heading: མདོ་སྡེ་ཇི་ལྟར་འཆད་པའི་ཚུལ་དང་པོར་དགོས་པ་དང་བརྗོད་བྱ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In this regard, one who wishes to explain a sūtra must first state its purpose, in order to engage listeners in taking it up with diligence and so forth. Without understanding the purpose, those who possess understanding will not engage in anything at all. Following that, in order to show the method for the sūtra’s purpose, the subject matter must be stated; for a sūtra that is empty of subject matter does not accomplish the desired purpose, just like the words of a "ten-pomegranate" [proverb]. Following that, in order for that subject matter to be easily grasped, the summarized meaning must be stated. Following that, in order for the summarized meaning to be understood, the meaning of the words must be stated. Following that, in order to show that the sequence is not contradictory, the connections between the words must be shown. Following that, in order to dispel contradictions with the logic of what precedes and follows, the responses to opponents must be stated; such is the method. In this regard, the name of this sūtra, *Vajracchedikā*, itself indicates the subject matter and the purpose. It is *Vajracchedikā* (Diamond Cutter) in two ways: because it cuts through the subtle obscurations of afflictions and of knowledge, which are like a diamond and difficult to destroy; this indicates that the purpose of this [text] is the abandonment of the two obscurations. Alternatively, it is called *Vajra*-like because the cutting is similar to the shape of a *vajra*, for a *vajra* is thick at both ends and thin in the middle. Likewise, this *Prajñāpāramitā* also fully reveals the vastness of the beginning and end—the stage of engaging through aspiration and the stage of Buddhahood. The thin middle indicates the stage of the pure superior intention. Therefore, this is like the form of a *vajra*, and by this, it is shown that these three stages are the subject matter of this [text].

heading: བསྡུས་དོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Regarding that, the introductory narrative is the cause for the emergence of the sūtra; it is indicated from the phrase "Thus have I heard" up to the phrase "the venerable Subhūti." This is stated in order to express that one should have confidence in the speaker, as he is the one who truly compiles it; this should be stated for all sūtras. The initiation of the dialogue is the contextual connection made for the sake of explaining the meaning of the sūtra; since speaking without context would result in everything being incoherent, it should be connected with the context in every instance to eliminate incoherence. This is indicated by the passage beginning with "Then the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat." The ensuring of the uninterrupted lineage of the Tathāgata is also indicated by that very same passage, for once the noble Subhūti realized that this prajñāpāramitā is what causes the lineage of the Tathāgata to remain uninterrupted, the elder Subhūti first set forth how the lineage of the Tathāgata would not be interrupted. The characteristics of the practice are indicated by the passage beginning with "How should a bodhisattva who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide?" and so forth. The state of that practice of the characteristics of the practice is the field in which the bodhisattva should abide, what should be practiced, and how the mind should be well-grasped; that is called its state. This is indicated from the phrase "Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus" up to the final verse beginning with "a star, a fault of vision." By these two, the characteristics of the practice and its state, the entire activity of the bodhisattva is shown to be complete; this is, for the time being, the summarized meaning.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: The meaning of the words and so forth shall also be stated; those are what are being expressed. Regarding the phrase "Thus," although the sound of this expression appears in many senses, such as agreement, here it is understood to be established by the power of the context and so forth. This establishes the entire meaning of the sūtra that follows below. The phrase "I" serves to exclude others and indicates that the meaning was heard directly. The intended meaning is that it was not heard by oneself having been passed down through a lineage from one to another. The word "heard" serves to negate [mere] conceptualization, because apart from the Buddha, there is no one else who has realized such teachings by themselves. This serves to dispel disbelief. The phrase "at one time" means at a single time, indicating that it is difficult to hear such precious teachings at all times. Alternatively, it indicates that one has heard much oneself. It shows that while one heard this at one time, at other times one heard other things as well. Alternatively, by connecting it with what follows, "at one time the Blessed One was dwelling," it is established that for the sake of benefiting those immeasurable beings to be tamed, he was dwelling elsewhere at other times. The term "Blessed One" (Bhagavān) is so called because he possesses the destruction of the four māras—the māra of the kleshas, the māra of the skandhas, the māra of the Lord of Death, and the māra characterized as the son of the gods—and thus, by way of etymology, he is called the Blessed One.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation:
Alternatively, it is called "well-endowed" because it possesses faculties and so forth. As it is said:
Possessing faculties,
Form, splendor, and fame,
Wisdom and diligence—
These six are called "well."
This is how it is explained. "Śrāvastī" is called the city of Śrāvastī because it is the dwelling place of the sage Śrāvastī; and because the specific region indicated by that name is also connected to it, it is called Śrāvastī. The reason the region is mentioned is to state that the region has become a place of pilgrimage, for it is said in this very text that this area has become a place of pilgrimage. Alternatively, because it perfectly gathers [the audience], all [the names] are mentioned to establish that the words of the speaker are worthy of being accepted; for if one speaks having included the location, the aspects, and the sovereign, the world will have faith, and others will accept the words; otherwise, they would not be worthy of acceptance. Because the region of Śrāvastī is very vast and it is not known where [the Buddha] is staying, "Prince Jeta’s Grove" is mentioned; it is called Prince Jeta’s Grove because it is the grove of that person called Prince Jeta. Furthermore, because it is possible that this might not be known to anyone, "in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada" is mentioned; the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is so named because he had compassion for those without protectors and gave them food, and because he was famous for that, he spread precious jewels for the sake of the Blessed One and purchased the park from Prince Jeta, and Prince Jeta also had the buildings and so forth decorated for the sake of the Blessed One, so the grove became famous for both of them. If only one of these were mentioned, one would not understand the specific region intended, so all three terms are mentioned. Alternatively, by this name "Śrāvastī," it is shown that because he is dwelling among many, the benefit for others is perfect.

source: རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་དབེན་པ་ན་བཞུགས་པས་རང་གི་དོན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །འདི་ལ་དབང་སུ་ཡོད་སྙམ་པ་ལ། དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བས་དགེ་སློང་དག་གོ། །བདུད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྒོལ་བ་དག་གིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པས་མང་པོ་དེ་དག་ལ་དགེ་འདུན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཕལ་ཆེ་བ་དང་མཐུ་གཉིས་ཏེ། དེས་ནི་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཕལ་ཆེ་བ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་སྙམ་པ་དང་། སྟོང་ཉིས་བརྒྱ་ལྔ་བཅུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེའི་ཚེ་ན་དེ་སྙེད་ཅིག་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རབ་ཏུ་མང་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་ཆེད་དུ་མདོ་སྡེ་འཆད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་དག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སྙིང་སྟོབས་ཆེ་བའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་གོ །ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་སྙིང་སྟོབས་ཡོད་པས་དེ་རྣམ་པར་གཅོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཆོས་དང་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། མོས་པ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་།ཚོགས་དང་། དུས་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམ་པ་བདུན་དང་ལྡན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དག་གོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆོས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: The Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s park, signifies that by dwelling in seclusion, the Tathāgata’s own purpose is perfected. Regarding the thought, "Who is present for this?" the text states "a great saṅgha of monks," meaning those who are monks because they are free from defilements. Because they cannot be divided by adversaries such as Māra, these many are called a "saṅgha." These great saṅghas of monks are twofold: those who are numerous and those who are powerful; this indicates their great power. Thinking, "What is meant by 'numerous'?" the text mentions "twelve hundred and fifty" and so forth, because that many were present at that time. The reason for mentioning the saṅgha of monks and the very many bodhisattvas is that the sūtra is being taught for their sake. They are called "bodhisattvas" because they possess the intention of having great courage for awakening. Because śrāvakas also have courage for awakening, in order to distinguish them, the term "mahāsattva" is stated; they are called "mahāsattvas" because they possess seven great characteristics: dharma, the generation of the mind, resolve, intention, accumulation, time, and perfect accomplishment. Among these, "great dharma" refers to the vastness of the teachings, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* in one hundred thousand verses, taught to the bodhisattvas.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: "Great generation of the mind" means generating the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. "Great resolve" means that they possess resolve for the profound and vast dharma. "Great intention" means they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. "Great accumulation" means they possess immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom. "Great time" means they attain awakening through three immeasurable great aeons. "Great perfect accomplishment" means they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. "Dwelling" refers to dwelling through the four postures, or alternatively, dwelling through the unsurpassed dwelling of the Brahmās, the gods, and the noble ones. "Te" indicates that the dwelling has already occurred. Regarding this, the saṅgha of monks is mentioned first because, having completed their tasks and out of compassion, they are known to always remain at the feet of the Tathāgata, and thus they are taught as being constant. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, since they have not yet completed the task of fulfilling the purpose of immeasurable sentient beings, and because they possess great compassion, they travel throughout the realms of the world to accomplish the purpose of beings and therefore do not always remain at the feet of the Bhagavan.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Therefore, the bodhisattva is not mentioned in the sūtras of the śrāvakas, because that is not for their sake and because they are impermanent. "Then" means after that. "Time" indicates certainty; this specifies the time for a meal. "Time is certain" means that this is the time when one must certainly eat. Since it is not known what that is, "in the morning" is stated to explain it; this is to be understood as meaning that it is both the morning and the time for a meal. The characteristic of "morning" is that it is the time for a meal for those who are observing the upoṣadha and those who have gone forth, and because it will be obtained later, the Bhagavan stated "time" in order to make it understood that it is to be explained as one. Otherwise, stating "in the morning" would not be understood as being exclusively that, for it is possible that the Bhagavan might do it at another time, and therefore all three terms are stated. "Lower garment" refers to wearing robes that are appropriate for dwelling in a house, and this is done to fulfill the respect that śrāvakas must have for the trainings. Otherwise, if one is not disciplined oneself, how could one discipline others? Regarding "wearing the dharma robes," wearing the dharma robes should be viewed as the characteristic of being dressed; anything else is not the occasion. "Great city" refers to a specific region, meaning the exclusion of Śrāvastī.

སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མོས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཟབ་ཅིང་ཆེ་བ་ལ་མོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསམ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཕན་པ་དང་བདེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བསམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཚོགས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དུས་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་གྲངས་མེད་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཞུགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྤྱོད་ལམ་བཞི་པོ་དག་གིས་སམ། ཡང་ན་ཚངས་པ་དང་ལྷའི་དང་། འཕགས་པའི་བཞུགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་བཞུགས་པའོ། །ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞུགས་ཟིན་པར་བསྟན་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ནི་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་དང་། སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ཉིད་ན་འདུག་པར་རིག་ནས་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོང་དུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་བྱ་བ་མ་བྱས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་ཆེ་བས་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སུ་རྒྱུ་བས་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་དྲུང་ན་མི་འདུག་པས་འོག་ཏུ་སྨོས་སོ། །

"Great generation of the mind" means generating the mind for unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. "Great resolve" means that they possess resolve for the profound and vast dharma. "Great intention" means they possess the intention to generate benefit and happiness for all sentient beings. "Great accumulation" means they possess immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom. "Great time" means they attain awakening through three immeasurable great aeons. "Great perfect accomplishment" means they perfectly accomplish unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. "Dwelling" refers to dwelling through the four postures, or alternatively, dwelling through the unsurpassed dwelling of the Brahmās, the gods, and the noble ones. "Te" indicates that the dwelling has already occurred. Regarding this, the saṅgha of monks is mentioned first because, having completed their tasks and out of compassion, they are known to always remain at the feet of the Tathāgata, and thus they are taught as being constant. Bodhisattvas are mentioned later because, since they have not yet completed the task of fulfilling the purpose of immeasurable sentient beings, and because they possess great compassion, they travel throughout the realms of the world to accomplish the purpose of beings and therefore do not always remain at the feet of the Bhagavan.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: If one asks why the Blessed One entered for the sake of alms, it is to lead the Śrāvakas toward having few desires, to benefit householders, the poor, the sick, the elderly, and others, to enable the blind and others to obtain eyes and the like, and to generate faith in the Blessed One among others by displaying various kinds of wonders; thus, one should understand that the purposes are immeasurable. The phrase "having performed the activity of eating" refers to one who has performed and completed the activity of eating, such as the consumption of food. If even those who are born from minor roots of virtue, such as Brahmā and others, do not perform the activity of eating because they are free from the desire for consuming morsels of food, how could the Blessed One, who has arisen from inconceivable roots of virtue, do so? In this regard, the noble *Dharmasaṃgīti* also states that the Tathāgata does not possess defilements or thirst, does not defecate or urinate, and his body is not frail. That is true, but if the body of the Blessed One were not ultimate, then at that time there would be room for all sorts of criticism. However, when this is the *nirmāṇakāya* of the Blessed One, which displays such modes of conduct and engages in accordance with the intentions of the sentient beings to be tamed, where would there be room for criticism? Because he shows a human body to those to be tamed in order to encourage them, saying, "Even if one who has become a human initiates diligence, one will attain such an unsurpassed state," he thus displays the manner of taking food.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: By demonstrating to the donors and the patrons for whom the alms are being purified that they generate joy, and by showing that those who, despite having the merit, have been born among the hungry ghosts and so forth due to certain karmic obscurations, will—if they are touched by the nectar-like fingernails of the Tathāgata—experience the supreme taste of the gods and, when they consume what is brought by the powerful yakṣas and others, will have their minds satisfied by supreme bliss and will also attain supreme samādhi, the activity of the Tathāgata’s food is immeasurable. If one asks in what way the activity of food is performed, for that reason it is stated, "afterwards," and so forth. Having taken everything, the meal that is consumed afterwards is the alms-meal consumed afterwards; this is the taking of what has been preceded by the proper acceptance for the sake of introducing the śrāvakas to the ascetic qualities. The word "consumed" means that it has been consumed. Alternatively, "afterwards" refers to that which is taken at the second time, which is called the later meal; the sentence is to be construed as saying that this later meal is both the meal afterwards and the alms. Alternatively, it is called by that name because it is the alms that consists of eating that afternoon meal. Therefore, because one possesses ascetic qualities and has abandoned untimely food, "consumed" means that one is free from those two. The word "having placed" means having set it down.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Even though Indra and others who are diligent in receiving the word in the presence of the Bhagavan always abide there, the Bhagavan himself set aside his alms bowl and robes to demonstrate that renunciation is something one must do for oneself. It is also to dispel the unhappiness of those with lesser merit who are unable to serve him. Although he has long since abandoned the appearance of impurity and places his lotus feet [on the ground], he is seen washing his feet to demonstrate that one should be respectful of the teachings—such as not treading on bedding or seats with soiled feet—or to accord with the intentions of sentient beings who are inclined toward the *kriyātantra* and the like. "Having arranged the seat" means it was arranged by gods and others. "Having straightened the body" means he did not sit too hunched nor too arched. Why did the Bhagavan abide in the deportment of renunciation when teaching the Dharma? It is to induce the world to exert effort in renunciation, by showing that only those who have renounced are capable of teaching, understanding, and listening to this Dharma, and not others. "Having established mindfulness beforehand" means that when he was previously a Bodhisattva, he made a vow, saying, "Once I have attained the unsurpassed rank, I shall act in such a way that the lineage of the Buddhas will not be interrupted," and he makes that vow manifest in his memory. Although the Buddhas, the Bhagavans, are always in meditative equipoise and thus abide in mindfulness at all times, that mindfulness which is not at the proper time does not accomplish anything, whereas remembering the vow at the proper time is fruitful. Since remembering at the proper time also demonstrates that the Bhagavan is always in meditative equipoise, there is no contradiction.

heading: གླེང་གཞི་བཤད་པ།
translation: Why is the phrase "many monks" mentioned? It is to show that when the Tathāgata was in Śrāvastī, not all of the monks of the sangha who were present there were gathered together at the time he was teaching the Dharma, but rather that a group of three or more had gathered there. This was stated in order to generate trust in others by accurately summarizing the situation. The word "gathered" means merely that they were in the vicinity. The word "sitting" means sitting on their seats. As for "the world," since it is common to establish a specific instance preceded by a general categorization, both terms are mentioned in accordance with worldly convention. Otherwise, the word "sitting" alone would have sufficed to express both. The meaning of the introductory words and so forth has been explained.

source: ད་ནི་གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བྱ་བ་བརྗོད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་བར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ལན་གཉིས་སུ་སྨོས་སོ། །བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བོད་པའོ། །བདག་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ནས་ཡང་དག་པར་གཤེགས་སོ། །ལེགས་པར་གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། ལེགས་པར་བསྟོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཡང་ན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་བག་ཆགས་དང་བཅས་པ་མ་ལུས་པར་སྤངས་ཏེ། གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། བུམ་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་གང་བ་ བཞིན་ནོ། །ཡང་ན་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་གཤེགས་པས་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ་སྟེ། རིམས་ནད་ཤིན་ཏུ་བྱང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཕན་གདགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་བྱེ་བྲག་སྟེ། ཕན་གདགས་པ་གང་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱིས་ཕན་གདགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །རྒྱལ་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དག་ཀྱང་འབངས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྟོན་པ་དག་ལ་ཅི་ནུས་ཀྱིས་རྗེས་སུ་འཛིན་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་འདིར་ངོ་མཚར་བ་ཅི་ཆེ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པ་ལ་ངོ་མཚར་གྱི་རྒྱུར། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །དངོས་པོའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་གསུངས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའོ། །ཡང་ན་སྔ་མ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ནས་གཤེགས་ཏེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་པ་རྙེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར། འདིར་ཡང་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའོ། །
translation: Now, I shall explain the introduction and the way in which the lineage of the Buddha is kept unbroken. It is mentioned twice in order to show that it is extremely wondrous. The term *Sugata* (bde bar gshegs pa) is a vocative. He has perfectly gone (gshegs so) by way of the path of the two selflessnesses. Because he has gone well (legs par gshegs pas), he is a *Sugata*, just as one says "praised well" (legs par bstod). Alternatively, because he has abandoned, without remainder, the afflictive and cognitive obscurations along with their latent tendencies, he has gone (gshegs pas), and is thus a *Sugata*, just as a vessel is completely full. Alternatively, because he has gone (gshegs pas) without returning, he is a *Sugata*, just as a fever is completely cleared away. The phrase "as many as" (ji snyed pas) refers to the specific nature of the benefit to be provided; the meaning is that he provides benefit to the extent of whatever benefit is to be provided. Since even kings and the like support their subjects and those who rely on them to the best of their ability, the Bhagavān, in order to provide a cause for wonder to those who might wonder what is so wondrous here, stated: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha." He is a *Tathāgata* because he has spoken exactly as the reality of things is. Alternatively, just as the former ones went by way of the path of the two selflessnesses and attained the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, so too, because he has gone (gshegs pas) in this way, he is a *Tathāgata*.

Why is the phrase "many monks" mentioned? It is to show that when the Tathāgata was in Śrāvastī, not all of the monks of the sangha who were present there were gathered together at the time he was teaching the Dharma, but rather that a group of three or more had gathered there. This was stated in order to generate trust in others by accurately summarizing the situation. The word "gathered" means merely that they were in the vicinity. The word "sitting" means sitting on their seats. As for "the world," since it is common to establish a specific instance preceded by a general categorization, both terms are mentioned in accordance with worldly convention. Otherwise, the word "sitting" alone would have sufficed to express both. The meaning of the introductory words and so forth has been explained.

heading: གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བཤད་པ།
translation: Because he is worthy of being worshipped by the entire world, or because he has vanquished the enemies, the defilements, he is an Arhat. Because he has thoroughly and completely understood all that is to be known, he is a Samyaksambuddha. By these terms, the Bhagavan has fully demonstrated the excellence of the essential nature, both in terms of wisdom and abandonment. This is to be understood as follows: that kings and others provide benefits to their subjects and the like is not something wonderful here, for they provide benefits to others while desiring their own interests, such as gain and honor. But the Bhagavan is a Tathāgata, and because he has attained all excellences as an Arhat and a Samyaksambuddha, it is shown that the benefits he provides are indeed wonderful here. Since there is no cause for the benefits provided by the Bhagavan other than his great compassion, this aspect demonstrates that the Bhagavan is solely of great compassion. To say "he has provided benefits" means he has attained supreme enlightenment; at the time the Bhagavan turned the wheel of the Dharma, he caused those Bodhisattvas whose roots of virtue had fully matured to attain the stages, for the sake of causing the Bodhisattvas to be firmly established in the nature of reality.

source: ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པ་ནི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་དག་ཕན་བཏགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ལ་གཏད་པ་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་འཇོག་ཏུ་གཞུག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ང་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ནི་ཁྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་ནས་དེ་དག་ཡོན་ཏན་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་། ཐོབ་པ་དག་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཉམས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་གྱིས་ཤིག་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཕན་བཏགས་པ་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་བཏགས་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ལྔས་དམ་པར་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དུས་དང་། ཁྱད་པར་དང་། རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། བསྟན་པ་དང་། ཁྱབ་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་དུས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་གཞན་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ནི་ཕྱི་རོལ་པ་དང་། ཉན་ཐོས་དང་། རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དག་པས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ནི་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དེ་དག་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བསྟན་པ་ནི་གཏན་དུ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཁྱབ་པ་ནི་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་དེ་བདག་དང་གཞན་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་དམ་པར་བལྟ་སྟེ། གནས་དང་ཆོས་ཉིད་རབ་ཏུ་འཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཀར་གདགས་པའོ། །
translation: Entrusting refers to entrusting those beginners whose roots of virtue have not yet matured to those very ones who have been benefited, for the sake of causing the Bodhisattvas to be firmly established in the nature of reality. The Bhagavan’s declaration that he is passing into parinirvāṇa means: "You must act in such a way that those who have not attained these qualities will attain them, and those who have attained them will not fall away from them." In this way, the two—providing benefits and entrusting—fully demonstrate that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted. Providing benefits to Bodhisattvas should be understood as excellent in five aspects: time, distinction, vastness, instruction, and pervasiveness. Regarding these, time refers to the fact that it concerns other lifetimes. Distinction refers to the fact that it is superior to the benefits provided by tirthankaras, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Vastness refers to the fact that those benefits are unsurpassable. Instruction refers to the fact that it is permanent. Pervasiveness refers to the fact that those benefits provide benefit to the continuums of oneself and others. Entrusting should also be viewed as excellent in three aspects: the attainment of the stage and the nature of reality, and the imposition of the mandate.

Because he is worthy of being worshipped by the entire world, or because he has vanquished the enemies, the defilements, he is an Arhat. Because he has thoroughly and completely understood all that is to be known, he is a Samyaksambuddha. By these terms, the Bhagavan has fully demonstrated the excellence of the essential nature, both in terms of wisdom and abandonment. This is to be understood as follows: that kings and others provide benefits to their subjects and the like is not something wonderful here, for they provide benefits to others while desiring their own interests, such as gain and honor. But the Bhagavan is a Tathāgata, and because he has attained all excellences as an Arhat and a Samyaksambuddha, it is shown that the benefits he provides are indeed wonderful here. Since there is no cause for the benefits provided by the Bhagavan other than his great compassion, this aspect demonstrates that the Bhagavan is solely of great compassion. To say "he has provided benefits" means he has attained supreme enlightenment; at the time the Bhagavan turned the wheel of the Dharma, he caused those Bodhisattvas whose roots of virtue had fully matured to attain the stages, for the sake of causing the Bodhisattvas to be firmly established in the nature of reality.

heading: གླེང་བསླང་བ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་བཤད་པ།
translation: What is the "stage"? It is because they are entrusted to spiritual friends so that they will not be wasted. What is the "attainment of the nature of reality"? It is because those Bodhisattvas who have been benefited are caused to benefit others through the nature of reality. What is the "imposition of the mandate"? It is because of the mandate given by saying, "You must provide benefits to other Bodhisattvas," and it is not done without respect. The introduction and the meaning of the words regarding ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted, and so forth, have already been explained.

Entrusting refers to entrusting those beginners whose roots of virtue have not yet matured to those very ones who have been benefited, for the sake of causing the Bodhisattvas to be firmly established in the nature of reality. The Bhagavan’s declaration that he is passing into parinirvāṇa means: "You must act in such a way that those who have not attained these qualities will attain them, and those who have attained them will not fall away from them." In this way, the two—providing benefits and entrusting—fully demonstrate that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted. Providing benefits to Bodhisattvas should be understood as excellent in five aspects: time, distinction, vastness, instruction, and pervasiveness. Regarding these, time refers to the fact that it concerns other lifetimes. Distinction refers to the fact that it is superior to the benefits provided by tirthankaras, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. Vastness refers to the fact that those benefits are unsurpassable. Instruction refers to the fact that it is permanent. Pervasiveness refers to the fact that those benefits provide benefit to the continuums of oneself and others. Entrusting should also be viewed as excellent in three aspects: the attainment of the stage and the nature of reality, and the imposition of the mandate.

heading: སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བཤད་པ།
source: སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་རྣམ་པ་དྲུག་གི་ཕྱིར་ཞུས་ཏེ། དོགས་པ་བཅད་པ་དང་། མོས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། དོན་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། མི་ལྡོག་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཡུན་རིང་དུ་གནས་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ཇི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གདུང་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པ་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དོགས་པ་བཅད་པའི་ཕྱིར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་མང་བར་བསྒྲགས་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་མོས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པ་རྣམས་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་བསྒྲུབས་པས་མནར་བ་དེ་ལེན་པ་དང་འཛིན་པ་ལ་རྩོམ་པ་རྣམས་བསོད་ནམས་མང་པོ་འདོད་པས་མི་ལྡོག་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཕན་གདགས་པ་ལྷག་པའི་བསམ་པ་དག་པ་རྣམས་བདག་གིས་ཆོས་དེ་རྟོགས་པར་མཐོང་ནས་མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་ཡུན་རིང་དུ་གནས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་དོགས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་སྨིན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་འདོད་པ་རྣམས་ཡང་དག་པར་འཛིན་དུ་གཞུག་པ་དང་། ལོག་པར་བསྒྲུབས་པས་མནར་བ་རྣམས་ཡང་དག་པར་གཟེངས་བསྟོད་པ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དག་པ་རྣམས་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པས་སོ། །
translation: We shall state the characteristics of the practice, and in reference to that, the word "how" is mentioned. The noble Subhūti asked for the sake of six things: to resolve doubts, to generate aspiration, to engage in the profound meaning, to ensure non-retrogression, to generate supreme joy, and to ensure the holy Dharma remains for a long time. Regarding that, in order to resolve the doubts of those who think, "How is this prajñāpāramitā the way the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted?", it is to generate aspiration for the prajñāpāramitā by proclaiming the great merit of Bodhisattvas whose continuums are not yet fully ripened. It is for the sake of those whose continuums are ripened to engage in the profound meaning. It is for the sake of ensuring that those who are tormented by incorrect practice, and who begin to take up and hold [this teaching], do not retrogress, as they desire great merit. It is for the sake of generating supreme joy in those with pure higher intentions of benefiting others, upon seeing that they have realized that Dharma. It is for the sake of ensuring that the Mahāyāna Dharma remains for a long time in the future. In summary, it is to correctly demonstrate [the teaching] to those with doubts, to cause those Bodhisattvas who are not yet ripened and who desire merit to correctly take it up, to correctly encourage those who are tormented by wrong practice, and to cause those with pure intentions to be supremely joyful. Regarding that, "to abide" is by way of aspiration and prayer. "To practice" is by way of entering into meditative equipoise.

What is the "stage"? It is because they are entrusted to spiritual friends so that they will not be wasted. What is the "attainment of the nature of reality"? It is because those Bodhisattvas who have been benefited are caused to benefit others through the nature of reality. What is the "imposition of the mandate"? It is because of the mandate given by saying, "You must provide benefits to other Bodhisattvas," and it is not done without respect. The introduction and the meaning of the words regarding ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted, and so forth, have already been explained.

heading: སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བཤད་པ།
translation:

translation: The vehicle of the bodhisattvas is the bodhisattva vehicle, by which a bodhisattva is definitively delivered. That is also comprised of the ten pāramitās and the ten bhūmis; to have entered into that correctly means to have entered with the mind of aspiration and the mind of engagement. This distinction is for the sake of excluding the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and others, for if one were to say only "having entered correctly into enlightenment," because there are three enlightenments, it would be understood as referring to another enlightenment as well. "Listen" means to accept the commitment. The meaning of the words regarding the characteristics of practice and so forth has already been explained.

source: ད་ནི་དེའི་གནས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེའི་གནས་དེ་ཡང་མདོར་བསྡུས་ན་རྣམ་པ་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་དེ། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་དང་། བསྒོམས་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་འདུན་པ་ལ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་པ་དང་། སངས་རྒྱས་འབྱུང་བ་མཉེས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། ཞིང་རྣམ་པར་དག་པར་སྨིན་པ་དང་།སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བསྟན་བཅོས་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་དང་། སེམས་ཅན་དང་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་རིལ་པོར་འཛིན་པའི་གཞིག་པར་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱ་བ་དང་། ལུས་དང་སེམས་དུབ་ནས་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ལས་ལོག་པ་དང་། མི་རྩོམ་པ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དག་དང་བྲལ་བ་སྟེ། ལུས་དང་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་དུབ་པ་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བརྩམས་པ་ལས་མི་ལྡོག །མ་བརྩམས་པ་ནི་མི་རྩོམ་ལ། བདག་ལ་གཞན་དག་གིས་འདི་ནི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱུར་ཀྱང་ཇི་མ་རུང་ཞེས་དད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ ནས་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་འདོད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་ཏེ་སྤང་བར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་ཇི་མི་སྙམ་པ་དང་། བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བ་དང་དབྲལ་བ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་དུས་ན་བདག་གོ་སྙམ་པའི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་དང་། གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་དང་། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་སྟེ། གནས་རྣམ་པ་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའོ། །གནས་དེ་དག་གིས་ས་གསུམ་བསྡུས་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་གནས་རྣམ་པ་བཅུ་དྲུག་གིས་མོས་པས་སྤྱོད་པའི་སའོ། །མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་གནས་གཅིག་པུས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་བསམ་པ་དག་པའི་སའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བས་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའོ། །སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྩོན་པ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་འཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་བསྐྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ནས་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། ཐ་མ་བདག་གོ་སྙམ་དུ་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ལ་ཐུག་པའི་བར་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་བགེགས་རྣམས་དང་སེམས་བྲལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ནས་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་འཚལ་ལོ། །དེ་ནས་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ནས་གོང་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཚོལ་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་གི་གོ་རིམས་ནི་དེ་ལྟའོ། །
translation: Now, the states of that [bodhisattva] shall be described. In brief, those states are eighteen in number, namely: generating the mind [of enlightenment]; engaging in the pāramitās; aspiring to attain the rūpakāya; aspiring to attain the dharmakāya; being free from arrogance regarding the excellence of one’s meditation; honoring and serving the buddhas as they appear; purifying and ripening buddhafields; ripening sentient beings; being free from attachment to the treatises; engaging in the destruction of the grasping at sentient beings and the receptacle world as a totality; making offerings and providing service to the Tathāgata; not turning back from exertion due to physical and mental fatigue; not being idle; and being free from [the desire for] gain and honor. That is to say, one who is physically and mentally exhausted does not turn back from having initiated exertion. One who has not initiated it does not begin, and even if others come to know that "this one is possessed of exertion," one is still motivated by the desire for gain and honor, thinking, "How wonderful!" Therefore, the bodhisattva must abandon all of these. [Other states include:] being indifferent to suffering; being free from the taste of meditative absorption; being free from the conceptualization of a "self" at the time of realization; seeking out the instructions; realization; and seeking the buddha-bhūmi. These eighteen states are what the bodhisattva must abide in, must cultivate, and must use to firmly hold the mind. These states encompass three bhūmis: the sixteen states constitute the bhūmi of engagement through aspiration; the single state of realization constitutes the bhūmi of pure superior intention; and seeking the buddha-bhūmi constitutes the buddha-bhūmi. Having generated the mind for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa, one exerts oneself in the pāramitās and generates the aspiration to attain the Tathāgata’s rūpakāya and dharmakāya. Then, one frees the mind from the obstacles to realization, starting from arrogance and ending with the conceptualization of a "self." Then, one seeks the instructions in order to realize. Then, one realizes. Then, one seeks the buddha-bhūmi above; therefore, that is their sequence.

བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་སྟེ། གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བར་བྱེད་པའོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བཅུ་དང་ས་བཅུས་བསྡུས་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ནི་སྨོན་པ་དང་འཇུག་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཞུགས་པའོ། །བྱེ་བྲག་དེ་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ཞེས་སྨོས་ན་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་གསུམ་ཡོད་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་གཞན་དུ་ཡང་གོ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཉན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁས་བླངས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཚིག་གི་དོན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །
[3-16] translation already produced for this document:
The vehicle of the bodhisattvas is the bodhisattva vehicle, by which a bodhisattva is definitively delivered. That is also comprised of the ten pāramitās and the ten bhūmis; to have entered into that correctly means to have entered with the mind of aspiration and the mind of engagement. This distinction is for the sake of excluding the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and others, for if one were to say only "having entered correctly into enlightenment," because there are three enlightenments, it would be understood as referring to another enlightenment as well. "Listen" means to accept the commitment. The meaning of the words regarding the characteristics of practice and so forth has already been explained.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: In relation to the generation of the mind for enlightenment, the phrase "however many sentient beings" was spoken. "However many" refers to a measure. Regarding the thought, "Do they have a measure?", the phrase "are included as sentient beings" was spoken. Although the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable, the expression "sentient being, sentient being" refers to that which is included as a sentient being, being what is known as a similar share of an essence that has been imputed based on the meaning of a word that is the reverse of the thought of that essence. Because this gathers together the meaning of what is seen and what is conceptually constructed, and superimposes an essence upon it, they are included by the distinctions of the aggregates such as form; therefore, they appear as if they were living beings. Having thus taught in general, in order to teach in particular, the phrase "born from eggs" and so forth was spoken. That definition of the particular is also taught through three classifications: by the classification of the place of birth, there are four types, such as "born from eggs." By the classification of the realm, it is because those with form and those without form have different abodes; those with form are those who wander in the desire and form realms. Those without form are those who are formless. By the classification of grasping at signs, it is the phrase "those with perception" and so forth; excluding the one part of those with great fruit and the sentient beings born in the peak of existence, all are those with perception.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: "Non-perception" is one aspect of the "Great Fruit." This is also a classification made in terms of grasping at signs, for it is distinguished by the absence of that [grasping] and is indicated by it. Those born in the Peak of Existence are not "non-percipient" nor "not non-percipient." This distinction was made for the sake of benefiting those of lesser intellect, but it was not elaborated upon in order to avoid disparaging others. In order to show that the statement "all phenomena are without sentient beings" and this explanation are not contradictory, and to show that the realm of sentient beings is the realm of sentient beings in terms of conventional truth, the words "as much as" and so forth were spoken. The term "designation" means knowing [something] as the nature of the specific five aggregates; the intended meaning is that it is not what is imagined by the tīrthikas as being fully known. By this, the extreme of nihilism is abandoned, for if it exists as a designation, one does not fall into nihilism. The "dhātu of nirvāṇa without remainder," which is non-abiding, is what is referred to by that term; the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas is not the dhātu of nirvāṇa here, for it is inferior. It is not logical for those who are compassionate to seek an inferior fruit when a supreme fruit exists.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: If you ask, "If a supreme fruit exists, but one is unable to attain it, is that why one seeks it in that way?" then according to your system, since there are three lineages and also those without lineage, it is the case that even an inferior fruit cannot be attained by everyone. However, if the two lineages of bodhisattvas are like this: those who are overcome by the force of great compassion think, "What can I do?" and, thinking "While other buddhas and bodhisattvas are present, what is the point of me making a prayer that has no purpose?" they abandon such conduct, cast aside reliance on others, and, seized by great compassion, seeing that beings are afflicted by the blazing fire of suffering, they make the prayer, "I alone shall protect them." As it is said: "Having abandoned the conceptualization of thinking 'is it difficult or not difficult,' you yourself have pledged, 'This world is helpless.'" If you ask, "If that is the case, then why not make a prayer for the supreme fruit, which one is unable to attain, just as one prays for a beloved son to become a king? Why do you seek only the inferior?" Therefore, the non-abiding nirvāṇa is rightly the dhātu of nirvāṇa without remainder here, for it is devoid of the remainder of the contaminated aggregates.

[3-19] translation already produced for this document:
"Non-perception" is one aspect of the "Great Fruit." This is also a classification made in terms of grasping at signs, for it is distinguished by the absence of that [grasping] and is indicated by it. Those born in the Peak of Existence are not "non-percipient" nor "not non-percipient." This distinction was made for the sake of benefiting those of lesser intellect, but it was not elaborated upon in order to avoid disparaging others. In order to show that the statement "all phenomena are without sentient beings" and this explanation are not contradictory, and to show that the realm of sentient beings is the realm of sentient beings in terms of conventional truth, the words "as much as" and so forth were spoken. The term "designation" means knowing [something] as the nature of the specific five aggregates; the intended meaning is that it is not what is imagined by the tīrthikas as being fully known. By this, the extreme of nihilism is abandoned, for if it exists as a designation, one does not fall into nihilism. The "dhātu of nirvāṇa without remainder," which is non-abiding, is what is referred to by that term; the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas is not the dhātu of nirvāṇa here, for it is inferior. It is not logical for those who are compassionate to seek an inferior fruit when a supreme fruit exists.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: If you ask, "Why is it not stated that one should pass beyond suffering?" it is because the first dhyāna and the like are to be excluded. The Bhagavan spoke of that as a synonym for nirvāṇa because it is devoid of the afflictions of the lower realms. If you ask, "Why is it not stated as the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder of the aggregates?" it is because the remainder of the aggregates of suffering has not been abandoned. The intention of bodhisattvas to lead all sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa should be viewed through three causes: it is to wait for another time for those born in states without leisure, and because the state of having no leisure is merely indicated, it is just a prayer and not an end in itself, for it is impossible to pass into complete nirvāṇa while remaining there. It is to bring those who are not yet mature to maturity, and to liberate those who are mature; therefore, it is not that one is unable to seek the goal. This intention to lead all sentient beings without exception to complete nirvāṇa demonstrates the vastness of the bodhicitta. Here, it is also shown how one should abide through the two of aspiration and prayer. Now, in order to show how one should accomplish this through meditative equipoise, it is stated, "In that way," and so forth. In that way, although conventionally all sentient beings are led to complete nirvāṇa, how is it that in the ultimate sense a bodhisattva does not perceive any sentient being? It is said that this is because they do not exist. In that way, one should investigate it through meditative equipoise.

However, if the two lineages of bodhisattvas are like this: those who are overcome by the force of great compassion think, "What can I do?" and, thinking "While other buddhas and bodhisattvas are present, what is the point of me making a prayer that has no purpose?" they abandon such conduct, cast aside reliance on others, and, seized by great compassion, seeing that beings are afflicted by the blazing fire of suffering, they make the prayer, "I alone shall protect them." If you ask, "If that is the case, then why not make a prayer for the supreme fruit, which one is unable to attain, just as one prays for a beloved son to become a king? heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: Rising, the thought, "In the ultimate sense, there is no sentient being whatsoever that I have led to parinirvāṇa," is the generation of the mind that reveals the profound, and it also reveals the ultimate bodhicitta. The former represents the conventional. Now, in order to show how the mind should be properly sustained here by subduing distraction, the words "For what reason?" are stated. The word "if" should be understood as having the same meaning as "supposing."

source: འོ་ན་སུ་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པ་དེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའམ་ཅི་ན། གང་གི་ཕྱིར་སེམས་ཅན་སྨོས་པ་དེ་ཁོ་ན་མཛད་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་། ཡང་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། ཅིག་ཤོས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དགོངས་པ་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། བློ་གྲོས་ངན་པ་དག་གི་ཡང་དེ་ནི་ཕུང་པོར་ལས་གཞན་པ་ནང་ན་བྱ་བ་དང་། ལོངས་སྤྱོད་བཞི་པོ་བྱེད་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པར་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་དང་སྲོག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྒྲར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་དང་། གང་དག་ཡང་གང་ཟག་བརྗོད་དུ་མི་རུང་བར་འདོད་པ་དེ་དག་གི་ཡང་དེ་ནི་ཕུང་པོར་གཏོགས་པའི་ཆོས་དང་མཚན་ཉིད་མི་འདྲ་བར་ཁས་བླངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་དོན་གཞན་པ་ཁོ་ནར་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བརྗོད་དུ་མི་རུང་བར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་ནི་ནམ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་མི་སྲིད་དོ། །དེ་ནི་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཚད་མ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། གནོད་པ་ཅན་ཡང་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེར་ལྟ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཁོ་ནར་འགྱུར་རོ། །གང་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དོན་དམ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། གཞན་ན་རེ་བདག་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཚད་མ་ཡོད་པ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ནམ། འདི་ལྟར་བཅིངས་པ་དང་། ཐར་པ་དང་། ལམ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་འབྲེལ་པ་དང་། དྲན་པ་དང་། ངོ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་གཞི་གཅིག་པ་གྲགས་པ་དག་ཡིན་ན། བདག་མེད་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཁྱེད་ཀྱི་ལུགས་ལྟར་ན་དེ་དག་གི་གཞིར་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་གཅིག་པུ་ནི་འགའ་ཡང་མེད་ན་གཞིར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཞིག་ཡིན། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་སོ་སོ་ནི་ཐ་དད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: If so, is it the case that one who engages in the perception of a person and so forth is called a bodhisattva, or what? Thinking that the Tathāgata acts precisely as the mention of "sentient beings" implies, the question "For what reason?" was asked, and the other also replied, "It should not be done." The intention is this: even for those of inferior intellect, having imagined that there is a person who exists within, distinct from the aggregates, who performs the four activities and enjoys the results, they apply conventional designations with terms such as "sentient being" and "life." And for those who hold that a person is inexpressible, because they accept that its characteristics are different from the phenomena belonging to the aggregates, they implicitly accept that it is a distinct entity; for if everything were inexpressible, it would follow that nothing could ever be expressed, which is impossible. Since there is no valid cognition to establish that, and because there is also contradictory evidence, a bodhisattva who views it in that way becomes entirely mistaken due to being intensely attached to a mistake. How could one who has become mistaken be an ultimate bodhisattva? Others might say, "Is it not just that there is valid cognition to establish the self?" Since it is well known that bondage, liberation, the path, the connection to the result, mindfulness, and recognition all share the same basis, according to your system of asserting no-self, if there is not even one thing that can be established as their basis, then what is it that becomes the basis? This is because the individual moments of the moments of consciousness are distinct.

Rising, the thought, "In the ultimate sense, there is no sentient being whatsoever that I have led to parinirvāṇa," is the generation of the mind that reveals the profound, and it also reveals the ultimate bodhicitta. The former represents the conventional. Now, in order to show how the mind should be properly sustained here by subduing distraction, the words "For what reason?" are stated. The word "if" should be understood as having the same meaning as "supposing."

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: It is not established that Devadatta is bound and later Yajñadatta is liberated. Nor is it the case that the result of an action performed by one is experienced by another. This is because it would lead to the absurd consequence of actions performed being wasted, and the consequence of encountering results of actions not performed. In this way, because the moment of consciousness designated as the agent is disconnected from the result, there is the fault of actions being wasted; and because the result is connected only to that which is not the agent, there is also the fault of encountering actions not performed. Furthermore, in the world, memory and the like are not known to exist in different locations. If one asks how they are, it is that they exist in the same location; it is not known that what is experienced by the mind of Devadatta is remembered or recognized by the mind of Yajñadatta, but rather it is known that the very one who experiences is the one who remembers and recognizes. Therefore, there exists a single person who follows through all states. As for the syllogism, those which are bondage and liberation share a single basis; for example, just as Devadatta is bound by iron shackles and is liberated. The statement that "the two, bondage and liberation, which are the basis of the dispute, are also bondage and liberation" is a syllogism of essence. In the same way, it is said that one should always apply the syllogism to establish that the agent also has a single basis.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: Now, if one were to establish here a person (puruṣa) who is independent, ultimate, permanent, and unitary, then at that time, because such a person is not established as being connected with any logical reason (hetu), it is inconclusive. Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are momentary, Devadatta and others are not established as having a permanent and unitary essence; therefore, the example is also lacking in what is to be established. For that very reason, the logical reason is contradictory, because it is connected with what is the opposite of that. However, if one asks why it is that when one establishes only a common basis, it is a case of establishing what is already established, it is because even then, one holds that bondage and so forth are in the same location because they exist in a single continuum (saṃtāna). In this way, when in a certain continuum, causes and results such as ignorance (avidyā) and so forth arise continuously without interruption, one designates that as "bondage." Again, when the noble path arises in that same continuum through the sequence of hearing and so forth, and ignorance and so forth are ceased, one designates the transformation of the basis as "liberation." However, it is not the case that these two are established as having as their object a permanent and unitary ultimate entity, because worldly bondage and liberation are also similar to that. In a continuum where virtuous and non-virtuous minds and experiences have arisen, because results such as happiness, suffering, and memory appear at another time—dependent upon the ripening of the continuum, just as the ripening of a continuum smeared with the juice of madhūka or lac and so forth—virtue and so forth are known as being in the same location; but there is no single agent, no single experiencer, and no single rememberer at all. This is because all these conventional designations are differentiated merely by cause and result.

source: ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ས་བོན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ནུས་པ་ངེས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རྒྱུའི་ནུས་པ་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་ཡང་དག་གང་གིས་ན་རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་ནི་གང་ཡང་མེད་དེ། གནས་སྐབས་གཞན་དུ་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་རྒྱུ་འདི་ལ་ཡང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ན། བདག་ཏུ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་འདིས་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ། བདག་ལ་ཡང་བརྟགས་ཏེ་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུའོ། །ཟབ་མོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གནས་སྐབས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་འབྲས་བུའོ་ཞེས་རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་དངོས་པོ་གདོན་མི་ཟ་བར་ཁས་བླང་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་གནས་སྐབས་དེ་གཉིས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའམ། གཅིག་ལ་གཅིག་ཕན་འདོགས་པ་མེད་པ་ན་ནམ་མཁའ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གྱུར་པས་ཟ་བ་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འགྲུབ་པར་ཡང་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། ནུས་པ་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པར་ཁས་བླང་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དང་འབྲེལ་པས་བདེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་གྱི་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་དགེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུར་གྱུར་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡོངས་སུ་སྣང་བ་དག་ཁོ་ན་བྱེད་པ་པོ་དང་ཟ་བ་པོ་ཡིན་ན་བལྟར་མི་སྣང་བའི་ངོ་བོ་བདག་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པས་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ། རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པས་བདག་དེ་མ་གྲུབ་ཏུ་ཆུག་ཀྱང་། འོན་ཀྱང་སྔར་ཤེས་པའི་མངོན་སུམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མངོན་སུམ་གྱིས་བདག་གྲུབ་པོ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ཡང་རིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེར་འཁྲུལ་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་ཤེས་པ་མངོན་སུམ་ཉིད་དུ་མི་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: It is not an overstatement, for just as the efficacy of seeds and the like is determinate, the efficacy of causes is likewise individually determinate. Regarding this, there is no single entity that follows along such that the nature of cause and effect becomes individually determinate, because they appear in different states. If this cause of sentient beings were to be similar to that, what is the use of this self that has been thoroughly imputed? The state that is the agent and so forth, having imputed it upon the self, is the cause. The state that is the profound and so forth is the effect; thus, one must inevitably accept the nature of cause and effect. If it were not so, and there were no arising in those two states, or if one did not assist the other, then, having become like space, how could the eater and so forth be established? One must accept that the efficacy is individually determinate; in this way, happiness and the like arise in connection with an individually determinate nature, but not from everything. Therefore, if the very things that appear as cause and effect, such as virtue, are the agent and the eater, what is the use of the self that has been thoroughly imputed as a nature that is not seen? If one says that even if that self is not established by inference, it is nevertheless established by direct perception because it is an object of previously known direct perception, that is also not logical, because it is mistaken in that regard, because it is accompanied by conceptualization, and because consciousness itself is not established as direct perception.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: When the awareness of "I" appears, how could it be that what is directly perceived is a self that is singular, permanent, and pervasive, as posited by one’s own philosophical tenets? Such a thing is not observed. One must certainly understand it in this way. It is not so; for if the awareness of "I" were directly perceived, then those who argue about the self as an object would not be in dispute, because the grasping of "I" would be of a definite nature, accompanied by conceptual construction. For there is no superimposition upon that which is made an object by certainty. Therefore, because one is deceived by the appearance of one thing after another as being similar, and because of the power of habituation from beginningless time, one superimposes a singular identity upon the aggregates—such as form—which are each distinct and definite, and thus, having engaged with the other, one thinks "I." This is because those very things, such as form, appear to that awareness. If this grasping of "I" had the body as its object, how could one grasp the distinction by saying "my body"? This is the same for that which has the self as its object; if this grasping of "I" had those as its object, how could one then think "my self"? If one argues that even though there is no difference in terms of the entity itself, one intends to know only that much by excluding other differences—just as one speaks of "the body of a statue"—and thus there is no contradiction in grasping it as distinct through conceptualization, then this is also the same for that which has the body as its object.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: The object of the self is also inconsistent with arising in sequence, as will be explained below. It is not possible to assert that the mere grasping of "I" is the self, nor that its objects, such as form and the rest, are the self, because their characteristics are not the same as that. Since those are perceived only in sequence, they do not exist as a single entity or as something independent. For that very reason, it is said: "The self is not the nature of the self; it is not so because the attendant is different." If one designates it as a name, then since it is merely a convention, there is no dispute regarding this. Therefore, there is not even the slightest valid cognition to establish a self. It has already been examined in another section that there is no valid cognition other than direct perception and inference. Valid cognition that acts as a refutation is observed only in the context of elimination; thus, if the self were not other than the aggregates, then at that time it would become momentary like the aggregates, or else the aggregates would become permanent like the self, because they would be non-distinct from it. The consequence that it would become multiple like the aggregates would also be difficult to avert. Therefore, it is only for the aggregates that the name "self" is intended, and there is no dispute regarding a name. However, if one asserts that the aggregates are distinct from the self, then at that time, because there is no connection with happiness and the like, it would not be established as the enjoyer or the like.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
source: སྦྱོར་བ་ནི་གང་ཞིག་བདེ་བ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འབྲེལ་པ་མེད་པ་དེ་ནི་བྱེད་པ་པོ་འམ་ཟ་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་ལ། གྲོལ་བར་བྱེད་པའམ་འཁོར་བར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་ཡང་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་མོ་གཤམ་གྱི་བུ་བཞིན་ལ། བདག་ཀྱང་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འབྲེལ་པ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁྱབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ནི་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་བདེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འབྲེལ་པ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ན་གཞི་དང་གནས་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ། ལྡན་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ། རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ་ཕྱོགས་གསུམ་དུ་འགྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཅི་ཡང་མི་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལྟར་འོག་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བའི་ཆོས་ཆུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་འོག་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བའི་གེགས་བྱེད་པས་གཞིར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་ན། བདེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ནི་ལུས་མེད་པས་འོག་ཏུ་འགྲོ་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱེད་ན་གཞིར་འགྱུར། གནས་པར་བྱེད་པས་ཀྱང་གཞི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གནས་པ་དང་གནས་པ་པོ་ཐ་མི་དད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཉིད་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་དགག་པར་བྱའོ། །གནས་པ་དང་ཐ་དད་ན་ཡང་དེ་གནས་པ་པོ་དེ་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་དེ། གནས་པ་དོན་གཞན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་ནི་གནས་པ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་མཐུ་ཡང་མེད་དེ། ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་མཐུ་མེད་པར་གསལ་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
translation: That which is not connected to happiness, suffering, and the like is neither an agent nor an experiencer, and it is not reasonable that it should be a liberator or a transmigrator, just like the son of a barren woman. The statement that the self is also not connected to actions and the like means that a pervasive agent is not observed. Nor is the logical reason unestablished, for if it were connected to happiness and the like, it would have to be in one of three categories: the characteristic of a basis and that which abides, the characteristic of being possessed, or the characteristic of cause and effect. For the time being, the first position is not the case, because it does nothing. Just as a phenomenon that moves downward, such as water, is posited as a basis because it acts as an obstacle to moving downward, if we posit the self as a basis, what does it do? Since happiness and the like have no body, it is impossible for them to move downward, so what would the self do to become a basis? It is also not a basis by way of causing abiding, because abiding and that which abides are not distinct, so it would be acting upon itself, which is also to be refuted. Even if it were distinct from abiding, it would not be beneficial to that which abides, because it would be acting upon a different entity. Furthermore, it lacks the power to produce abiding, for it is to be made clear that it lacks power in all respects.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: There is nothing that acts as a basis for an entity that is by nature changing, for it is already in the process of abiding. If it were otherwise, it would only result in the destruction of that entity, not in its being made to abide. Furthermore, what would an agent of abiding do for an entity that is by nature unchanging, since it already abides in a nature of stability? Therefore, because it does nothing, a relationship of being possessed is also untenable, as it would lead to the fallacy of over-extension. If that were the case, then everything would become a cause for everything else to be possessed. It is not reasonable for one distinct entity to be possessed by another distinct entity, because, like an iron probe, everything abides in its own nature. Moreover, if the self were to become happy or suffering by the power of being possessed, then at that time, that which is possessed would be singular; because there is no differentiation, it would not be connected to the specific, determined nature of happiness and the like. Therefore, the self alone would not become happiness or suffering through happiness and the like. If one were to assert that it is determined by the power of what is not perceived, then if it is determined by that alone, what is the point of imagining a possessor? That is because it lacks power in any respect. Even regarding the imputation of difference based on the difference of those that are connected, in ultimate reality, there is no difference in the nature of things; so, what could possibly be the basis for a difference in functional activity that depends upon a difference in nature? Therefore, this relationship is merely something imagined by a poor intellect.

That which is not connected to happiness, suffering, and the like is neither an agent nor an experiencer, and it is not reasonable that it should be a liberator or a transmigrator, just like the son of a barren woman. The statement that the self is also not connected to actions and the like means that a pervasive agent is not observed. Nor is the logical reason unestablished, for if it were connected to happiness and the like, it would have to be in one of three categories: the characteristic of a basis and that which abides, the characteristic of being possessed, or the characteristic of cause and effect. For the time being, the first position is not the case, because it does nothing. Just as a phenomenon that moves downward, such as water, is posited as a basis because it acts as an obstacle to moving downward, if we posit the self as a basis, what does it do? Since happiness and the like have no body, it is impossible for them to move downward, so what would the self do to become a basis? It is also not a basis by way of causing abiding, because abiding and that which abides are not distinct, so it would be acting upon itself, which is also to be refuted. Even if it were distinct from abiding, it would not be beneficial to that which abides, because it would be acting upon a different entity. Furthermore, it lacks the power to produce abiding, for it is to be made clear that it lacks power in all respects.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: It is also not connected by way of cause and effect, because happiness and the like appear to arise in sequence. It is not reasonable for a result that possesses a complete set of causes to sometimes arise and sometimes not, because there is no distinction. As for the self, which others cannot distinguish or which possesses an unceasing power, there is no reliance upon auxiliary causes by which it would arise in sequence, nor is there any reliance upon auxiliary conditions. Therefore, if it were bound because it is the cause that produces suffering, then at that time it would be bound in all respects and would not become liberated, because it does not abandon that kind of nature. If it were to abandon it, how could it be permanent? If, on the other hand, it were liberated because it is the cause that produces a state devoid of suffering, then at that time it would be liberated in all respects and would never be bound; if so, how could one posit the basis of bondage and liberation? Similarly, if it were an agent because it is capable of performing or producing the characteristics of thought and the like, then at that time it would be an agent in all respects; how could it be an experiencer? If, on the other hand, it were an experiencer because it is the cause that produces happiness and the like, then at that time it would be an experiencer in all respects; how could it be an agent? Even the immutable, sky-like self posited by the Sāṃkhyas as an experiencer of happiness and the like is not logically sound, because it would lead to the fallacy of over-extension.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: If it were to change, then its permanence would be lost. A mere cause does not become an agent or an experiencer, for that would lead to an unacceptable consequence. Likewise, it should be applied that a rememberer and so forth cannot be established as the basis for that. Therefore, only in the system that asserts selflessness are the designations of liberation, bondage, and the like logically sound, because those designations are differentiated merely by the distinction between cause and effect. Furthermore, the reality of cause and effect exists only for the impermanent, not for the permanent, because the latter lacks the power to produce any result whatsoever in succession, as previously explained. Nor is it simultaneous, for the essence of the power to produce such a result would have to follow along, and it is illogical for it to be devoid of producing a result, as before. If it does not follow along, then the former essence would be lost. Apart from succession and simultaneity, there is no other mode by which something can perform a function, because those two are characterized by being mutually exclusive. For that very reason, great Buddhist scholars assert that all things that are not momentary—whatever they may be, such as space and other entities imagined by others—are objects of conceptual imputation that do not exist, because they lack the capacity to perform a function.

heading: སེམས་བསྐྱེད་བཤད་པ།
translation: To designate things such as the horns of a rabbit as non-existent is simply due to the cause of their lacking the capacity to perform a function. Conversely, to designate something as existent is to refer to a domain that possesses the capacity to perform a function, for existence and non-existence are defined by the characteristic of being mutually exclusive. If one were to apply the name "entity" to things like the horns of a rabbit, which are devoid of all capacity in that manner, and which are no different from such things, then there would be no dispute regarding the name. However, those who possess an understanding of the intent of what is meaningless argue that it is not logical to designate as an entity something that is no different from the son of a barren woman, which is of the nature of not being observed in that manner. Therefore, the logical reason is not unestablished. Nor is it uncertain, as that would lead to the absurdity of space and the like being agents. Nor is it contradictory, as it exists in what is concordant with the thesis. Since there is no other characteristic of a self, it is therefore like the son of a barren woman. If persons were to perish, it would lead to the absurdity of them being included solely within the aggregates, because the aggregates encompass all conditioned things. If they do not perish, then at that time, because they are unlike the phenomena belonging to the aggregates, they would be entirely different entities from them, and the fault of that has already been stated. Therefore, there is not even the slightest entity that can be called inexpressible. Thus, the lion's roar of the Tathāgata—that all phenomena are devoid of self—is what causes the entire herd of tirthika elephants to tremble and remain uncrushed, so there is no need for more.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Focusing on the engagement with the pāramitā, the text states, "Again," and so forth. This should be viewed as having the nature of two types of statements: a general rule and a specific exception. The intended meaning is: "A bodhisattva should indeed practice generosity, but should not abide in objects." By the term "generosity," this refers to the three types of generosity, thereby indicating all six pāramitā, not merely generosity alone. Among these, the generosity of material goods indicates the pāramitā of generosity. The generosity of fearlessness indicates the pāramitā of ethical discipline and the pāramitā of patience. The generosity of the Dharma indicates the pāramitā of diligence, the pāramitā of meditative concentration, and the pāramitā of wisdom; for without diligence, one becomes weary of grasping and teaching the Dharma and fails to teach it. Without meditative concentration, one desires to act beyond mere faith and becomes a teacher afflicted by kleshas. Without wisdom, one teaches it in a distorted manner. Therefore, without all three, the generosity of the Dharma cannot be accomplished. Others explain that diligence pervades all. The phrase "should practice generosity" indicates how one should abide in all six pāramitā through aspiration and prayer.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: The phrase "not abiding in objects" and so forth indicates how one should accomplish this through the meditative equipoise of a yogin. The phrase "a bodhisattva should practice generosity in this way" and so forth indicates how, having overcome distraction, one should firmly hold the mind. Regarding this, "not abiding in objects" indicates that the engagement with the pāramitā exists just as it is. To be fixated on the reality of objects such as the thing to be given, the giver, and the recipient is what is called "abiding." If a bodhisattva engages in the pāramitā while being fixated on objects, they are engaging incorrectly, because in the ultimate sense, there is no object whatsoever that is not subject to fixation, and thus they are fixated in a distorted manner. This is because there is no valid cognition to establish it, and because there are refutations. For instance, the view held by others that the object of cognition is distinct from consciousness cannot be established through direct perception, as it is not reasonable for consciousness to grasp a different object. If one were to wonder whether the grasping of an object by consciousness occurs with aspects, without aspects, or as an external aspect, it is not the case that it occurs with aspects; for when one sees things like a painted image, because it is non-distinct from the singular consciousness, the aspects would also be reduced to a singular essence, or else consciousness itself, being non-distinct from the aspects, would be reduced to a multiplicity of essences.

Focusing on the engagement with the pāramitā, the text states, "Again," and so forth. This should be viewed as having the nature of two types of statements: a general rule and a specific exception. The intended meaning is: "A bodhisattva should indeed practice generosity, but should not abide in objects." By the term "generosity," this refers to the three types of generosity, thereby indicating all six pāramitā, not merely generosity alone. Among these, the generosity of material goods indicates the pāramitā of generosity. The generosity of fearlessness indicates the pāramitā of ethical discipline and the pāramitā of patience. The generosity of the Dharma indicates the pāramitā of diligence, the pāramitā of meditative concentration, and the pāramitā of wisdom; for without diligence, one becomes weary of grasping and teaching the Dharma and fails to teach it. Without meditative concentration, one desires to act beyond mere faith and becomes a teacher afflicted by kleshas. Without wisdom, one teaches it in a distorted manner. Therefore, without all three, the generosity of the Dharma cannot be accomplished. Others explain that diligence pervades all. The phrase "should practice generosity" indicates how one should abide in all six pāramitā through aspiration and prayer.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: It is also not reasonable for it to be many, because there is no experience of a consciousness that apprehends merely a single atom, and therefore a single consciousness is not established. If that is not established, then the many are also not established, because the many are of the nature of a collection of ones. Since consciousnesses are without body, it is impossible for there to be an arising of apprehension through consciousness abiding in coverage of the object, which would make it well-reasoned to posit that many consciousnesses arise for the purpose of establishing the form of an image. Furthermore, if one were to wonder whether it might be similar in its entirety or in part, for the time being, it is not in its entirety, because then consciousness would become of the nature of an insentient object, just like the object. It is also not by way of parts, because there are no parts to a single entity. Even if one were to impute parts by way of distinctions of exclusion, since such things exist in all similar phenomena, it would follow that everything would be known by everything. If, however, one were to posit that it is known by the two of being produced from it and being similar, then it would follow that the immediately preceding condition would also be apprehended as a similar object. Even if one were to allow that there is similarity, in the ultimate sense, an external object is not established as directly perceived, because consciousness knows that the aspect of blue and so forth exists within itself. There is no second consciousness that knows the aspect of blue and so forth, by which the object would also be directly perceived.
