heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If one asks, "Is it the case that consciousness itself apprehends the object?" [I reply:] It is so only from the perspective of imputation, but in the ultimate sense, there is no such cognition, because it only cognizes the aspect that exists within itself. How could there be such a thing as "it is only the aspect of that consciousness, because the object is extremely hidden"? The cause is not established as being produced solely by the creation of its own essence, because it appears as a delusion. Atoms are not the object of a consciousness that appears as coarse, because they are subtle. They are not an aggregation either, because they are not different from the objects themselves. The object of conceptualization also does not exist, because there is no substantial entity. If the aggregation were something else, it would not be reasonable for it to be a single entity, because it would appear as having distinct directions and because it would possess contradictory characteristics such as being obstructed and unobstructed. Even if it were a multiplicity of aggregations, it would just be those very atoms, and it would not be a different object. The position that there is "no aspect" is also not the case, because it does not perform any function regarding blue and so forth. If one were to cognize merely by existence, then all consciousness would cognize everything, because there would be no distinction among all things. Therefore, it would not be possible to establish that "this is the cognition of blue, but not of yellow," because there would be no distinction in the cause of the establishment.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If one accepts a single particular, then one is accepting that very thing as having an aspect; for in a consciousness that is merely the nature of conceptualization and lacks any particularity, there is nothing other than the aspect itself. The position of there being an "other aspect" is also not tenable, for that would lead to an unacceptable over-extension. If that were the case, then a consciousness of an aspect would also have to be examined as having form as its object. Therefore, the object is not established through direct perception. It is not established through inference either, because that object, which has not become an object of direct perception, is not established as being connected with any sign, such as consciousness. If one were to infer that consciousness is merely a cause that is distinct from the effect, then one’s desired conclusion would not be established, because there exist other immediate conditions as well. There is no other valid cognition either. Therefore, for the time being, an external object is not established. The ultimate nature of consciousness is also not established through direct perception, because there is no individual awareness of a non-dual nature. If it were not so, then everything would not be seen as it truly is. It is not established through inference either, because that kind of aspect is not established as being connected with any sign. If one asks how, then, there can be defilement and purification, it is not so, because according to your view, neither of those two is established as being connected with anything at all.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Those two are not established as being connected to the ultimate entity in any way or by any means. They are not established as connected by the characteristic of being produced from it, because that is entirely hidden from view. A connection to what is hidden from view cannot be grasped by anyone who sees only what is manifest. When one does not examine ignorance and the rest, there is no contradiction in the fact that attachment is the root of all defilement; but when one examines ignorance and the rest, if attachment is reversed, then the characteristic of the arising of a state that is not in harmony with purification—which is the attachment that exists solely when one does not examine—is also reasonable. At that time, since there is no entity in the ultimate sense, how could it follow that those two also do not exist? This consequence applies to one who asserts that those two are definitely one without a cause, but it does not apply to one who speaks of dependent origination in the conventional sense. Therefore, there is not even the slightest nihilism that denies the establishment of the nature of an ultimate entity. That which is subject to refutation truly exists; for instance, that which is devoid of the nature of being one or many does not exist in the ultimate sense, just like a sky-flower. As for the claim made by others that all forms of entities, which are of the nature of the knower and the knowable, are empty of the nature of being one or many, this is in effect a failure to perceive the pervader, because being one or many pervades the nature of an entity.

translation: Those two are also not present in that. In this regard, for the time being, those external entities such as form and the like are not single, because contradictory phenomena such as being obstructed and being unobstructed are observed. Even while possessing contradictory phenomena, if they were single, everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and perish simultaneously. They are also not multiple, because if one were to break them down into multiples, they would become distinct atoms, and since atoms also lack parts, they cannot exist in a "further" or "nearer" side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not even appear to exist as pervading directions; thus, one must admit that there are distinct directional parts. If one admits that, how could they be single? Therefore, it is established that, for the time being, external objects are devoid of the nature of being single or multiple. Cognition that appears as blue and so forth is also not of a single nature, because it appears to grasp the form of a painting, just like the multiple moments of consciousness that exist in separate continua. It is also not appropriate to say that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously, as in the case of a series, because for those that lack parts and lack a body, it is not logical for them to exist in a "nearer" or "further" side.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If such existence is absent, then it would not appear in that way. If one were to argue that consciousness is solely single, and that because false aspects appear to it, it does not incur the fault of being multiple, then if that were the case, how could those false aspects appear to it? To be "appearing" means to be of the nature of luminosity; if that is a phenomenon included within the nature of consciousness, then if those false aspects were entirely non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit and so forth, how could they appear? Therefore, if you admit that the aspects of the nature of luminosity are themselves false, what other essence of consciousness remains that would be your "truth"? Consciousness itself does not have any such thing as a "nature of luminosity," because it is in dependence upon the exclusion of others that one applies conventional designations to particulars alone. If the particulars are false, then it becomes entirely clear that everything is false, for there is no connection—neither by way of the characteristic of the essence of the consciousness that is the nature of truth, nor by way of the characteristic of arising from it—by which those things that are not existent could definitely appear to it. If there is no connection, then it is not logical for them to appear, because that would lead to the fallacy of over-extension. Therefore, the logical reason is not unestablished.

དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་མེད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་གང་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་དེ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བསྒྲིབས་པ་དང་མ་བསྒྲིབས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཆོས་འགལ་བ་དང་ལྡན་བཞིན་དུ་ཡང་གཅིག་པ་ཉིད་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རྫས་གཅིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྱུང་བ་དང་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུ་མ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་དུ་མར་བཤིག་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཏུ་ཐ་དད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུལ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་ནི་མེད་དེ་སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཁྱབ་པར་གནས་པར་སྣང་བར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ཞིག་ན་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླང་བར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ནི་གཅིག་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དོན་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་བོ། །སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་རི་མོའི་རྣམ་པ་འཛིན་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་གཅིག་པུའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐ་དད་པའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་དུ་མ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དུ་མ་རྣམ་གྲངས་བཞིན་དུ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཅིག་ཅར་འབྱུང་ངོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ཡང་མི་རུང་སྟེ། ཆ་ཤས་མེད་པ་དང་ལུས་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ནི། ཚུ་རོལ་དང་ཕ་རོལ་ན་གནས་པ་མི་རིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Those two are also not present in that. In this regard, for the time being, those external entities such as form and the like are not single, because contradictory phenomena such as being obstructed and being unobstructed are observed. Even while possessing contradictory phenomena, if they were single, everything would become a single substance, and therefore they would arise and perish simultaneously. They are also not multiple, because if one were to break them down into multiples, they would become distinct atoms, and since atoms also lack parts, they cannot exist in a "further" or "nearer" side, just like mind and mental factors. Therefore, they would not even appear to exist as pervading directions; thus, one must admit that there are distinct directional parts. If one admits that, how could they be single? Therefore, it is established that, for the time being, external objects are devoid of the nature of being single or multiple. Cognition that appears as blue and so forth is also not of a single nature, because it appears to grasp the form of a painting, just like the multiple moments of consciousness that exist in separate continua. It is also not appropriate to say that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously, as in the case of a series, because for those that lack parts and lack a body, it is not logical for them to exist in a "nearer" or "further" side.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation:
Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is not uncertain. Because it exists in the concordant class, it is not contradictory. Therefore, entities are connected in whatever way they are conceptualized. For that very reason, it is said:
"However entities are conceptualized,
They lack a nature that is true.
In this way, they do not exist
As having the nature of one or many."
The Blessed One also stated in the Noble Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
"Just as forms appear in a mirror,
Devoid of both oneness and otherness,
Though they appear, they do not exist there.
Such is the nature of entities;
When analyzed by the intellect,
No nature can be grasped.
Therefore, they are said to be inexpressible,
And devoid of any nature."
Likewise, it is also stated in the Noble Samādhirāja Sūtra:
"Just as when a person seeking the pith
Systematically dismantles a fresh plantain tree,
No pith is found either inside or outside,
Know all phenomena to be just like that."

དེ་ལྟར་གནས་པ་མེད་ན་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་སྣང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འོན་ཏེ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི་གཅིག་པུ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ལ། རྣམ་པ་བརྫུན་པ་རྣམས་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བས་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་གོ་བརྫུན་པ་དེ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་དེ་ལ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར། སྣང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ལ་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དུ་གཏོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཡིན་ན་བརྫུན་བ་རི་བོང་གི་རྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བར་ཤིན་དུ་མེད་ན་གོ་སྣང་བར་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པ་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཁས་ལེན་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་བདེན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཤེས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་ཅི་ཞིག་ལུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་གསལ་བའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གཞན་རྣམ་པར་བཅད་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་ཁོ་ན་ལ་སྤྱིར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བྱེ་བྲག་རྣམས་བརྫུན་ན་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་བརྫུན་པར་ཤིན་དུ་གསལ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པའི་ངོ་བོའི་ཤེས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དེ་ལ་གང་གིས་ན་དེ་ལ་ངེས་པར་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ། དེ་ལས་འབྱུང་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འབྲེལ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །འབྲེལ་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་སྣང་བར་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

If such existence is absent, then it would not appear in that way. If one were to argue that consciousness is solely single, and that because false aspects appear to it, it does not incur the fault of being multiple, then if that were the case, how could those false aspects appear to it? To be "appearing" means to be of the nature of luminosity; if that is a phenomenon included within the nature of consciousness, then if those false aspects were entirely non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit and so forth, how could they appear? Therefore, if you admit that the aspects of the nature of luminosity are themselves false, what other essence of consciousness remains that would be your "truth"? Consciousness itself does not have any such thing as a "nature of luminosity," because it is in dependence upon the exclusion of others that one applies conventional designations to particulars alone. If the particulars are false, then it becomes entirely clear that everything is false, for there is no connection—neither by way of the characteristic of the essence of the consciousness that is the nature of truth, nor by way of the characteristic of arising from it—by which those things that are not existent could definitely appear to it. If there is no connection, then it is not logical for them to appear, because that would lead to the fallacy of over-extension. Therefore, the logical reason is not unestablished.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Therefore, because all entities are like illusions and are pleasant when not examined, one should practice giving without being fixated in that way. The meaning of the statement that one should not abide in entities is logical here. In this way, it is fully demonstrated that the application to giving and so forth exists just as it is, and not otherwise. If one thinks, "Since there are no entities in the ultimate sense, one should not practice giving by abiding in entities; therefore, one should practice giving by being fixated on the non-existence of entities," then it is to address this that the statement "one should not abide in anything" was spoken. A Bodhisattva should also abandon the conceptualization of the non-existence of entities, for that does not exist if there is no grasping at entities. Conventionally, there are objects to be given, givers, and so forth; therefore, it is intended that being fixated on the non-existence of entities is also not reasonable.

Because there is no other aspect of an entity, it is not uncertain. Because it exists in the concordant class, it is not contradictory. Therefore, entities are connected in whatever way they are conceptualized. For that very reason, it is said:
"However entities are conceptualized,
They lack a nature that is true.
In this way, they do not exist
As having the nature of one or many."
The Blessed One also stated in the Noble Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
"Just as forms appear in a mirror,
Devoid of both oneness and otherness,
Though they appear, they do not exist there.
Such is the nature of entities;
When analyzed by the intellect,
No nature can be grasped.
Therefore, they are said to be inexpressible,
And devoid of any nature."
Likewise, it is also stated in the Noble Samādhirāja Sūtra:
"Just as when a person seeking the pith
Systematically dismantles a fresh plantain tree,
No pith is found either inside or outside,
Know all phenomena to be just like that."

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།

A sign (nimitta) is the defining characteristic of an entity, that is, a mark. That also refers to non-arising and so forth. Conceptualizing about that is perception (saṃjñā). Not conceptualizing about that is not abiding in it.

[3-43] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, because all entities are like illusions and are pleasant when not examined, one should practice giving without being fixated in that way. The meaning of the statement that one should not abide in entities is logical here. In this way, it is fully demonstrated that the application to giving and so forth exists just as it is, and not otherwise. If one thinks, "Since there are no entities in the ultimate sense, one should not practice giving by abiding in entities; therefore, one should practice giving by being fixated on the non-existence of entities," then it is to address this that the statement "one should not abide in anything" was spoken. A Bodhisattva should also abandon the conceptualization of the non-existence of entities, for that does not exist if there is no grasping at entities. Conventionally, there are objects to be given, givers, and so forth; therefore, it is intended that being fixated on the non-existence of entities is also not reasonable.

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: By this, the statement "one should not abide in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, this entire passage also teaches the profundity, and it teaches the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and negation. For those who have objects of apprehension, the possibility of perfecting the accumulations of merit and wisdom in this view is denied; for instance, one who wishes to make offerings and provide benefits generates great faith in what is given, but this is not based on the non-apprehension of the object to be given, the giver, and the recipient. If, because they do not exist, the object to be given and so forth are not apprehended, or if it is because there is no object [of perception], then the first alternative would lead to the consequence of there being no merit, since no one has given anything at all. Since sentient beings do not exist, the efforts made by Bodhisattvas for the sake of the benefit of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, it is not the case that they simply do not exist. Because the Tathāgata perceives the entities of the object to be given and so forth, they are not objects [of apprehension].

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Having kept in mind all the objections—such as the claim that if it were not so, how could the Tathāgata have given away his children and so forth—he asks, "For what reason?" and in response, he says, "Subhūti, whatever a Bodhisattva..." and so forth. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from right view are completely pure, and therefore they bring about the realization of highly superior and desirable fruits, whereas those arising from inverted views do not. This is like the limbs of morality and so forth that arise from wrong view. Because entities such as the object to be given do not exist in the manner previously stated, apprehending them as such is purely an inversion, just like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the methods of prajñāpāramitā that arise from that are weak in power, as they arise from causes that are not completely pure, just like giving and so forth that arise from the inversion of self and what belongs to self. Not apprehending the object to be given and so forth as things to be known is non-inverted, because in the sense of ultimate reality, it is the object, just like apprehending a mirage as a mirage. Therefore, because they arise from causes that are extensive, giving and so forth from that are of great fruit, just like sprouts and so forth that are realized from healthy seeds.

དེས་ནི་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་འདི་མཐའ་དག་གིས་ནི་འདིས་ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ལ། སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པ་དང་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་དགག་པ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །དམིགས་པ་ཅན་རྣམས་ལྟ་བ་འདི་ལ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱ་བར་རུང་བ་བཀག་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་མཆོད་པ་དང་ཕན་གདགས་པར་འདོད་པས་གང་བྱིན་པ་དེ་ཤིན་དུ་དང་བ་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱི། སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་པོ་དང་། ལེན་པ་པོ་མི་དམིགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མི་དམིགས་སམ་འོན་ཏེ་ཡུལ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་སུས་ཅི་ཡང་བྱིན་པ་མེད་པས་བསོད་ནམས་མེད་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་ཅན་དག་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་གྱི་ཕྱིར་ཡོངས་སུ་ངལ་བར་བྱས་པ་དེ་ཡང་དོན་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་མེད་པ་ཁོ་ན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་གཟིགས་པས་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

By this, the statement "one should not abide in anything whatsoever" is taught. Alternatively, this entire passage also teaches the profundity, and it teaches the refutation of the extremes of superimposition and negation. For those who have objects of apprehension, the possibility of perfecting the accumulations of merit and wisdom in this view is denied; for instance, one who wishes to make offerings and provide benefits generates great faith in what is given, but this is not based on the non-apprehension of the object to be given, the giver, and the recipient. If, because they do not exist, the object to be given and so forth are not apprehended, or if it is because there is no object [of perception], then the first alternative would lead to the consequence of there being no merit, since no one has given anything at all. Since sentient beings do not exist, the efforts made by Bodhisattvas for the sake of the benefit of sentient beings would also become meaningless; therefore, it is not the case that they simply do not exist. Because the Tathāgata perceives the entities of the object to be given and so forth, they are not objects [of apprehension].

heading: ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: Therefore, generosity and so forth that abide in non-apprehension arise from right view and thus generate great faith in the wise, but this is not the case for others. It is not that one holds that the objects of giving and so forth are absolutely non-existent, which would lead to a lack of merit because one would not engage in generosity and so forth; rather, one acknowledges that they exist conventionally. Nor is it the case that there is no apprehension at all, because in the state of non-meditative equipoise, one apprehends them as being like an illusion. At that time, it is established as non-apprehension arising from aspiration. In the state of meditative equipoise, however, there is truly no apprehension at all, and at that time, one does not claim to engage in generosity and so forth; thus, one cannot be faulted for the activities of the initial preparatory stage or the subsequent post-meditative state. By this, the vastness of the application to the prajñāpāramitā is expressed because of the greatness of the fruit. By demonstrating the entities of cause and effect conventionally, the extreme of nihilism is also refuted. In three ways, merit is like the sky: because it is all-pervasive, vast, and inexhaustible. It is all-pervasive because it generates both mundane and supramundane merit; mundane merit is generated in the state of non-meditative equipoise, and supramundane merit is the state of meditative equipoise. It is vast because it proceeds to excellence by entering into excellence. It is inexhaustible because it will not be exhausted as long as saṃsāra continues.

Having kept in mind all the objections—such as the claim that if it were not so, how could the Tathāgata have given away his children and so forth—he asks, "For what reason?" and in response, he says, "Subhūti, whatever a Bodhisattva..." and so forth. The intention is this: giving and so forth that arise from right view are completely pure, and therefore they bring about the realization of highly superior and desirable fruits, whereas those arising from inverted views do not. This is like the limbs of morality and so forth that arise from wrong view. Because entities such as the object to be given do not exist in the manner previously stated, apprehending them as such is purely an inversion, just like apprehending a mirage as water. Therefore, all the methods of prajñāpāramitā that arise from that are weak in power, as they arise from causes that are not completely pure, just like giving and so forth that arise from the inversion of self and what belongs to self. Not apprehending the object to be given and so forth as things to be known is non-inverted, because in the sense of ultimate reality, it is the object, just like apprehending a mirage as a mirage. Therefore, because they arise from causes that are extensive, giving and so forth from that are of great fruit, just like sprouts and so forth that are realized from healthy seeds.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: If, because that does not exist, one should give a gift without dwelling on form, then one might wonder how a Bodhisattva who desires to attain the rūpakāya of a Tathāgata should engage in giving and the like; anticipating this objection, by saying "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth, the text demonstrates the basis for aspiring to attain the rūpakāya. In this context, the meaning is that it eliminates the discordant factor characterized by the pride of identifying the rūpakāya as a Tathāgata.

source: མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཚན་དང་དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོས་བརྒྱན་པ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་མཚན་རྣམས་ནི་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལ་འཁོར་ལོ་མངའ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ཏེ། ཚིག་མངས་ཀྱིས་དོགས་པས་མ་བྲིས་ཀྱི་མདོ་ལས་ཇི་སྐད་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཡུལ་ན་གནས་པ་དང་། གསལ་བ་དང་། རྫོགས་པས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའོ། །དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོ་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་དག་ནི་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་ཀྱི་མདོག་འདྲ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། མདོ་ལས་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །མཚན་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་བཞིན་དུ་བརྫུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་ཏོ། །འདི་ལྟར་མཚན་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་བསགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དམ། དེས་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་གྱི་གཟུགས་ཞིག་ཏུ་གྱུར་གྲང་ན། རེ་ཞིག་ཕྱོགས་དང་པོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སྔར་བཤིག་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་པ་མེད་ན་དེས་ན་བརྩམས་པ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། སྒྲིབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འགལ་བའི་ཆོས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་དག་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་སྨྲས་པ་ལས་དགོངས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས། དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་ཏེ་ཞེས་གསལ་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་མཚན་རྣམས་བརྫུན་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན་འོ་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མདོ་སྡེ་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ལས་མཚན་རྣམས་གསུངས་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། དེ་ཉིད་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨྲས་ཏེ། མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་དོན་དམ་པར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྱུ་མས་སྤྲུལ་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་བཞིན་དུ་དེས་བརྫུན་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཁོ་ནར་གསུངས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྨྲས་པའི་དོན་དེ་ཉིད་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བསྐང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །
translation: By mentioning "perfect marks," one is merely speaking of signs, which fully demonstrates the Tathāgata’s rūpakāya, adorned with all the major marks and minor signs. Regarding these, the major marks are the thirty-two, such as having wheels on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet; as I fear being wordy, I have not written them out, so please understand them just as they appear in the sūtras. These are also perfect in that they are situated in their proper place, are clear, and are complete. The eighty minor signs are such as having nails the color of copper, and so forth; please understand them as they appear in the sūtras. These marks and so forth are also false, just like the marks of a Buddha conjured by magic. Therefore, the text teaches that one should dwell with aspiration and prayer for such a rūpakāya. In this way, are these marks the essence of accumulated atoms, or are they a composite form produced by them? The first position is not the case, because the atoms have already been refuted. The second is also not the case, because if there is no creator, there is no composite, and because the previously explained contradictory phenomena, such as obscurations, are observed. Therefore, the intention behind what was said is explained; having examined this, Subhūti clarifies, "That is not so." If the marks were truly false, one might think, "Why then did the Bhagavān speak of the marks in such and such sūtras?" and ask, "For what reason?" The text states, "Because that itself lacks perfect marks," meaning that the perfect marks were not taught in the ultimate sense; rather, the implication is that they were taught as having the nature of being false, just like a Buddha conjured by magic. In order to fulfill the meaning of what the noble Subhūti said, the Bhagavān spoke the words beginning with "To what extent..."

If, because that does not exist, one should give a gift without dwelling on form, then one might wonder how a Bodhisattva who desires to attain the rūpakāya of a Tathāgata should engage in giving and the like; anticipating this objection, by saying "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth, the text demonstrates the basis for aspiring to attain the rūpakāya. In this context, the meaning is that it eliminates the discordant factor characterized by the pride of identifying the rūpakāya as a Tathāgata.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: The phrase "to the extent that there are perfect major marks" means that, in ultimate reality, to the extent that one is attached to the perception of perfect major marks, to that same extent one is attached to a misconception; this is the intended meaning. It is as previously explained.

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ།
translation: The phrase "to the extent that there are no perfect major marks" should be understood as an explanation by way of inversion. This indicates how one who is engaged in yogic meditative equipoise should practice. It shows how to abandon the two extremes and thereby firmly grasp the mind: the phrase "in that way" means that one should view the Tathāgata through the major marks just as one views a Buddha emanated by illusion. This eliminates the extreme of deprecation, because in conventional reality, one does not deprecate the rūpakāya of the Bhagavan. One should view the "no major marks" in terms of ultimate reality, because no major marks are established whatsoever. This eliminates the extreme of superimposition. By making a vow for the sake of attaining the rūpakāya of the Tathāgata, one expresses the vastness; by not perceiving it, one expresses the profundity. The section on the aspiration to attain the rūpakāya has been explained.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Regarding that, because in the future the five degenerations will be prevalent among sentient beings, and because this precious Dharma is extremely profound and vast in its fruition, [the Buddha] asked, "Will there be [those who believe]?" out of concern that there might be a lack of faith in the dharmakāya of teaching. The phrase "Will there be?" is to be connected with the meaning of the passage: "Will there be any sentient beings who, when this kind of sūtra is taught, will generate a correct perception?" Regarding the phrase "the last five hundred," a collection of five centuries is five hundred; because it is well known that the teaching of the Bhagavan will remain for five periods of five hundred years, the term "last" is specifically used, for at that time the five degenerations are prevalent.

source: དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་ནི་མོས་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ལུང་ནོད་པ་དང་། འཆད་པ་དང་།ཉན་པ་དང་། སེམས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་པའོ། །འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའོ། །མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མདོ་སྡེ་བསྟན་པའི་ངག་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདི་དག་གིས་དོན་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་མཐའ་དག་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡང་ན་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཚིག་དག་ནི་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །བཤད་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །བཤད་པ་དག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དང་པོ་ལྟར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་ནི་དོན་སྟོན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དོན་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། སྒྲ་ཇི་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མི་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྲུབ་ན་ཡང་དག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཡང་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་དག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གཟིགས་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་དོགས་པ་དེ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འབྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་སོ། །
translation: The degeneration of the holy Dharma is the decline of conviction, reading, recitation, receiving the transmission, explaining, listening, and reflecting, and so forth. The phrase "such as this" refers to that which is profound in meaning and vast. The phrase "the words of the sūtra" refers to the utterances that teach the sūtra, for it is by these that one understands and knows the meaning. This mere expression of the signs fully reveals the entire dharmakāya of teaching. Alternatively, "the words of the sūtra" is a term for what is to be expressed. In this explanation, the phrase "such as this" is to be connected with "profound and vast." The phrase "regarding the explanation" means, in the first case, "regarding the expressions," and in the second case, it is a term for "regarding those that reveal the meaning." To have a non-erroneous perception of the meaning is what is meant here by "correct perception," but one should not have a perception that thinks, "This is correct," by becoming attached to the literal words. By this, when the meaning is established, it eliminates the perception that is not correct. Because the Tathāgata knows everything without obstruction, he saw those who would appear as if they were right before him, and in order to dispel that doubt of Subhūti, he said, "They will appear." The phrase "great bodhisattva" is stated in order to correctly reveal the qualities of those bodhisattvas.

དེ་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཆོས་དཀོན་མཆོག་འདི་འདྲ་བ་ཡང་འབྲས་བུ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་ཅིང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཡིད་མི་ཆེས་སུ་དོགས་ནས་མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་ཞུས་ཏེ། མཆིས་ལགས་སམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་ནི་ཅི་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ལ་ལ་དག་འདི་ལྟ་བུའི་མདོ་སྡེའི་ཆོས་བཤད་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འབྱུང་བ་དག་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གི་དོན་དེ་དང་སྦྱར་རོ། །ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་ པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་མཛད་དེ། དེའི་ཚེ་སྙིགས་མ་ལྔ་པོ་དག་ནི་ཤས་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[3-53] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding that, because in the future the five degenerations will be prevalent among sentient beings, and because this precious Dharma is extremely profound and vast in its fruition, [the Buddha] asked, "Will there be [those who believe]?" out of concern that there might be a lack of faith in the dharmakāya of teaching. The phrase "Will there be?" is to be connected with the meaning of the passage: "Will there be any sentient beings who, when this kind of sūtra is taught, will generate a correct perception?" Regarding the phrase "the last five hundred," a collection of five centuries is five hundred; because it is well known that the teaching of the Bhagavan will remain for five periods of five hundred years, the term "last" is specifically used, for at that time the five degenerations are prevalent.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་། རྒྱུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་ཡང་དག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུས་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལྷག་པའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་སེམས་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་གོ་རིམས་བཞིན་ཏེ། བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ཤེས་རབ་ལོགས་ཤིག་དུ་སྨོས་པ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི་འདིར་བསམ་གཏན་ལས་བྱུང་བ་བཟུང་སྟེ། བ་ལང་དང་གླང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་མའི་དུས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་ནི་ན་བཟའ་དང་ཞལ་ཟས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱས་པ་དང་། གདུགས་དང་རྒྱལ་མཚན་དང་བ་དན་ལ་སོགས་པས་མཆོད་པའོ། །
translation: The Bhagavan fully reveals what kind of practice that is, what kind of cause leads to its perfect accomplishment, what kind of support from a spiritual friend one possesses, and what kind of correct perception leads to the state of perception. The statement "endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with qualities, endowed with wisdom" indicates, in that order, the accomplishment of the three trainings: the higher ethical discipline, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. The qualities mentioned separately as ethical discipline and wisdom here refer to those arising from meditative concentration, in the manner of what is called "the ox and the bull." Regarding the thought of how such a person endowed with qualities like ethical discipline could appear in the later, afflicted times, he spoke the words beginning with "Subhūti." To "honor" means to provide service with robes, food, and the like, and to "worship" means to offer parasols, victory banners, pennants, and the like.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Generating the roots of virtue should be viewed as a matter of taking the instructions and teachings upon one's head and then applying oneself diligently to the perfection of qualities such as ethical discipline. The Bhagavan fully reveals what kind of practice that is, what kind of cause leads to its perfect accomplishment, what kind of support from a spiritual friend one possesses, and what kind of correct perception leads to the state of perception. The statement "endowed with ethical discipline, endowed with qualities, endowed with wisdom" indicates, in that order, the accomplishment of the three trainings: the higher ethical discipline, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. The qualities mentioned separately as ethical discipline and wisdom here refer to those arising from meditative concentration, in the manner of what is called "the ox and the bull." Regarding the thought of how such a person endowed with qualities like ethical discipline could appear in the later, afflicted times, he spoke the words beginning with "Subhūti." To "honor" means to provide service with robes, food, and the like, and to "worship" means to offer parasols, victory banners, pennants, and the like.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The statement "They are seen by the Tathāgata" refers to their physical forms. This indicates that they are fully supported by a spiritual friend. This was spoken in order to encourage those who have entered upon the right path and to generate a sense of shame in those who have entered upon the wrong path. If it were not so, what difference would there be between this and the statement that the Bhagavan is "omniscient" because he knows all things? Alternatively, this should be viewed as primarily teaching that they possess the potential; the meaning is that he knows them as having the potential.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, in order to show the complete gathering of their heap of merit, the phrase "all those sentient beings" is stated. "Generating" refers to the time when merit arises. By all of this, it is shown that one should abide with both aspiration and prayer, having dispelled incorrect conceptualization and generated correct conceptualization; the vastness of this state is fully indicated.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The phrase "For what reason" is an inquiry into the logic of how one knows that they have made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and here the phrase "those bodhisattva mahāsattvas" and so forth are spoken. This fully indicates how one should accomplish the meditative absorption into yoga. The profundity is also expressed. The grasping at the existence of a self, thinking "I am," is the perception of a self.

If it were not so, what difference would there be between this and the statement that the Bhagavan is "omniscient" because he knows all things? Alternatively, this should be viewed as primarily teaching that they possess the potential; the meaning is that he knows them as having the potential.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Grasping at the existence of a self is the perception of a sentient being. Grasping at the duration of that very self for as long as it remains is the perception of a life-force. Grasping at the repeated movement into various states of existence is the perception of a person.

The phrase "For what reason" is an inquiry into the logic of how one knows that they have made offerings to many hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and here the phrase "those bodhisattva mahāsattvas" and so forth are spoken. This fully indicates how one should accomplish the meditative absorption into yoga. The profundity is also expressed. The grasping at the existence of a self, thinking "I am," is the perception of a self.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one thinks that, in the absence of perceptions of a self and so forth, there might be a perception of phenomena such as form, just as there is for the śrāvakas and others, the phrase "there is no perception of phenomena" is stated, with the intention that in the ultimate sense, no phenomena whatsoever exist. If one then thinks, "Is there then a perception of non-existence, like that of the nihilists?" the phrase "nor is there a perception of non-existence" is stated. Because phenomena exist in a way that is pleasing when not analyzed in conventional terms, it is not logical for those abiding on the conventional path to have a perception of the non-existence of phenomena. Nor is it logical for those abiding in ultimate wisdom, because at that time, no phenomena whatsoever are observed, the negation of which would lead to a perception of the non-existence of phenomena. That is because if there is no grasping at phenomena, there is no non-existence. It is impossible anywhere to negate something without an object. For example, even if it is true that there is only consciousness, if one conceptualizes, "This is only consciousness," one is merely abiding in the idea of "only consciousness"; likewise, even if it is true that phenomena do not exist, if one realizes that phenomena do not exist, it is impossible to abide in that, so all are the same. If one thinks, "If there is no self and so forth, then even if those perceptions do not occur, this will become a perception of attachment to names, thinking, 'This is just a name, such as "self" or "form,"'" the phrase "and perception" is stated. Because names are included within the form aggregate, they are just as false as form and so forth, and they exist only as designations, not as entities. Therefore, the intention is that even the perception of them is merely an attachment to a perversion.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If it is thought that in such a state, because one is devoid of all perceptions, one becomes like a dead person or one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation, and thus is no longer a yogi, it is said that "one does not enter into the perceptionless." At that time, there exists the yogi’s primordial wisdom, which is the nature of the authentic conventional, by which they are a yogi. When rising from that, pure mundane primordial wisdom arises from it. If it were not so, it would be entirely without cause. If one asks who realizes that primordial wisdom of the yogi which is the nature of the conventional, it is by that very same reasoning: just as the realization of the selflessness of the person is present to oneself through self-cognition, so too is it the same here. It is not that primordial wisdom and cognition are not accepted as conventional. The yogi does not focus on the selflessness present in that [state] after having made the own-character manifest individually, because at that time the past and so forth are not near and are infinite. If one asks what it is like, they focus simultaneously on that which is established by gathering all phenomena that become objects through the analysis of non-nature into a general selflessness. Although that primordial wisdom of theirs is without an object in the ultimate sense, it is established as valid because it is not deceptive, like the cognition of a true dream. In that generality, the nature of its own essence is also included, and there is no separate object of focus for it. Therefore, because both realize selflessness, it is evident that they have made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. It is impossible for those who have not made offerings to the Buddhas to realize this, just like the non-Buddhists. This is the intention, thinking that this is not something familiar in saṃsāra. By this, it has been fully shown how one should practice this by entering into meditative attainment, what kind of authentic perception makes it that perception, and its profundity has also been fully shown.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Because there is no self and so forth, even if one does not perceive them as a self and so forth, is it not the case that those who perceive the characteristics of what is well-spoken—such as the collection of words—and what is ill-spoken as Dharma and non-Dharma will certainly emerge from them? That is not so. If bodhisattvas were not to perceive them in that way, one might worry: "Having abandoned the phenomena of the non-Buddhists that are produced by incorrect reasoning, how should one generate the aspiration to realize the phenomena spoken by the Tathāgata?" It is to address this doubt that the question "For what reason?" was asked, and the reply "Subhūti, if..." was spoken. The intention is this: when analyzed individually as to whether they are of the nature of one or many, phenomena characterized by form and so forth do not exist; the phenomena that are spoken of are likewise the same. Whoever has a perception of them as Dharma has certainly not abandoned the perception of them as a self and so forth, because the root of that is grasping at the characteristics of Dharma. Since mental engagement that possesses grasping at the characteristics of Dharma is mental engagement with "thatness," and mental engagement with compassion and so forth is not mental engagement with "thatness," it does not abandon the view of a self. For that very reason, it is said, "The vehicle is only one, namely, the Great Vehicle." Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who perceives them as Dharma has not yet generated the path of seeing, how could such a person abandon the perception of them as a self and so forth, since that is something to be abandoned by the path of seeing? For that reason, it is said, "Having analyzed all of them, they will grasp at them as a self." The intention is that this is because it is the cause of that, and because the latent tendencies of that have not been abandoned. If that were not the case, since they are of different types, how could the very perception of them as Dharma become a grasping at a self? Here, phenomena are considered to be the characteristics of the scriptural teachings produced by reasoning. Those that are the reverse of that are non-Dharma. If that is so, one might wonder how it is that the Tathāgata taught the bodhisattvas to fully grasp the holy Dharma in various sūtras; it is to address this that, having analyzed it, the question "For what reason?" was asked, and in reply, "Subhūti," and so forth, was spoken.

heading: བཤད་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "One should not grasp it incorrectly" means that one should not grasp it with the characteristic of being perversely attached to a wrong path; the intended meaning is that one should not be attached to the thought that "it is true." The intention is that this is not a rejection of grasping the characteristics of what has been taught as being like a raft for the purpose of accomplishing the goal. The phrase "therefore" and so forth connects this same meaning with other words. Because the attachment to the thought that "it is true" regarding all phenomena and non-phenomena is a perverted attachment, those collections of teachings generated by reasoning, which were taught to ferry one across the ocean of saṃsāra and are like a raft, should also be abandoned once one has reached the other shore because they are no longer needed; what need is there to even mention those non-phenomena, like the teachings of the tīrthikas, which are generated by incorrect reasoning? The Tathāgata spoke in this way, saying that He did not permit relying upon them even for the sake of a purpose. Regarding that, it is not so; if phenomena and non-phenomena and so forth were to exist as true entities, then at that time, because the attachment to them would be an object in the ultimate sense, they would become the very nature of reasoning even for those who have reached the other shore of saṃsāra; why then would the Tathāgata cause them to be rejected? This is the summarized meaning.

[3-67] translation already produced for this document:
If all phenomena, such as the *dharmas*, were in ultimate reality of a false nature, then the statement that the Bhagavan, having attained perfect and complete enlightenment, taught all *dharmas* would also become false. Therefore, in order to address the thought that a bodhisattva should not aspire to attain the *dharmakāya*—which is realized through the cause of the Tathāgata’s primordial wisdom—and to generate the aspiration to attain that *dharmakāya* which has primordial wisdom as its cause, the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" were spoken. By this, it is shown in essence that while holding to the attainment of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in ultimate reality is taught as a discordant factor, it also teaches that in the nature of valid conventional reality, one should generate the aspiration and make the prayer to attain the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata’s primordial wisdom, which has primordial wisdom as its cause.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Thinking that there is neither any perfect awakening nor any teaching of the Dharma, he asked, "Why is that?" The statement "it cannot be grasped" is because, in terms of ultimate reality, it is not even an object of non-conceptual primordial wisdom, as was explained previously. The statement "it cannot be expressed" is because it is not even an object of language, for the sphere of all language is merely the generality of conceptual imputation, and that generality itself lacks any substantial existence. These two are stated as the reasons for there being no perfect awakening and no teaching of the Dharma, respectively.

[3-68] translation already produced for this document:
The expression "unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment" merely indicates the sign, and by fully expressing it, it also fully reveals the *kāya* of realization, which has primordial wisdom as its cause and is differentiated by the distinctions in the realizations of *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and so forth. The qualities of *śrāvakas* and others are also things to be realized by the bodhisattva. If it were not so, how could the stage of omniscience be attained? In terms of conventional reality, however, it is like this: perfect enlightenment, the act of becoming perfectly enlightened, the act of teaching, and the teaching itself, and so on, all exist as synonyms.

Because the Bhagavan, with the intention of referring to ultimate reality, stated that "everything is merely false," the venerable ārya Subhūti, having grasped the intention behind that statement, requested, "As I understand the meaning of what the Bhagavan has said..." The phrase "as I understand" is an explanation of that intention.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: གལ་ཏེ་དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟུང་དུ་མེད་ཅིང་བརྗོད་དུ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་། འོན་ཀྱང་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་འཛིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་གནས་པ་ཁོ་ནའོ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མ་ལགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དམ་པར་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་འཛིན་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་གོ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་མེད་པ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་ལྟ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ཆོས་མ་མཆིས་པ་ཡང་མ་ལགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ནི་མེད་པ་དགག་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏེ། སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པ་དང་། སྐུར་བའི་མཐའ་ཡང་བཀག་གོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་འདིར་འཐད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འདིར་ལན་དུ་འདུས་མ་བྱས་ཀྱིས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨྲས་སོ། །འདུས་མ་བྱས་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཡང་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་མཚན་ཉིད་ཁོ་ན་ལ་གནས་ཏེ། སྔར་ཇི་སྐད་དཔྱད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡང་དག་པར་སྡུད་པ་ལས་བཤད་པ། ཀུན་དགའ་བོ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་དང་། འཇིག་པ་མེད་པ་དང་། གནས་པ་མེད་པ་དང་། གཞན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
translation: Even if all phenomena are ungraspable and inexpressible, one might think that because they possess their own intrinsic characteristics, the essence of phenomena must exist in an ultimate sense. To this, the response "that is not even a phenomenon" is offered. This is because it is impossible for all phenomena, in an ultimate sense, to possess an intrinsic characteristic that is by nature beyond suffering. If that were the case, one might think that the Bhagavan had perfectly awakened to nothingness; to this, the response "it is not that there is no phenomenon" is offered. This is the essence of the negation of non-existence. By this, the meditative equipoise of the yogi is indicated, and the extremes of superimposition and deprecation are also negated. The question "Why is that?" is asked here to request the reasoning, and the reply is given that it is because it is distinguished by the unconditioned. The unconditioned is the ultimate nature of phenomena. When analyzed through reasoning, it abides solely in the characteristic of non-arising, just as was analyzed previously. As the Bhagavan explained in the *Sūtra of the True Gathering of the Buddha*: "Ānanda, that which is the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-abiding, and non-changing of phenomena is called the noble truth."

Thinking that there is neither any perfect awakening nor any teaching of the Dharma, he asked, "Why is that?" The statement "it cannot be grasped" is because, in terms of ultimate reality, it is not even an object of non-conceptual primordial wisdom, as was explained previously. The statement "it cannot be expressed" is because it is not even an object of language, for the sphere of all language is merely the generality of conceptual imputation, and that generality itself lacks any substantial existence. These two are stated as the reasons for there being no perfect awakening and no teaching of the Dharma, respectively.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Ānanda, this is like what the Tathāgata said when, having this in mind, he taught that the noble śrāvakas are distinguished by the unconditioned. This is "unconditioned" because, whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear, it exists as such eternally and is unchanging. Because they realize this, noble individuals are distinguished by it, for noble ones are distinguished by their realization of the suchness of phenomena. It is not reasonable for anything else to be the essence of suchness. This unconditioned is not a non-existence in the sense of a negation of non-existence, for it is the essence of the nature of phenomena. If it were not so, noble ones would not have realized the nature of phenomena, as they would have realized some other essence that is not that. If there were no grasping at phenomena, then because it would be non-existent, it would follow that there is only grasping at phenomena. Therefore, in the *Sūtra Unraveling the Intent* and other sūtras, it is said that suchness is not a thing other than phenomena, for it would follow that what was just stated is a fault. It does not exist as the essence of a phenomenon in an ultimate sense, because no essence of a phenomenon is established. It would follow that it is merely conditioned, like the essence of a phenomenon. Therefore, because it exists in phenomena rather than being non-existent, it becomes an essence that is not suchness. It would follow that it is realized by everyone just as the essence of the nature of phenomena is. It is also difficult to avoid the consequence that it would be the cause of defilement. For that very reason, in the *Sūtra Unraveling the Intent* and those others, it is said that suchness is not a thing other than the phenomenon. Therefore, it is said, "In an ultimate sense, it is not even a phenomenon, nor is it that there is no phenomenon." By this, the essence of negating phenomena, non-phenomena, existence, non-existence, and so forth is taught. By this, the overcoming of distraction is also taught. By all of this, the profundity of this position is also taught. If the Bhagavan had not perfectly awakened or taught any phenomenon, then, considering how a bodhisattva who desires to attain the dharmakāya, which has merit as its cause, should engage in grasping the holy Dharma, he generates the aspiration to attain the dharmakāya, which has merit as its cause.

[3-71] translation already produced for this document:
Even if all phenomena are ungraspable and inexpressible, one might think that because they possess their own intrinsic characteristics, the essence of phenomena must exist in an ultimate sense. To this, the response "that is not even a phenomenon" is offered. This is because it is impossible for all phenomena, in an ultimate sense, to possess an intrinsic characteristic that is by nature beyond suffering. If that were the case, one might think that the Bhagavan had perfectly awakened to nothingness; to this, the response "it is not that there is no phenomenon" is offered. This is the essence of the negation of non-existence. By this, the meditative equipoise of the yogi is indicated, and the extremes of superimposition and deprecation are also negated. The question "Why is that?" is asked here to request the reasoning, and the reply is given that it is because it is distinguished by the unconditioned. The unconditioned is the ultimate nature of phenomena. When analyzed through reasoning, it abides solely in the characteristic of non-arising, just as was analyzed previously. As the Bhagavan explained in the *Sūtra of the True Gathering of the Buddha*: "Ānanda, that which is the non-arising, non-ceasing, non-abiding, and non-changing of phenomena is called the noble truth."

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་ནི་གསེར་དང་། དངུལ་དང་། ཤེལ་དང་། བཻ་ཌཱུརྱ་དང་། རྡོའི་སྙིང་པོ་དང་། སྤུག་དང་། མུ་ཏིག་དམར་པོའོ། །འཕགས་པ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་པདྨ་དཀར་པོ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་སོ། །གླིང་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟོང་ལ་སྟོང་གི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སོ། །དེ་སྟོང་ལ་སྟོང་གཉིས་སོ། །
translation: "Subhūti, what do you think?"—this is what was spoken. Regarding that, the seven precious substances are gold, silver, crystal, beryl, emerald, carnelian, and red pearl. These are those that appear in the *Ārya-saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*. A "thousand-fold world system" is one that includes the four continents and so forth. A "two-thousand-fold world system" is a thousand of those.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: A "three-thousand-fold great thousand-fold world system" is a thousand of those. The phrase "from that basis" means that this merit arises from that basis of giving precious substances; it is an expression meaning "arising from that cause." Merit is all virtuous intention and the habitual tendencies produced by it; the mass of that is the accumulation. Because the result is abundant, it is also "abundant." The word "abundantly" is a specification. By saying "abundant" twice, it is stated as "very abundant."

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If, in the ultimate sense, all things are unborn, how could the mass of merit arise from that basis? Thinking this, he asks, "For what reason?" and, understanding his own intention, he replies by saying, "Because there is no mass." The phrase "in the ultimate sense" is what remains to be understood. Because the masses are merely imputed, there is no mass of merit that has become a substantial entity. Merit itself is also merely imputed based on the distinction of states in the nature of habitual tendencies. A bodhisattva is also merely an imputed existence, because, since things are without movement, he does not engage through the mode of mental construction. Even if one examines them individually in terms of being one or many, they are merely of a deceptive nature. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is no mass of merit. By this, the meditative equipoise of the yogin is fully indicated. The extreme of superimposition is also refuted.

[3-75] translation already produced for this document:
If, in the ultimate sense, all things are unborn, how could the mass of merit arise from that basis? Thinking this, he asks, "For what reason?" and, understanding his own intention, he replies by saying, "Because there is no mass." The phrase "in the ultimate sense" is what remains to be understood. Because the masses are merely imputed, there is no mass of merit that has become a substantial entity. Merit itself is also merely imputed based on the distinction of states in the nature of habitual tendencies. A bodhisattva is also merely an imputed existence, because, since things are without movement, he does not engage through the mode of mental construction. Even if one examines them individually in terms of being one or many, they are merely of a deceptive nature. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is no mass of merit. By this, the meditative equipoise of the yogin is fully indicated. The extreme of superimposition is also refuted.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: By this, it is taught that since the dharmakāya realized by the Tathāgatas necessarily arises from the dharmakāya that is explained as having merit as its cause, if even just a four-line verse from that is taught, it becomes a source of merit; what need is there to speak of the dharmakāya realized by the Tathāgatas that has merit as its cause? Although this lacks a literal meaning, there is no fault in this, as it is understood through implication. Therefore, even if in the ultimate sense there is no teaching of Dharma or attainment of perfect buddhahood, because in conventional terms there is a teaching of the body of merit, the intention is that a bodhisattva should engage in the path with the thought of attaining merit. By teaching that merit is excellent, this indicates the vastness of this [practice]. It also indicates the aspiration to generate it and the making of prayers. Because there is also a six-line root verse, it is specified as a "four-line" verse. The term "verse" here does not refer to effort, but rather, from the mere words, the words of the four-line root verse are also grasped. "Having grasped" means having recited them. "To explain" refers to the words. "To teach correctly" refers to the meaning. "Countless" means because they are extremely numerous. "Immeasurable" means because they are not objects of comparison. By this, in terms of meaning, it thoroughly eliminates the opposing side that does not generate merit. By mentioning merely the name "merit," it indicates the entire collection of merit of the Tathāgata.

source: འདི་ཅི་ཡིད་ཆེས་པར་བྱ་བར་ཟད་དམ། འོན་ཏེ་རིགས་པས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡང་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འདིར་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ནི་འདི་ལས་བྱུང་སྟེ་ཞེས་རིགས་པ་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཏོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡང་འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་བསོད་ནམས་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་ལ་ལུས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་བསོད་ནམས་དེ་ནི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འཁོར་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཕལ་པ་འཐོབ་སྟེ། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོའི་འབྲས་བུ་འཐོབ་ཀྱི་དེ་དག་ཉི་ཚེས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གོ་འཕང་དཔེ་མེད་ཅིང་ཟད་མི་ཤེས་པ་ཐོབ་པས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་མི་མངོན། ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཀྱིས་ཕན་བཏགས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་གཞན་ལ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་གཞན་དག་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན་པའི་རིམ་གྱིས་ཆོས་འདི་ལས་མྱུར་བ་ཁོ་ནར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་འཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་རྣམས་ལས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གཞན་དག་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པའི་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པས་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྦྱིན་པ་ལས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྦྱིན་པ་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་སོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལས་འབྱུང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་གྲུབ་པ་སྟེ། སྤྱད་པ་བཅུ་རྣམས་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེའི་འོག་ཏུ་གཅིག་ནས་གཅིག་ཏུ་བརྒྱུད་དེ་ཐོབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སྤྱད་པ་བཅུ་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཡི་གེར་འདྲི་བ་དང་། མཆོད་པ་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ་དང་། བཀླག་པ་དང་། མཉན་པ་དང་། གཟུང་བ་དང་། ལུང་ཕོག་པ་དང་། ཁ་ཏོན་དུ་བྱ་བ་དང་། བསམ་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་པའོ། །
translation: Is this merely to be believed, or is it also to be understood through reasoning? Thinking thus, and having asked, "For what reason?", the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, here taught the reasoning, saying, "Subhūti, the unexcelled, perfectly complete enlightenment of the Buddhas arises from this." The thought that "merit is great" refers to the fact that it is great because of its great fruit; it is not great in its own essence, because it lacks a body. Merit arising from precious substances attains only ordinary fruits of cyclic existence, such as great wealth and the like; but if seized by prajñāpāramitā, one attains the fruit of great enlightenment, such as generosity and the like, and these are not merely temporary. Since the gift of the Dharma attains the incomparable and inexhaustible rank of the Tathāgata, why would it not be manifest as great? Just as the Dharma is beneficial, precious substances do not benefit others to the same extent; for in this way, through the sequence of teaching others, one attains the rank of Buddhahood more quickly from this Dharma than from precious substances. Therefore, it is intended that the gift of the Dharma is superior to the gift of precious substances because it is the supreme way of benefiting others. The phrase "arises from this" means that it is perfectly established; it is the implication that, relying upon the ten practices, one attains it subsequently through a continuous succession. Those ten practices are: writing down, making offerings, giving, reading, listening, grasping, teaching, reciting, reflecting, and meditating.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If, in the ultimate sense, all phenomena are indeed unborn, then at that time all the qualities of a Buddha would also be unborn; so how could this unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment arise from them? Thinking that the Buddhas are not distinct from enlightenment, and having asked, "For what reason?", the response given here is the phrase "the qualities of a Buddha." The qualities of a Buddha are those phenomena characterized by unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment and so forth, which serve as the cause for designating a Buddha. Therefore, although in the ultimate sense the Buddhas are not distinct from enlightenment, the intention is that because they serve as the cause for that designation, it is taught that the Buddhas are born from this. Since those too are unborn in the ultimate sense, even though the qualities of a Buddha do not exist, in dependence upon the conventional, the Tathāgatas have taught that the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment of the Tathāgatas arises from this, and so forth; in the ultimate sense, however, it is not so.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: For that very reason, the intention is that the "qualities of a Buddha" cannot be expressed in the ultimate sense from this or that other perspective, because they are to be known by each individual for themselves and are therefore inexpressible. By this, meditative equipoise and the overcoming of distraction are indicated, and profundity is also indicated. Here, some might say: "Since there is no distinction in the Dharmakāya, how can these three types of distinct bodies exist? Or, if one attains the Dharmakāya, and because it is the natural outflow of the Dharmakāya, are the nature of merit and the nature of teaching not called 'Dharmakāya' by way of imputation?" If they say this, then they would claim that the Rūpakāya also becomes the Dharmakāya, because it is the natural outflow of attaining it and is the cause for attaining it. That is not true; the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the Bhagavats, is established as the nature of perfectly pure primordial wisdom and whatever is its general reality. This is not a distinction of its ripening, nor is it the case that "Dharma" is taught here by imputing it upon teachings and merits. If so, what is it like? It is the entity itself; it teaches the Dharma. This is because it is renowned as such by itself, as in the phrase "the Dharma is gathered," and so forth.

If, in the ultimate sense, all phenomena are indeed unborn, then at that time all the qualities of a Buddha would also be unborn; so how could this unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment arise from them? Thinking that the Buddhas are not distinct from enlightenment, and having asked, "For what reason?", the response given here is the phrase "the qualities of a Buddha." The qualities of a Buddha are those phenomena characterized by unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment and so forth, which serve as the cause for designating a Buddha. Therefore, although in the ultimate sense the Buddhas are not distinct from enlightenment, the intention is that because they serve as the cause for that designation, it is taught that the Buddhas are born from this. Since those too are unborn in the ultimate sense, even though the qualities of a Buddha do not exist, in dependence upon the conventional, the Tathāgatas have taught that the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment of the Tathāgatas arises from this, and so forth; in the ultimate sense, however, it is not so.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: That which is taught as "dharmas" by grasping their own and general characteristics is common to all entities, and thus the Rūpakāya is not taught as the Tathāgata, for it is not that which makes [one] know [the ultimate]. Even if it were taught by way of imputation, the Rūpakāya would not result in the Dharmakāya, for it is the natural outflow of merit. As it is said: "In brief, the Jina's Dharmakāya arises from the accumulation of wisdom, while the Rūpakāya of the Buddhas arises from the accumulation of merit." Therefore, because only the accumulation of wisdom is the cause for attaining it, it is impossible for the Rūpakāya to attain it; since there is no cause for imputing it as such, one does not call the Rūpakāya the Dharmakāya. The "teaching body" is the fruit of authentic primordial wisdom, and since the nature of the accumulation of merit is also the cause for attaining it, it is logical that it is taught as the "accumulation of Dharma" by way of imputation; thus, there is no need for more. Other inferior objections have not been written down for fear of excessive words, thinking that those possessed of wisdom will distinguish for themselves whether they are logical or illogical. The explanation of the place of aspiring to attain the Dharmakāya is finished.

For that very reason, the intention is that the "qualities of a Buddha" cannot be expressed in the ultimate sense from this or that other perspective, because they are to be known by each individual for themselves and are therefore inexpressible. By this, meditative equipoise and the overcoming of distraction are indicated, and profundity is also indicated. Here, some might say: "Since there is no distinction in the Dharmakāya, how can these three types of distinct bodies exist? Or, if one attains the Dharmakāya, and because it is the natural outflow of the Dharmakāya, are the nature of merit and the nature of teaching not called 'Dharmakāya' by way of imputation?" If they say this, then they would claim that the Rūpakāya also becomes the Dharmakāya, because it is the natural outflow of attaining it and is the cause for attaining it. That is not true; the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the Bhagavats, is established as the nature of perfectly pure primordial wisdom and whatever is its general reality. This is not a distinction of its ripening, nor is it the case that "Dharma" is taught here by imputing it upon teachings and merits. If so, what is it like? It is the entity itself; it teaches the Dharma. This is because it is renowned as such by itself, as in the phrase "the Dharma is gathered," and so forth.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: From this point forward, the twelve locations should be understood as the antidotes to the twelve types of discordance, in their respective order. These twelve types of discordance are: manifest pride; having little learning even without manifest pride; having much learning but meditating while focusing on a small object; meditating while focusing on an object that is not small but neglecting sentient beings; not neglecting them but becoming attached to and engaging with external treatises; not engaging in that but lacking skill in means to suppress the signs of entities; having skill in means but not accumulating the accumulation of merit; accumulating the accumulation of merit but experiencing alms through laziness, gain, and honor; not experiencing them but being unable to endure suffering; being indifferent to suffering but not accumulating the accumulation of wisdom; accumulating the accumulation of wisdom but strongly grasping at a self; and not strongly grasping at a self but lacking oral instructions. Regarding this, although the Tathāgata has extensively taught the selflessness of persons and phenomena, due to the power of having firmly accumulated the manifest attachment to a self since beginningless time, one thinks: "If one who engages in the perception of 'sentient beings' and so forth is not called a bodhisattva, then how is it that the Tathāgata said, 'At that time, in that period, I was the king named Dīpaṃkara'?"

གང་ཡང་རང་དང་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་འཛིན་པས་ཆོས་རྣམས་སོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པ་དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་ཐུན་མོང་ཡིན་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་མ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བཏགས་ནས་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་ཐལ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱིས་རྒྱུ་མཐུན་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། མདོར་ན་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཆོས་སྐུ་ནི། །ཡེ་ཤེས་ཚོགས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་སྟེ། །སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་ནི། །བསོད་ནམས་ཚོགས་ལས་བྱུང་བའོ། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུས་ནི་དེ་འཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མི་སྲིད་དེ། དེའི་གདགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མེད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ། །བཤད་པའི་སྐུ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་ལ། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དེ་འཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པས་བཏགས་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བསྟན་པར་རིགས་པ་ཉིད་དེ་མང་དུ་ནི་མི་དགོས་སོ། །ཀླན་ཀ་ངན་པ་གཞན་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅན་དག་གིས་རིགས་སམ་མི་རིགས་འབྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་གྲང་སྙམ་དུ་སྟེ་ཚིག་མངས་ཀྱིས་དོགས་ནས་མ་བྲིས་སོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་གནས་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །
[3-82] translation already produced for this document:
That which is taught as "dharmas" by grasping their own and general characteristics is common to all entities, and thus the Rūpakāya is not taught as the Tathāgata, for it is not that which makes [one] know [the ultimate]. Even if it were taught by way of imputation, the Rūpakāya would not result in the Dharmakāya, for it is the natural outflow of merit. As it is said: "In brief, the Jina's Dharmakāya arises from the accumulation of wisdom, while the Rūpakāya of the Buddhas arises from the accumulation of merit." Therefore, because only the accumulation of wisdom is the cause for attaining it, it is impossible for the Rūpakāya to attain it; since there is no cause for imputing it as such, one does not call the Rūpakāya the Dharmakāya. The "teaching body" is the fruit of authentic primordial wisdom, and since the nature of the accumulation of merit is also the cause for attaining it, it is logical that it is taught as the "accumulation of Dharma" by way of imputation; thus, there is no need for more. Other inferior objections have not been written down for fear of excessive words, thinking that those possessed of wisdom will distinguish for themselves whether they are logical or illogical. The explanation of the place of aspiring to attain the Dharmakāya is finished.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "I shall teach the Dharma to you all," and so forth, will follow. The absence of the perception of sentient beings and so forth—the thought that "I shall not think in that way"—is because one is free from the pride that has become an obstacle; thus, focusing on the fifth stage, he spoke, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The external meaning here is this: even those who have attained the final śrāvaka stage, such as the srota-āpanna, who have not attained nirvāṇa because they have realized the selflessness of phenomena—if they have no attachment to "I" and "mine," then it goes without saying that those who have realized both types of selflessness and have abandoned all obscurations without remainder [are free from such attachment]. The phrase "At that time, I..." and so forth is intended for those who wish to understand the meaning of establishing worldly conventions; it is merely a negation in the continuum of another, similar to the conventions of "army" or "forest," and is not an attachment to a singular or permanent entity. Those who abide in the wisdom of suchness are unable to express conventions together with the world. Therefore, because one is free from the pride that has become an obstacle, one is caused to hold correctly that "you also should not cling to a self." In this context, the characteristic of the path that does not see the going to the great city of nirvāṇa is the "stream" (srota). "Entered" (āpanna) means attained; one who has abandoned all defilements to be abandoned by seeing is called a srota-āpanna. Furthermore, by abandoning attachment to the agent, the action, and the instrument, this demonstrates the realization of selflessness, as it is only by realizing this much that the condition is understood. "Of self" refers to attachment to the agent. "Fruit" refers to attachment to the action. "Attained" refers to attachment to the instrument. By this, it is shown in terms of meaning that the discordant side is the thought, "I have attained."
