heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The noble Subhūti also, by expressing the intention of the Tathāgata, established the ultimate truth and, in order to lead [others] to enter into the meditative equipoise of yoga, petitioned, "Tathāgata, he has not entered into anything at all." Regarding the thought of why this is, he petitioned, "He has not entered into form," and so forth. By this, it is demonstrated that in the ultimate sense, there is no fruit of either of the two types to be attained. In this way, if the essence of what is to be attained were to become a fruit, would it be conditioned or unconditioned? Regarding that, for the time being, the unconditioned is merely that which has not arisen; because it does not exist, it is like the horns of a rabbit, and it is not reasonable for it to be attained, as there is no difference between it and the state of not having been attained. The conditioned is momentary and perishes immediately upon arising; because it does not abide, it cannot be attained by anyone in any way. It is merely said that one "attains the fruit" when the causal conditions for the characteristics of the path of selflessness have approached in a continuum, and the result—the characteristic of a state that is completely incompatible with the arising of defilements—has come into being; but in the ultimate sense, this is not the case. In this way, could the entity to be attained and the entity that attains it exist at different times or at the same time? For the time being, the first alternative is not the case, because both must exist; if the times are different, when one has approached, the other does not exist, so how could both exist? It is also not the case that they are at the same time, because once both have been established, there is no mutual benefit between them.

[3-85] translation already produced for this document:
The statement that a Srotaāpanna does not think, "I have attained [the fruit of a Srotaāpanna]," fully demonstrates the abandonment of all manifest pride by merely expressing a sign. It also demonstrates the aspiration and the making of prayers regarding that.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If there is no benefit, then the entity that is to be attained and the entity that attains it cannot be logically established, for that would lead to an absurd overextension. It is also not logical for the entity to be attained and the entity that attains it to be connected simultaneously by the characteristic of producing a mutual relationship. This is because, for one thing, those entities that lack a body do not reside in a location, and thus there is no mutual relationship. Furthermore, they do not become the entity to be attained and the entity that attains it merely by being simultaneous, for that would lead to an absurd overextension. It is also not from a single cause alone, for that is common to both, and thus it would not be certain which is the entity to be attained and which is the entity that attains it. Those that do have a body, if they were to be connected in their entirety, would result in being one; if they were connected by only a part, it would result in having limbs. Attainment does not occur from residing without an interval either, for that is common to both, and since there is no distinction, there is no certainty. Therefore, this is merely something imputed by conceptualization. By this, one should clearly understand all the conventional terminology such as the agent and the action. The term "dharmas" refers to the *dharma-āyatana*. This also includes the unconditioned, because the *dharma-āyatana* is of the nature of seven substances. The remainder, such as form and a portion of the *dharma-āyatana*, indicates the conditioned. This is an illustration; therefore, the eye and so forth should also be understood.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If he were to become attached in that way, thinking, "I have attained it," then why would he not be called a "Stream-enterer"? Regarding this, he asked, "Blessed One, if..." and so forth. Whoever becomes attached, thinking, "I have attained it," has not abandoned the view of a self. One who has not abandoned the view of a self has not given rise to the noble path. One who has not given rise to the noble path is an ordinary person; therefore, how could he be a Stream-enterer? This is the intention. In this way, whoever is attached, thinking, "I have attained it," is one in whom the view of a self arises. By this, the firm grasping of the mind is indicated. By all of this, the profundity of this point is expressed.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The statement, "There is not any dharma whatsoever called an Arhat," means that because this designation is applied to the continuum of wisdom that has abandoned such types of afflictive obscurations, and because the continuum itself is merely a conventional existence, in the ultimate sense, there is nothing there at all, for it is a superimposition. Now, the Noble Subhūti, because he himself is the witness and in order to make his words worthy of being accepted, speaks of himself by way of the special quality of "abiding without afflictions" and the common quality of being an Arhat, and in order to demonstrate the state of having perfectly restrained the mind, he makes the request beginning with "I." "Abiding without afflictions" refers to a specific type of meditative absorption. This means that an Arhat who is liberated in both ways, having focused on the self, thinks, "It is not appropriate for afflictions to arise in others," and thus enters into meditative equipoise; and having emerged from that, he focuses on those others so that afflictions do not arise in them. Those who possess the disposition of abiding in that "absence of afflictions" are spoken of in that way. This distinction is a joyful one. The statement, "I have not taught," means that at that time, because the view of a self has not been abandoned, it is difficult for me to even attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, so there is no need to even mention the "abiding without afflictions" that is to be attained by an Arhat who is liberated in both ways. Regarding the thought of how to abide without afflictions, he makes the request, "Abiding in nothing whatsoever." The intended meaning is that because of the mental attachment of thinking, "I have attained some fruit, whether conditioned or unconditioned," one who does not abide in that way is what is meant in some quarters by "abiding without afflictions," and it is not anything else.

heading: མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐོས་པ་ཉུང་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If there is nothing at all to be attained in the ultimate sense, and nothing that attains it, then how did the Bhagavan, having become a Bodhisattva, receive the Dharma from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? If he did not receive it, then why, at that time, should those of us who desire to receive the Dharma seek to please the Tathāgata when he appears? Thinking in this way, those who have come to such a realization, because they are free from the obstacles of having heard little, and with the sixth stage in mind, the Tathāgata spoke the words: "Do you think that there is any Dharma that the Tathāgata, Arhat, perfectly awakened Buddha received from Dīpaṃkara?" Subhūti, also holding to the previous intention, replied, "That does not exist." As previously explained, there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been received by way of an entity that is to be attained or an entity that attains in the ultimate sense. This is also because all phenomena are by nature peaceful. Nevertheless, due to the power of the Tathāgata, the mere arising of a consciousness that perceives a variety of verbal aggregates and so forth is designated as "receiving," and thus the pursuit of hearing is fruitful. In essence, this means that when a Bodhisattva is in the process of seeking to hear, he should please the Buddha who has appeared. Following that, it points out that the attachment of thinking, "I shall receive the Buddha's teachings," is a discordant factor, and it also shows that one should abide in aspiration and prayer to abandon that. By stating, "Was any Dharma received from Dīpaṃkara?" as a mere aspect, it turns back all signs of receiving a Dharma. By the statement, "That Dharma which was received does not exist," it establishes that the ultimate reality of phenomena cannot be grasped, and it also shows how to enter into meditative equipoise and how to overcome distraction regarding that. The profundity of this point is also expressed.

[3-93] source:
ད་ནི་བདག་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པར་གནས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-93] translation already produced for this document:
Now, I have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, as the foremost among those who dwell without defilements.

[3-94] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ལགས་ཀྱང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། འོ་ན་ཇི་ལྟ་ཞེ་ན། ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་ནི་བདག་གིས་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །
[3-94] translation already produced for this document:
The statement, "Bhagavan, even though I am an Arhat free from attachment," is not due to an attachment to a self. If one asks, "How is that?" it is due to an attachment to mere conventional designation, and that has already been explained by me previously.

heading: ཐོས་པ་མང་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If action and the agent and so forth do not exist in the ultimate sense, then at that time, in order to accomplish the complete purification of the buddha-fields, how should a bodhisattva think to make a vow? Because those who think in this way are free from the obstacles of meditating on inferior objects of focus, the text, taking the seventh stage as its basis, states, "Whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. "Untrue" means false. If that is the case, then how does the Bhagavan think about how he has spoken of the various perfect purifications of the buddha-fields of the bodhisattvas? And in response to the question, "For what reason?" he spoke of "the arrays of the fields" and so forth. "Many fields" refers to the arrays of the fields. "Without those arrays" means that in the ultimate sense, there is no entity of a composite whole, nor is there any array composed of accumulated atoms.

heading: ཐོས་པ་མང་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Those arrays certainly do not exist; however, just as the arrays of fields perceived in a dream exist conventionally as mere delights when not examined, it is taught that they exist conventionally. For that very reason, it is said, "the arrays of the fields." If it were not so, the intention would be that the ultimate nature is inexpressible and thus would not be expressed. Although "not abiding" was explained above, for the sake of benefiting those who are forgetful, and in order to bring it to mind by way of a summary, it is said, "therefore," and so forth. "In this way" means that because no entity is established in the manner previously mentioned, one should generate the mind without abiding in it; this is the intended meaning. The remainder is as before. By saying, "that is speaking falsely," this indicates, in terms of the meaning, the opposing side of the mental attachment that thinks, "I will accomplish the arrays of the fields in the ultimate sense." By mentioning "the arrays of the fields" as mere signs, it completely indicates being free from all meditations that focus on inferior objects of focus. It also indicates the aspiration and the making of vows for the sake of meditating on inferior objects of focus. By saying, "the Tathāgata has spoken of those arrays as non-existent," this indicates the profound, by leading one into meditative equipoise through the establishment of the ultimate.

heading: ཐོས་པ་མང་ཡང་དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་བསྟན་པ།

Those arrays certainly do not exist; however, just as the arrays of fields perceived in a dream exist conventionally as mere delights when not examined, it is taught that they exist conventionally. For that very reason, it is said, "the arrays of the fields." If it were not so, the intention would be that the ultimate nature is inexpressible and thus would not be expressed. Although "not abiding" was explained above, for the sake of benefiting those who are forgetful, and in order to bring it to mind by way of a summary, it is said, "therefore," and so forth. "In this way" means that because no entity is established in the manner previously mentioned, one should generate the mind without abiding in it; this is the intended meaning. The remainder is as before. By saying, "that is speaking falsely," this indicates, in terms of the meaning, the opposing side of the mental attachment that thinks, "I will accomplish the arrays of the fields in the ultimate sense." By mentioning "the arrays of the fields" as mere signs, it completely indicates being free from all meditations that focus on inferior objects of focus. It also indicates the aspiration and the making of vows for the sake of meditating on inferior objects of focus. By saying, "the Tathāgata has spoken of those arrays as non-existent," this indicates the profound, by leading one into meditative equipoise through the establishment of the ultimate.

heading: དམིགས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ་བསྒོམས་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་འདོར་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Even if it is accepted that sentient beings are not separate from the aggregates, is it not the case that there exists something that is not distinct? Otherwise, if one thinks, "How should a Bodhisattva proceed in order to bring sentient beings to full maturity?" that thought would become an obstacle, characterized by the abandonment of sentient beings. In order to dispel this, and focusing on the eighth position, the Blessed One spoke the words, "For example." The phrase "a person" refers to the lord of the asuras, Rāhu; his body in the desire realm is the size of Mount Meru. Even though it is vast, it is without essence, and thus it is "great." Wishing to express the intention behind why the Blessed One taught this, he asked, "Why is that?" and in order to express that very intention, he stated, "It is not a thing." In the ultimate sense, because it is devoid of the nature of being one or many, it is indeed without intrinsic nature; just like the body dreamt of in a dream, the Tathāgata spoke of it as being conventional, not ultimate. Therefore, the phrase "is called a body" is a statement of what is acceptable here. The intention is that this is merely conventional, and that is why it is called so; if it were not so, it would not be spoken of in that way, because in the ultimate sense, no phenomenon is established. In order to refute those, such as the Rgyal-dpog-pa, who claim that what does not exist is a thing, he stated, "Because it is not a thing." Since "not a thing" is characterized by the absence of things, how could it not be of a nature that is inconsistent with them? Therefore, it is called a body. If it were not so, since no body is established in the ultimate sense, what would be meant by the term "body" here? Therefore, by teaching that it is not a thing, this is fully demonstrated: even though the size of the body is that of Mount Meru, when it is ultimately without intrinsic nature and thus not one's own body, how could the bodies of others be possessed of intrinsic nature or possessed of a self? In this context, the effort to bring sentient beings to full maturity by a Bodhisattva is shown to be a discordant factor if one is ultimately attached to sentient beings as real; the aspiration to abandon that and the making of a vow are also taught. The phrase "a person" is mentioned merely as a sign, indicating all the various and distinct bodies, such as those born from eggs and so forth.

translation: Sublimity is what is known in the world as being extremely rare, which is what is taught by the statement, "Filled to the brim with the seven types of precious substances." The field is superior because it possesses the perfection of the welfare of self and others. Regarding that, the perfection of the welfare of others is because it teaches without error the things to be abandoned and the things to be adopted, which is what is taught by the statement, "By the Tathāgata." Because he speaks of the suchness of things exactly as it is, in terms of etymology, he is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-gone/Thus-spoken). The perfection of the welfare of self is of two types, due to the distinction between the perfection of primordial wisdom and the perfection of abandonment. Regarding that, the term "Arhat" indicates the perfection of abandonment, for in terms of etymology, one is called an "Arhat" because one has vanquished the enemy of the defilements.

translation: The term "Samyaksambuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One) indicates the perfection of primordial wisdom. Therefore, the general summary of the meaning is that the three terms mentioned include the result. The phrase "should be resolved" means to desire; "one should generate resolution" and "one should understand" mean that one should realize, which is a synonym for generating prajñā. In this, the former is the result of the latter, or alternatively, the latter is the explanation of the former. "Explanation" refers to the verbal expression. "Incalculable" means that its power cannot be estimated or that it is incomparable. "Recite" means that one personally performs the verbal recitation of the text. "Teach" means to correctly show the meaning of the words to others. Alternatively, "recite" is the words, and "teach" is the meaning. "Becomes a stūpa" means that it is worthy of being honored. It is that which has become a stūpa itself, just as one says "has become under one's control."

Sublimity is what is known in the world as being extremely rare, which is what is taught by the statement, "Filled to the brim with the seven types of precious substances." The field is superior because it possesses the perfection of the welfare of self and others. Regarding that, the perfection of the welfare of others is because it teaches without error the things to be abandoned and the things to be adopted, which is what is taught by the statement, "By the Tathāgata." Because he speaks of the suchness of things exactly as it is, in terms of etymology, he is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-gone/Thus-spoken). The perfection of the welfare of self is of two types, due to the distinction between the perfection of primordial wisdom and the perfection of abandonment. Regarding that, the term "Arhat" indicates the perfection of abandonment, for in terms of etymology, one is called an "Arhat" because one has vanquished the enemy of the defilements.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The intention is that if one becomes a stūpa even by teaching a verse merely on the selflessness of the person, then it goes without saying that this applies if one teaches both types of selflessness. "Taking" refers to the words. "Holding" means not forgetting. "Reading" means having made it into a book. "Comprehending" refers to the meaning. By this, it is indicated that one holds it through the prajñā that arises from hearing. Because one also holds it through reflection and the prajñā of reflection, the phrase "in accordance with reality" is stated, which is a synonym for understanding the meaning without error. In some versions, only the word "holding" appears; in that case, "holding" should be viewed as referring to both the words and the meaning. "Most wondrous" is because such profound and extensive Dharma is understood. "The Teacher resides" refers to the Dharma preacher, for because they perform the activity of the Teacher, it is a synonym for saying that the Tathāgata, the Bhagavan, is present in person. "Any such as a Guru" refers to anyone such as the Ārya Mañjuśrī and so forth; one should view that Dharma preacher as residing there in order to accomplish his activity.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In some versions, the two words "other" and "others" appear; this is an enumeration of anyone such as a Guru, because it indicates that they reside there. By all of this, the extensiveness of this place is indicated. In terms of meaning, it indicates that abandoning the holding of the holy Dharma and becoming attached to external treatises is a discordant factor; it shows the aspiration and the dedication to abandon attachment to those and to strive in the Dharma. The phrase "from this enumeration of Dharma" mentions only the sign, thereby abandoning attachment to external treatises and fully indicating that one should strive in all holy Dharma. Because this enumeration of Dharma possesses inconceivable power, and because it is stated that merit arises for sentient beings even by merely hearing its name for the sake of benefiting others, the Ārya Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this?"

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Prajñāpāramitā" is the name given to that which is so named. Because it is both wisdom and it realizes and fully determines the further shore, it is "prajñāpāramitā." This is a compound [meaning] that it is both wisdom and it is the further shore. Alternatively, the "further shore of wisdom" is the further shore of wisdom, and because it realizes and fully determines that, it is so named. That also implicitly refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which possesses the excellence of all aspects, for by other wisdom, the further shore cannot be measured. Alternatively, "prajñāpāramitā" means that one has arrived; this is the very meaning of the term. That is wisdom exactly as stated, for it is impossible for others to go to its further shore. By this, the pāramitā of generosity and so forth are also explained. Because it will be expressed, this enumeration of Dharma is also so named, just as poetic compositions are constructed such as "the shore found, not taken away," and so on.

In some versions, the two words "other" and "others" appear; this is an enumeration of anyone such as a Guru, because it indicates that they reside there. By all of this, the extensiveness of this place is indicated. In terms of meaning, it indicates that abandoning the holding of the holy Dharma and becoming attached to external treatises is a discordant factor; it shows the aspiration and the dedication to abandon attachment to those and to strive in the Dharma. The phrase "from this enumeration of Dharma" mentions only the sign, thereby abandoning attachment to external treatises and fully indicating that one should strive in all holy Dharma. Because this enumeration of Dharma possesses inconceivable power, and because it is stated that merit arises for sentient beings even by merely hearing its name for the sake of benefiting others, the Ārya Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this?"

The phrase "How should this be held?" fully indicates that by holding it, one also comes to possess immeasurable merit.

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡལ་བར་མི་འདོར་ཡང་ཕྱིའི་བསྟན་བཅོས་་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་ཏེ་འཇུག་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thinking that the Blessed One, because it is to be realized individually by each person and is therefore non-shared, and because it is also unborn in the ultimate sense, cannot be expressed by words, [Subhūti] inquired, "For what reason?" and in response, the Tathāgata spoke the words, "Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the prajñāpāramitā." Although it cannot be expressed by words because it is to be realized individually in the ultimate sense and is therefore non-shared, and because all phenomena are in the ultimate sense completely unborn, nevertheless, one superimposes [a name] externally upon the nature of the image of conceptualization; and since that conceptualization is itself erroneous by nature, the form that is superimposed by it is also false. Therefore, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of and made intelligible through words as the prajñāpāramitā, which has become an image of conceptualization, is itself not the [true] pāramitā; it is not the Tathāgata’s wisdom, for that [true wisdom] has reached the further shore of the knowable in terms of conventional truth. If it were not so, how could the Blessed One be omniscient? This is because the one who realizes, being erroneous, does not understand that it and the image of conceptualization are distinct. Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata has spoken of that very wisdom in the ultimate sense as the essence of knowing. Therefore, he intended that there is no contradiction in such a teaching. Alternatively, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the essence of realizing what is the Tathāgata’s wisdom is itself non-existent in the ultimate sense, for in the ultimate sense, there is no going to the further shore. The word "itself" should be viewed as being placed after the phrase "there is no pāramitā." By this, he has fully indicated how one should practice by establishing it in the ultimate sense and entering into meditative equipoise upon it.

"Prajñāpāramitā" is the name given to that which is so named. Because it is both wisdom and it realizes and fully determines the further shore, it is "prajñāpāramitā." This is a compound [meaning] that it is both wisdom and it is the further shore. Alternatively, the "further shore of wisdom" is the further shore of wisdom, and because it realizes and fully determines that, it is so named. That also implicitly refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which possesses the excellence of all aspects, for by other wisdom, the further shore cannot be measured. Alternatively, "prajñāpāramitā" means that one has arrived; this is the very meaning of the term. That is wisdom exactly as stated, for it is impossible for others to go to its further shore. By this, the pāramitā of generosity and so forth are also explained. Because it will be expressed, this enumeration of Dharma is also so named, just as poetic compositions are constructed such as "the shore found, not taken away," and so on.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Although the selflessness of all phenomena has already been taught extensively in this way, those who are beginners—thinking, "How should one meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena?"—lack the skillful means to suppress the marks of entities. Therefore, focusing on the tenth stage, he says, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. This teaches that one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena by realizing, through two types of means, that they are devoid of the nature of being one or many. The two types of means are the means of thinning out and the means of making them appear as non-existent. Regarding this, the phrase "as many as the atoms" teaches the means of thinning out, for if one realizes that they are devoid of a singular nature, then this world system is not correctly viewed as a single entity, because it possesses clear phenomena such as the obscured and the unobscured. Therefore, if one breaks it down into many, one must accept that the atoms are broken down. For this reason, it teaches that if one meditates on the atoms, one will abandon the notion of singularity.

Although the selflessness of all phenomena has already been taught extensively in this way, those who are beginners—thinking, "How should one meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena?"—lack the skillful means to suppress the marks of entities. Therefore, focusing on the tenth stage, he says, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. This teaches that one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena by realizing, through two types of means, that they are devoid of the nature of being one or many. The two types of means are the means of thinning out and the means of making them appear as non-existent. Regarding this, the phrase "as many as the atoms" teaches the means of thinning out, for if one realizes that they are devoid of a singular nature, then this world system is not correctly viewed as a single entity, because it possesses clear phenomena such as the obscured and the unobscured. Therefore, if one breaks it down into many, one must accept that the atoms are broken down. For this reason, it teaches that if one meditates on the atoms, one will abandon the notion of singularity.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: This indicates the vastness. Since those atoms also do not exist, as they are not distinct due to the differentiation of their parts, one might wonder, "How can those atoms become many?" Based on the intention of such an objector, the question "Why?" is asked, and in response, the phrase "Whatever are the atoms of earth" is stated. That which is taught as the nature of atoms—because it is clear that one is grasping those many atoms as a single entity—is actually devoid of atoms; for in the ultimate sense, just like the nature of a magical illusion, they are devoid of atoms and are merely a nature imputed by the mind. This is taught merely as a means for grasping at singularity, but it is not so in the ultimate sense.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Therefore, the statement "they are called atoms of earth" is made because they exist conventionally according to reasoning. If it were not so, one might think that because they do not exist ultimately and because their own characteristics cannot be expressed, they would not be expressed at all. It is also not reasonable to teach them as conventionalities of expression, because their own nature is not apparent to others either. This indicates that the method for realizing that they are devoid of a nature of multiplicity is to make them appear as non-existent. In this way, by finally analyzing the atoms individually through reasoning and making them appear, one comes to realize that the world systems are devoid of a nature of multiplicity, and subsequently, one realizes that they are devoid of intrinsic nature.

[3-115] translation already produced for this document:
This indicates the vastness. Since those atoms also do not exist, as they are not distinct due to the differentiation of their parts, one might wonder, "How can those atoms become many?" Based on the intention of such an objector, the question "Why?" is asked, and in response, the phrase "Whatever are the atoms of earth" is stated. That which is taught as the nature of atoms—because it is clear that one is grasping those many atoms as a single entity—is actually devoid of atoms; for in the ultimate sense, just like the nature of a magical illusion, they are devoid of atoms and are merely a nature imputed by the mind. This is taught merely as a means for grasping at singularity, but it is not so in the ultimate sense.

heading: དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པ་ལ་ཐབས་མི་མཁས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: In this way, since the world of the receptacle is devoid of the nature of being one or many, it is stated that it is only devoid of intrinsic nature; and because the world of sentient beings is also stated, the question "What is the world system?" is asked. Here, "world system" refers to the world of sentient beings, for the other has already been explained. The statement "that world system is not a world system" is intended to mean that it is devoid of the nature of being one or many. In this regard, to begin with, that which is the form aggregate is explained by the world of the receptacle itself. The remaining four aggregates are as previously analyzed regarding how they do not possess the nature of being one or many. Because it is not so, yogins see all phenomena as being like an illusion, devoid of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense. This also expresses the profound. In terms of meaning, it fully indicates that the mental attachment to the world of the receptacle and sentient beings as real entities in the ultimate sense is the opposing side. In order to abandon that, the aspiration and the making of prayers are also taught; by merely mentioning the "great trichiliocosm world system" as a sign, it fully indicates that one should meditate on all entities as being devoid of intrinsic nature. The statements "those atoms are not atoms" and "that world system is not a world system" fully indicate how one should practice by entering into the meditative equipoise of this ultimate establishment.

Therefore, the statement "they are called atoms of earth" is made because they exist conventionally according to reasoning. If it were not so, one might think that because they do not exist ultimately and because their own characteristics cannot be expressed, they would not be expressed at all. It is also not reasonable to teach them as conventionalities of expression, because their own nature is not apparent to others either. This indicates that the method for realizing that they are devoid of a nature of multiplicity is to make them appear as non-existent. In this way, by finally analyzing the atoms individually through reasoning and making them appear, one comes to realize that the world systems are devoid of a nature of multiplicity, and subsequently, one realizes that they are devoid of intrinsic nature.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Although the method for realizing that all phenomena are devoid of self has been taught in this way, those who are attached to body and life, and who are greedy for gain and honor—those who have become attached to laziness, gain, honor, and alms—are, for the sake of being free from that attachment, addressed with the twelfth stage in mind, and he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman..." By this, it is indicated that since this body—a place of hundreds of thousands of sufferings—is devoid of essence, one should not be attached to it; for even if one were to abandon this body entirely, the merit that would not be attained is what one is obstructing, and therefore it is appropriate to strive for this with a mind that does not regard body and life. By this, in terms of meaning, laziness and the like are indicated as discordant factors. In order to abandon them, it is also taught that one should generate aspiration and prayer for the sake of upholding the holy Dharma and so forth. By merely mentioning the marks in the phrase "from this discourse on the Dharma," the hearing and so forth of the entire Great Vehicle is indicated. By the phrase "merely the merit," the vastness is expressed. The phrase "by the power of the Dharma" means by the power of faith in the Dharma. The fact that the noble Subhūti shed tears should also be viewed as being for the purpose of generating intense faith in others who are lazy, by the Bhagavan’s blessing, through the proclamation of the marvelous Dharma of the Great Vehicle.

Having heard of such merit that has reached excellence, those who have initiated exertion and are engaging [in the path], but who would come to perceive this Dharma according to the literal words, address him with the phrase "most marvelous" in order to abandon their faults. This is because they have faith in such [teachings] that generate vast merit, which are difficult for base individuals to believe in, and because they have faith in the profound selflessness of persons and phenomena; thus, those who realize merely the selflessness of persons, like myself, will possess this "most marvelous" [quality]. The phrase "correct perception" refers to perceiving the meaning without error; it does not refer to being attached to the literal words and perceiving, "This is correct." This is because here, [the Tathāgata] taught with the ultimate truth in mind—that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature—and not because they are devoid of intrinsic nature in conventional reality. Therefore, he intends that this is not contradictory to what is seen and so forth. If there were a "correct perception," then the object to be perceived would also have to exist in the ultimate sense, for if there were no object to be perceived, it would follow that there would be no perception either.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because it exists merely as a joy when not examined, the Tathāgata speaks of it as "correct perception." If it were not so, he would not speak of it, as it would be non-existent in every respect. By this, he establishes the ultimate sense, and he teaches both how one should accomplish [the path] by entering into meditative equipoise and how one should subdue distraction. He also expresses its profundity. He has also abandoned the extremes of superimposition and denigration.

[3-125] translation already produced for this document:
Having heard of such merit that has reached excellence, those who have initiated exertion and are engaging [in the path], but who would come to perceive this Dharma according to the literal words, address him with the phrase "most marvelous" in order to abandon their faults. This is because they have faith in such [teachings] that generate vast merit, which are difficult for base individuals to believe in, and because they have faith in the profound selflessness of persons and phenomena; thus, those who realize merely the selflessness of persons, like myself, will possess this "most marvelous" [quality]. The phrase "correct perception" refers to perceiving the meaning without error; it does not refer to being attached to the literal words and perceiving, "This is correct." This is because here, [the Tathāgata] taught with the ultimate truth in mind—that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature—and not because they are devoid of intrinsic nature in conventional reality. Therefore, he intends that this is not contradictory to what is seen and so forth. If there were a "correct perception," then the object to be perceived would also have to exist in the ultimate sense, for if there were no object to be perceived, it would follow that there would be no perception either.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "In order to generate wonder in those who are lazy, he asks, 'Bhagavan, it is not a wonder to me that I should contemplate and have faith in the explanation of this Dharma discourse; but, Bhagavan, in the future time, in the final five-hundred-year period, those sentient beings who take up, hold, and fully understand this Dharma discourse will be possessed of supreme wonder.' The summarized meaning of this is as follows: in the future, during the time when the holy Dharma is being thoroughly destroyed, there will arise bodhisattvas who hold this Dharma discourse and who do not grasp it in terms of a person and so forth; if such beings appear, then since you do not have such practice even during the time when you have the feast of the holy Dharma, this is a place of great shame for you. Regarding this, 'I' refers to the realization of the selflessness of the person. 'This' refers to the complete demonstration of the selflessness of the person and phenomena. 'Explanation' refers to what the Bhagavan has made manifest and clear. 'Contemplate' refers to the mode of clarity, meaning he demonstrates it clearly. 'Faith' refers to the mode of conviction. 'Those sentient beings' refers to those who will arise in the future time, Bhagavan. The words 'take up' and so forth mentioned here have already been explained previously. This is taught as follows: it is not a wonder that one who has realized merely the selflessness of the person, and who, by the power of having heard it directly from the Bhagavan, has become one who merely has faith and conviction in such a Dharma that demonstrates the mode of the two selflessnesses; rather, those who, in the future time of the Bhagavan, realize this kind of Dharma discourse through the sequence of holding it and so forth, and then fully understand it, will be possessed of supreme wonder, for he thinks that it is extremely rare for faith to arise in this when there are many who abandon the Mahāyāna in the time of the Bhagavan. By this, he has abandoned laziness and taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for holding the holy Dharma and so forth. Because he also shows that they will not only possess the oral transmission but will also possess perfect realization, he asks, 'Bhagavan.'"

[3-126] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having examined the objection of those who think, "How can it be established that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense?", he asks, "Why is that?" and in response, he asks, "Bhagavan, what is 'correct perception'?" Because it is devoid of an object to be perceived, because it is non-existent, and because it is free from the nature of being one or many, that very thing is, in the ultimate sense, without perception; therefore, it is taught that one should not perceive that "correct perception" as a "correct perception."

གང་གི་ཕྱིར་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཡང་དག་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་གསུང་ངོ་། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གསུང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་ཅིང་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བ་ཚར་གཅད་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་གཉི་ག་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དོ། །སྒྲོ་འདོགས་པ་དང་སྐུར་པ་འདེབས་པའི་མཐའ་ཡང་སྤངས་སོ། །
[3-127] translation already produced for this document:
Because it exists merely as a joy when not examined, the Tathāgata speaks of it as "correct perception." If it were not so, he would not speak of it, as it would be non-existent in every respect. By this, he establishes the ultimate sense, and he teaches both how one should accomplish [the path] by entering into meditative equipoise and how one should subdue distraction. He also expresses its profundity. He has also abandoned the extremes of superimposition and denigration.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The mention of "self" and so forth is intended to illustrate; in that context, they do not engage in the perception of phenomena, because they realize both selflessness simultaneously. If one thinks, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time the perception of them must surely also engage," then, having asked, "Why is that?" the response is given as "the perception of a self." By this, it is taught that, leaving aside for a moment the self and so forth as previously mentioned, even that perception of a self—which is commonly known to all beings as the thought "this is I"—is unable to bear the burden of analysis and is therefore nothing at all; so, what need is there to mention that there is no existence of the self and so forth, which are not even experienced? By this, the meditative equipoise is demonstrated.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Even if the self and so forth do not exist, one might wonder: "What is the meaning of the statement that, having fallen into error regarding them, one does not engage in the perception of a self and so forth?" Having considered this question, which is posed internally, one asks, "Why is that?" The response is given: "Because the Tathāgata Bhagavāns are free from all perceptions." The meaning here is this: they are called Tathāgata Bhagavāns because they have fully realized all phenomena, without exception, just as they truly are. In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever to be perceived, and therefore they do not engage in perception anywhere. If it were otherwise, it would be an error. Bodhisattvas engage in practice by following the Buddha.

The mention of "self" and so forth is intended to illustrate; in that context, they do not engage in the perception of phenomena, because they realize both selflessness simultaneously. If one thinks, "If selflessness and so forth exist, then at that time the perception of them must surely also engage," then, having asked, "Why is that?" the response is given as "the perception of a self." By this, it is taught that, leaving aside for a moment the self and so forth as previously mentioned, even that perception of a self—which is commonly known to all beings as the thought "this is I"—is unable to bear the burden of analysis and is therefore nothing at all; so, what need is there to mention that there is no existence of the self and so forth, which are not even experienced? By this, the meditative equipoise is demonstrated.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If it were otherwise, how could that state be attained? Therefore, just as the Tathāgata Bhagavāns have trained in being free from all perceptions, so too should Bodhisattvas train. For this reason, it is certain that those Bodhisattvas who follow in their footsteps do not engage in the perception of a self and so forth. The statement "It is just so" was spoken by the Bhagavān twice after he had affirmed it, in order to ensure that those to be trained would be certain. Up to this point, the teaching has been given with a focus on turning away from exertion. Now, because some individuals, upon hearing this profound Dharma, become mentally terrified and do not initiate exertion from the very beginning, the passage beginning with "What living beings..." was spoken to free them from that lack of exertion. If one is terrified, one does not initiate exertion. In the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Bhagavān taught that "this is merely Dharma; there is no person here at all," whereas in the Mahāyāna, he taught that "even those mere Dharmas are illusory." Because of this, those who have not cultivated the body—who possess a core connected to the innate view of self from beginningless time—become terrified upon hearing that there is no person, thinking, "I do not exist." To refute this, the words "do not become terrified" were spoken. Those who are intensely attached to mere Dharmas become terrified upon hearing the teaching that there is no self in Dharmas, thinking, "Alas, I am ruined," because even that which is merely Dharma does not exist; and since they see no refuge even when looking in the ten directions, they become terrified. To refute this, the words "do not become frightened" were spoken. At the time of reflection, one is unable to apply the non-existence of both, and thus one becomes frightened. To refute the initial terror of thinking, "How can we realize the non-existence of both?" the words "will not become terrified" were spoken. Some say that because the two types of selflessness are not realized, the terror is explained in three stages—small, medium, and great—by these three phrases in sequence. Others say that the three types of terror occur at the times of hearing, reflecting, and meditating.

Even if the self and so forth do not exist, one might wonder: "What is the meaning of the statement that, having fallen into error regarding them, one does not engage in the perception of a self and so forth?" Having considered this question, which is posed internally, one asks, "Why is that?" The response is given: "Because the Tathāgata Bhagavāns are free from all perceptions." The meaning here is this: they are called Tathāgata Bhagavāns because they have fully realized all phenomena, without exception, just as they truly are. In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever to be perceived, and therefore they do not engage in perception anywhere. If it were otherwise, it would be an error. Bodhisattvas engage in practice by following the Buddha.

heading: ལེ་ལོ་དང་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Now, in order to dispel attachment to gain and honor, and to benefit those who wish to hear how these will possess supreme wonder, he himself puts forward a question and states, "Why is that?"

translation: In order to show that it is not just I alone who have taught this as supreme, but that all Buddhas have also taught this as supreme, he states, "What is the supreme prajñāpāramitā?" By this, he teaches that if even what is spoken by a single Buddha is to be grasped as *tathatā* because its meaning is unerring, then what need is there to mention that which all Buddhas have unanimously intended? Therefore, if one practices this supreme teaching with one's whole being, how could it not possess supreme wonder? This teaching of the "supreme" serves as the second instance of pointing out a cause for shame; it is as if to say, "If this teaching is supreme, then for you to be attached to gain and honor and to remain heedless in this way is a cause for great shame." By this, he teaches the firm restraint of the mind.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Although the causes for shame have already been explained, those who are unable to endure suffering and are therefore unwilling to initiate great diligence are, in order to be freed from that inability to endure suffering, addressed by the Tathāgata—based on the thirteenth location—beginning with the words, "Subhūti." This section teaches how one endures, by what signs that endurance is known, what its aspects are, what those aspects are like, and what the antidote to the basis of non-endurance is.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
source: ཇི་ལྟར་བཟོད་ཅེ་ན། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་མི་དམིགས་པ་སྟེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་སྟེ། དོན་དམ་པར་དུ་བཟོད་པ་དང་། གང་གིས་བཟོད་པ་དང་། གང་ལ་བཟོད་པ་དང་། གང་བཟོད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཟོད་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་དམིགས་པས་དེ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། ། དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་ལྟར་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །འདིས་ནི་བཟོད་པ་དེ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཟབ་པ་ཡང་བརྗོད་དོ། །
translation: How does one endure? It is the non-apprehension of the nature of all phenomena. That which is the Tathāgata’s *prajñāpāramitā* of patience is precisely what is taught as "there is no *pāramitā*." In the ultimate sense, because the patience, the one who endures, that which is endured, that which is to be endured, and the patience itself are all not apprehended, it is the very state of having no *pāramitā*. The intention is that, because they are not produced in the ultimate sense, there is no "going to the other shore." By this, he teaches that patience is unborn by its own nature, and he also expresses its profundity.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The statement "I have no perception whatsoever" refers to the perception of another's body, the perception of a weapon, the perception of cutting, the perception of another, and the perception of endurance, and so forth; by this, he expresses the non-apprehension of all phenomena. Regarding the thought that if there is no perception whatsoever, it would be like the state of a Victorious One where there is no thinking, he stated, "It is not that one has become without perception." At that time, the yogi’s wisdom realizes that all phenomena are selfless, while intending that the authentic conventional nature exists.

source: དེའི་ཡང་ཅི་མངོན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པའི་འདྲི་བ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་བཀའ་སྩལ་ནས། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །གནོད་སེམས་ཀྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དགོངས་པ་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། གང་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ལ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ན་ངེས་པར་བདག་ལ་ཆགས་པ་འབྱུང་ངོ་། །དེ་ལྟར་བདག་ལ་ཆགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ན། གདོན་མི་ཟ་བར་བདག་གི་དང་གཞན་དུ་རྟོག་པ་འབྱུང་སྟེ། འདི་ལྟར་དེས་གང་ཞིག་བདག་ལ་ཕན་འདོགས་པར་བསྡུས་པ་དེ་ལ་ནི་བདག་གིར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་ལ། གཞན་ལ་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་གོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་གི་དང་མཐུན་པར་འཇུག་གོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་དང་བདག་གི་དང་མཐུན་པར་འཇུག་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པ་དང་དེ་དང་འགལ་བ་ལ་ཞེ་སྡང་སྟེ། དེ་དང་འབྲེལ་པ་ཉེས་པའི་ཚོགས་མཐའ་དག་ཀྱང་འབྱུང་ངོ་། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར། བདག་ཡོད་གཞན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཏེ། །བདག་གཞན་བྱེད་པས་ཡང་འཛིན་སྡང་། །འདི་དག་དང་ནི་འབྲེལ་པ་ཡིས། ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་རབ་ཏུ་འཕེལ། ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །གང་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉེས་པའི་ཚོགས་འབྱུང་བ་དེ་ལ་ང་ཇི་ལྟར་བཟོད་པ་སྨྲ་བར་གྲགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གང་གིས་ན་བཟོད་པའི་མཐུས་ཀ་ལིང་ཀའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་དེའི་ཚེ་དེ་ཁོ་ན་སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བར་འགྲོ་བར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །འདིས་ནི་གནོད་པ་བྱས་པ་ན་འགྱུར་བ་མེད་པས་གནོད་སེམས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་རྣམས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་བདག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་བྲལ་བའི་རྟགས་ཀྱིས་བཟོད་པ་དེ་འདྲ་བ་དེ་ཤེས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བཟོད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏེ། འདིར་ཀ་ལིང་ཀའི་རྒྱལ་པོས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་བཟོད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །ཡན་ལག་དང་ཉིང་ལག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་དུ་ལེན་པའི་བཟོད་པའོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་ང་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་ཆོས་ལ་ངེས་པར་རྟོག་པའི་བཟོད་པའོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཅིང་། འདུལ་བ་རྣམས་དེ་སྤང་བ་དང་། ཇི་སྐད་སྨོས་པའི་བཟོད་པ་སྐྱེད་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་འཛིན་དུ་འཇུག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་འདིས་ནི་གདུལ་བའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གང་གི་ཚེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཉིད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་བཟོད་པ་མཆོག་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་བསྒོམས་པ་དེ་ནི་བདག་ཅག་གིས་འདི་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་མི་བསྒོམ་སྟེ། བྱ་དཀའ་བའི་ལས་མ་བྱས་ན་རྙེད་དཀའ་བའི་གོ་འཕང་མི་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་གདུལ་བ་དེ་དག་དེ་ལ་སྤྲོ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཡན་ལག་དང་ཉིང་ལག་རྣམས་ཞེས་མཚན་མ་ཙམ་ཞིག་བརྗོད་པས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་དུ་ལེན་པའི་བཟོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation:
Having examined the inquiry that thinks, "What is the meaning of that?" he himself spoke, saying, "For what reason?" and in response, he said, "Subhūti, if..." The intention of the statement "even the perception of malevolence" is this: for whomever there is a perception of a self, by that very fact, attachment to the self necessarily arises. When one is thus possessed of attachment to the self, the conceptualization of "mine" and "other" inevitably arises; in this way, one conceptualizes as "mine" whatever is gathered to benefit the self, and one conceptualizes as "other" those who are external. Therefore, one proceeds in accordance with "mine." Consequently, because one proceeds in accordance with self and "mine," there is attachment to that, and anger toward what is contrary to that, and thus the entire collection of faults associated with that also arises. For that very reason, it is said:
"There is a perception of self and other;
By making self and other, one grasps and hates.
Through association with these,
All faults greatly increase."
For one in whom the collection of faults such as malevolence arises, how could it be renowned that I speak of patience? For he intended that by the power of patience, the King of Kaliṅga would at that time have gone to the hell realms. By this, it is shown that because there is no change when harm is done, and because the faults such as malevolence that necessarily arise are absent, that kind of patience is known by the sign of being free from perceptions of self and so forth. By this very passage, three types of patience are also shown: here, the words "the King of Kaliṅga" demonstrate patience toward those who do harm; the words "major limbs and minor limbs" demonstrate patience in accepting suffering; and the words "at that time, I..." and so forth demonstrate patience in the certain realization of phenomena. By this, in essence, he shows the opposing factors of conceptualizing phenomena and persons, and causes those to be trained to abandon them and to truly grasp the generation of the patience mentioned. In this way, he causes the beings to be trained to think, "When the Blessed One himself practiced such supreme patience for the sake of enlightenment, why should we not practice it? If one does not perform difficult deeds, one will not attain the hard-to-obtain state." Therefore, he generates enthusiasm for that in those to be trained. By mentioning only the signs of "major limbs and minor limbs," all patience in accepting suffering is fully indicated.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Now, in order to demonstrate what that patience is like, the passage "Subhūti, I recall" is spoken. This refers to the occasion when the King of Kaliṅga cut off my limbs and minor limbs, though it is not mentioned in the *Prajñāpāramitā* itself. That patience is taught as being of two types: that which has as its object the constant suffering caused by others' harm, and that which has as its object the unbearable suffering caused by others' harm. Regarding that, the object of constant suffering and so forth is what is meant by "for five hundred lifetimes," which expresses the vastness of this. The object of unbearable suffering and so forth is what is meant by the statement "my limbs and minor limbs." The bases of impatience are the three types of suffering: the suffering of saṃsāra, the suffering of sentient beings engaging in wrong paths, and the suffering of lacking resources. Regarding that, the passage "therefore" is spoken as the antidote to the first base of impatience. By all of this, impatience is abandoned, and it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for bodhi, with the intention that if one generates the mind for bodhi, no one will be touched by the suffering of saṃsāra.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Even if one has generated the bodhicitta a few times, because one is afraid due to the perception of the three types of suffering through the gateway of habitual attachment to a self, one does not generate it again; therefore, the passage "having abandoned all perceptions" is spoken. Here, "all perceptions" refers to the perception of a self and so forth, and the perception of the three types of suffering. Habitual attachment to form and so forth is like the śrāvakas and others who, having thoroughly examined saṃsāra and being distressed in mind by that suffering, do not generate the bodhicitta even on rare occasions; therefore, the passage "should not abide in form" and so forth is spoken. Habitual attachment to form and so forth is abiding in them, which is explained here just as it was previously. There is no redundancy in the wording here. By this, the antidote to the base of impatience is stated. The former passage is the application to the pāramitā.

Regarding that, the object of constant suffering and so forth is what is meant by "for five hundred lifetimes," which expresses the vastness of this. The object of unbearable suffering and so forth is what is meant by the statement "my limbs and minor limbs." The bases of impatience are the three types of suffering: the suffering of saṃsāra, the suffering of sentient beings engaging in wrong paths, and the suffering of lacking resources. Regarding that, the passage "therefore" is spoken as the antidote to the first base of impatience. By all of this, impatience is abandoned, and it is taught that one should abide with aspiration and prayer for bodhi, with the intention that if one generates the mind for bodhi, no one will be touched by the suffering of saṃsāra.

Here, "all perceptions" refers to the perception of a self and so forth, and the perception of the three types of suffering. Habitual attachment to form and so forth is like the śrāvakas and others who, having thoroughly examined saṃsāra and being distressed in mind by that suffering, do not generate the bodhicitta even on rare occasions; therefore, the passage "should not abide in form" and so forth is spoken. Habitual attachment to form and so forth is abiding in them, which is explained here just as it was previously. There is no redundancy in the wording here. By this, the antidote to the base of impatience is stated. The former passage is the application to the pāramitā.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Is it because one is angry at abiding in form and so forth while they exist, or is it to abandon the wrong habitual attachment to their mere non-existence that one asks, "Why is that?" and in response the passage "that which is abiding does not abide" is spoken? The meaning here is this: your mind, due to the power of habitual attachment to form and so forth as real entities since beginningless time, abides in form and so forth; yet, whatever habitual attachment to them as true exists, it does not abide in the ultimate sense because form and so forth do not exist as entities. Therefore, this concluding phrase indicates abiding in the second aspect here; by the term "giving," it is intended that all six pāramitā are included here as before. The passage "Subhūti" and so forth is also spoken as an antidote to the second base of impatience. By all of this, it is fully taught: if a Bodhisattva is eager to undertake the practice of the extremely difficult pāramitā for the sake of sentient beings, yet those sentient beings do not exist in the ultimate sense, and the perception of them as sentient beings also does not exist in the ultimate sense, then how could they become discouraged by the wrong engagement of such sentient beings? By refuting sentient beings and the perception of them, both types of selflessness are stated.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The phrase "for the sake of all sentient beings" indicates the vastness here. The remaining entirety indicates the profundity. Having thus shown that it is reasonable to be patient through logic, he now speaks the phrase "speaks correctly" and so forth to show that it is also reasonable through faith in the Tathāgata. The first part is the teaching; the remainder is the explanation. Alternatively, it teaches the four truths, which should be applied in order. Alternatively, "speaks correctly" indicates what is to be established. "Tathāgata" indicates the reason, for the Buddha, the Bhagavān, has abandoned the obscurations of the kleshas and of knowables; because he has gone (gata) in that same way (tathā) as the Tathāgatas who have come before, he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, he speaks correctly and without error, and because he possesses no obscurations—the cause of teaching erroneously—he establishes that the cause is not observed. Thinking, "How is it established that this is the Tathāgata alone?" the phrase "speaks truthfully" is spoken. "Truthfully" means he has the nature of speaking the characteristics of the four noble truths; therefore, it is certain that he is the Tathāgata. The meaning of "extremely difficult to fathom" is that it is impossible to teach it correctly in every respect, as it is said: "That which arises from method and its cause, being hidden, is extremely difficult to explain." Thinking, "How is it known that what he speaks is true?" the phrase "speaks the suchness" is spoken. Because he speaks the suchness of entities without error, exactly as it is, he is the one who "speaks the suchness."

Is it because one is angry at abiding in form and so forth while they exist, or is it to abandon the wrong habitual attachment to their mere non-existence that one asks, "Why is that?" and in response the passage "that which is abiding does not abide" is spoken? The meaning here is this: your mind, due to the power of habitual attachment to form and so forth as real entities since beginningless time, abides in form and so forth; yet, whatever habitual attachment to them as true exists, it does not abide in the ultimate sense because form and so forth do not exist as entities. Therefore, this concluding phrase indicates abiding in the second aspect here; by the term "giving," it is intended that all six pāramitā are included here as before. The passage "Subhūti" and so forth is also spoken as an antidote to the second base of impatience. By all of this, it is fully taught: if a Bodhisattva is eager to undertake the practice of the extremely difficult pāramitā for the sake of sentient beings, yet those sentient beings do not exist in the ultimate sense, and the perception of them as sentient beings also does not exist in the ultimate sense, then how could they become discouraged by the wrong engagement of such sentient beings? By refuting sentient beings and the perception of them, both types of selflessness are stated.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: He speaks of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, just as it exists, along with its method; how then could he not be speaking the truth? One might wonder, even if that is the case, how can it be certain that the four truths taught by him exist in that way? To this, he says, "It is not a false teaching." The meaning is that because he speaks without error and in accordance with valid cognition, and does not speak of anything that is contradicted by valid cognition, it is therefore true. By all of this, the Tathāgata is established as a valid authority through the logical mark of the result. For that very reason, it is said: "From the Protector, the teaching is perfectly complete; the unique knowledge is established." In the ultimate sense, since not even a single nature of any entity is established, it is difficult to establish even one truth, so how could there be a view of four truths? Yet, by stating the four truths, he speaks correctly. For instance, if the Tathāgata says that the five skandha are like an illusion, how can their nature be the truth of suffering? Since suffering is also ultimately false, the truth of its origin and the truth of its cessation do not exist at all; for things that are utterly non-existent, such as the horns of a rabbit, those two are impossible. Because there is no cessation, the path leading to it also does not exist in the ultimate sense; if there is no destination, there is no going. It is as stated: "Having established enlightenment, if one does not see even one truth established, how can one see four?" Having examined this, in order to abandon the extreme of superimposition for those who are attached to the literal meaning of what is correctly spoken, he says "Subhūti" and so forth. The statement "there is no truth" is because, in the ultimate sense, no nature is established. Regarding the statement "there is no falsehood," since falsehood exists by way of negating truth, if that which is to be negated does not exist, by what would it be false? Alternatively, "there is no truth" means that the nature of what is known is false, like an illusion. "There is no falsehood" means that if one does not examine it, it remains as a mere appearance. By negating these two extremes, he demonstrates the Middle Way. In order to abandon the attachment to a self held by the Śrāvakas, the four truths were taught merely as a partial aspect of the selflessness of persons, but not for the sake of everything; thus, there is no contradiction.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Furthermore, regarding the question of what the difference is between one who apprehends the body and so forth and seeks them as an object, thereby performing the act of giving, and one who does not apprehend them and thus does not seek them as an object—the reflection upon this is the antidote to the third basis of non-forbearance, and thus the passage beginning with "For example" was spoken. One who is attached to the nature of the body, existence, and enjoyments as being solely happiness, and who performs the act of giving while having fallen into seeking those as objects, is like a person who has entered into darkness; even though they possess eyes, because they do not apprehend the reality of things, they do not know what should be abandoned and what should be adopted, and thus they fall into a state of all-encompassing suffering, which is the nature of delusion. Therefore, the Bodhisattva becomes completely deprived of the happiness of great enjoyment. Because they do not possess that [wisdom], they are afflicted by suffering just like the Śrāvakas and others, and thus they turn away from enlightenment. One who does not fall into the reality of things performs the act of giving. Not apprehending the body and other such things, and not performing the act of giving while seeking them as objects, is like a person who possesses eyes and, because there are various forms, sees them; and having seen them, they completely abandon what should be abandoned and take up what should be adopted.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: To address the thought that if the sun were to rise, it might not be seen in a hundred cases, the words "when the sun has risen" were spoken. Even if the sun has risen, to address the thought that one might not see it if one were in a house or other such place that is dark, the words "when the dawn has broken" were spoken. The term "dawn has broken" indicates darkness; therefore, it means "in a place where there is no darkness." Even if those conditions are met, to address the fear that a blind person might still not see it in a hundred cases, the words "endowed with eyes" were spoken; in such a way, a bodhisattva should view things without falling into substantialism. That is the breaking of the dawn of the darkness of ignorance, and when the sun of wisdom has risen, one sees the various types of knowable objects exactly as they are. One completely abandons the objects of inverted perception, which are the basis of all suffering, because they are false and the suffering is to be abandoned. One also desires to attain the state of the true nature of anuttarasamyaksambodhi, which is the basis of all happiness, and begins to engage in it. Therefore, bodhisattvas, having found great and perfect enjoyment, have their bodies steadied by supreme happiness and are considered to be those who will not turn back from awakening. For that very reason, they will not turn back; previously, it was shown that one abides in that merely by conceptualization, whereas here, it is falling into the nature of being attached to that by having made conceptualization the precursor. For that reason, "falling" is mentioned here. In the former, "abiding" was mentioned. By all of this, the complete capturing of the mind is shown.

translation: Even though they have been introduced to patience in this way, those who experience the taste of meditative stabilization and, becoming attached to that very thing, do not strive in the Mahāyāna teachings—which are the cause for fully accumulating the collection of wisdom—are lacking the collection of wisdom and are separated from it; therefore, focusing on the fourteenth stage, the Tathāgata spoke the words beginning with "Subhūti." This section fully demonstrates the excellence of the qualities of striving in the holy Dharma through five aspects, for the sake of being separated from experiencing the taste of meditative stabilization. These are: the Tathāgata’s mindfulness, the gathering of superior merit, the Dharma, the instruction on how to practice it, the making of offerings by gods and others, and the complete purification of negative deeds. Regarding that, the Tathāgata’s mindfulness is what is expressed by the words beginning with "The Tathāgata knows them." The explanation of the words beginning with "take up" is as before.

Even though they have been introduced to patience in this way, those who experience the taste of meditative stabilization and, becoming attached to that very thing, do not strive in the Mahāyāna teachings—which are the cause for fully accumulating the collection of wisdom—are lacking the collection of wisdom and are separated from it; therefore, focusing on the fourteenth stage, the Tathāgata spoke the words beginning with "Subhūti." This section fully demonstrates the excellence of the qualities of striving in the holy Dharma through five aspects, for the sake of being separated from experiencing the taste of meditative stabilization. These are: the Tathāgata’s mindfulness, the gathering of superior merit, the Dharma, the instruction on how to practice it, the making of offerings by gods and others, and the complete purification of negative deeds. Regarding that, the Tathāgata’s mindfulness is what is expressed by the words beginning with "The Tathāgata knows them." The explanation of the words beginning with "take up" is as before.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Reflecting on the thought, "What is the excellence of that mass of merit, such that it becomes immeasurable?" and in order to demonstrate the gathering of supreme merit, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, whatever man or woman," and so forth. The specific circumstances of the sun, light, earth, water, and so on, are what constitute "morning." Because he wished to show that "time" is designated only by such specific circumstances, and not by something falsely imagined through distinctions of the qualified and so forth, he made a distinction using the word "time" and the term for that [circumstance] as being of the same basis. If it were not so, because it would be a single entity, there would be no way to distinguish it as "this is morning" and so forth. If one were to accept that it is distinguished by the differences of others, then since that very difference is the cause for designating the specific circumstances of the sun and so forth as "morning" and so on, he thought, "What is the point of imagining a time that does nothing and whose power is not seen?" It is also not logical for it to be characterized by signs such as dullness or sharpness of intellect, because it contradicts the fact that such things as dullness of intellect arise gradually from their own causes. That has already been explained. There is no need to elaborate on the valid cognition that acts as a refutation, as it was already explained in the context of refuting the self. In order to show that the term "life" is used to make a distinction—meaning that the term "time" is applied to such specific circumstances as living beings due to conventions created by mere whim, and not because of an imagined connection between the word and the meaning—he made a distinction using the word "life." If he had mentioned only one, it would not have shown the intended meaning as explained, so he mentioned all three terms. Because they are objects of convention, he superimposed the conventional term and made them of the same basis. Here, this is stated because it is separated from the savoring of meditative absorption, and in the former case, it is not redundant because the object to be given and this type of temporal distinction were not shown.

[3-149] translation already produced for this document:
Because the Bhagavan is omniscient, he is all-knowing and all-seeing. Reflecting on the thought, "What is so wondrous about them?" and in order to demonstrate the excellence of gathering merit, he spoke the words, "all those sentient beings." The intended meaning is that because they have generated immeasurable masses of merit, he knows that they possess the fortune [to attain awakening].

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The statement, "From that very basis, one generates merit that is extremely vast, incalculable, and immeasurable," indicates the vastness [of the merit]. This is because it surpasses the merit arising from giving that is distinguished by the specific differences of number, substance, and time. Thus, the phrase "as many as the grains of sand of the Gangā" indicates the distinction of number. The word "body" refers to that which is difficult to fathom, which is the distinction of substance. The phrase "hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas" refers to the distinction of time. Those billions of kalpas are also multiplied by billions. And to that, the word "hundreds of thousands" is added. Regarding the thought of how this is to be understood, in order to show the distinction of praising the Dharma, [the Buddha] spoke the words "Subhūti" and so forth.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The statement, "This discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable," indicates that it is extremely profound, having the characteristic of all phenomena being devoid of intrinsic nature; it is to be personally realized by the Tathāgatas themselves, and is beyond the capacity of others, such as the Śrāvakas, to conceive. The statement, "It is incomparable," means that because such a mode [of teaching] is not taught elsewhere, there is nothing that is equal to or superior to this.

The statement, "From that very basis, one generates merit that is extremely vast, incalculable, and immeasurable," indicates the vastness [of the merit]. This is because it surpasses the merit arising from giving that is distinguished by the specific differences of number, substance, and time. Thus, the phrase "as many as the grains of sand of the Gangā" indicates the distinction of number. The word "body" refers to that which is difficult to fathom, which is the distinction of substance. The phrase "hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas" refers to the distinction of time. Those billions of kalpas are also multiplied by billions. And to that, the word "hundreds of thousands" is added. Regarding the thought of how this is to be understood, in order to show the distinction of praising the Dharma, [the Buddha] spoke the words "Subhūti" and so forth.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because it is neither equal nor superior, this teaches that an inconceivable result arises from an inconceivable cause. Regarding the thought of how it is incomparable, the phrase "those who have correctly entered the supreme vehicle" was spoken. "Extremely gone beyond" means "supreme," and the phrase "this discourse on the Dharma for those who are Śrāvakas and so forth" was spoken. The phrase "supreme vehicle" is analyzed by joining the words, meaning either that it is the vehicle of the supreme ones, or that it is both a vehicle and it is supreme; and it is said in that way for those who have correctly entered it. Similarly, the phrase "those who have correctly entered the vehicle that is gone beyond" is also consistent, and these two are included as synonyms. The intention behind teaching these synonyms is to benefit the beings to be trained, because different people are transformed by different things. Others say that it is "supreme" in relation to vehicles other than this one. They say it is "gone beyond" because all obscurations of the afflictions and of knowledge are completely purified. Alternatively, "supreme" means "excellent."

[3-151] translation already produced for this document:
The statement, "From that very basis, one generates merit that is extremely vast, incalculable, and immeasurable," indicates the vastness [of the merit]. This is because it surpasses the merit arising from giving that is distinguished by the specific differences of number, substance, and time. Thus, the phrase "as many as the grains of sand of the Gangā" indicates the distinction of number. The word "body" refers to that which is difficult to fathom, which is the distinction of substance. The phrase "hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas" refers to the distinction of time. Those billions of kalpas are also multiplied by billions. And to that, the word "hundreds of thousands" is added. Regarding the thought of how this is to be understood, in order to show the distinction of praising the Dharma, [the Buddha] spoke the words "Subhūti" and so forth.
