ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ནི་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཟབ་པ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སོ་སོ་རང་གིས་རིག་པར་བྱ་བ་ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཞན་དག་གིས་བསམ་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་འདིར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚུངས་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་དུ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་མ་བསྟན་པས། འདི་དང་མཚུངས་པའམ། ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

The statement, "This discourse on the Dharma is inconceivable," indicates that it is extremely profound, having the characteristic of all phenomena being devoid of intrinsic nature; it is to be personally realized by the Tathāgatas themselves, and is beyond the capacity of others, such as the Śrāvakas, to conceive. The statement, "It is incomparable," means that because such a mode [of teaching] is not taught elsewhere, there is nothing that is equal to or superior to this.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།

Since the Śrāvakas and others are not vessels for this kind of Dharma teaching, it was spoken for the sake of the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is established that this discourse on the Dharma has no equal. The phrase "spoken by the Tathāgata" is used because it is not the domain of others.

[3-153] translation already produced for this document:
Because it is neither equal nor superior, this teaches that an inconceivable result arises from an inconceivable cause. Regarding the thought of how it is incomparable, the phrase "those who have correctly entered the supreme vehicle" was spoken. "Extremely gone beyond" means "supreme," and the phrase "this discourse on the Dharma for those who are Śrāvakas and so forth" was spoken. The phrase "supreme vehicle" is analyzed by joining the words, meaning either that it is the vehicle of the supreme ones, or that it is both a vehicle and it is supreme; and it is said in that way for those who have correctly entered it. Similarly, the phrase "those who have correctly entered the vehicle that is gone beyond" is also consistent, and these two are included as synonyms. The intention behind teaching these synonyms is to benefit the beings to be trained, because different people are transformed by different things. Others say that it is "supreme" in relation to vehicles other than this one. They say it is "gone beyond" because all obscurations of the afflictions and of knowledge are completely purified. Alternatively, "supreme" means "excellent."

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The phrase "this Dharma discourse" and so forth serves to thoroughly establish the meanings previously explained, to conclude the discussion, and to demonstrate the excellence of praising that which brings about such establishment. Because this Dharma discourse is inconceivable and immeasurable, its maturation is also inconceivable; therefore, the intent of the statement "whoever holds this Dharma discourse" and so forth is that it is established. "Innumerable" is what is taught. The rest is what has been explained.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།

"Immeasurable" means that even if all sentient beings were to calculate it, they would be unable to measure it. "Limitless" means that it cannot be measured even by great realms and the like, because it is even more vast than space. Alternatively, this and all the others are included as synonyms.

[3-154] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the thought that even in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle there is something excellent in comparison to the Śrāvaka vehicle, the phrase "those who have correctly entered the vehicle that is gone beyond" was spoken. "Extremely gone beyond" means "supreme," and because this is extremely gone beyond among the many vehicles of the Śrāvakas and so forth, the term "supreme" is used here; that is the Mahāyāna itself. Since the Śrāvakas and others are not vessels for this kind of Dharma teaching, it was spoken for the sake of the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is established that this discourse on the Dharma has no equal. The phrase "spoken by the Tathāgata" is used because it is not the domain of others.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The statement "all those sentient beings will carry my enlightenment on their shoulders" means that it is like carrying the burden of enlightenment upon one's shoulders. By this, it is taught that one should abandon the tasting of the flavor of meditative stability and remain with aspiration and prayer, focused on the adoption of the Dharma that is the cause for fulfilling the accumulation of wisdom. Why did the Tathāgata speak this for those who have truly entered the supreme vehicle, and not for others?

[3-155] translation already produced for this document:
The phrase "this Dharma discourse" and so forth serves to thoroughly establish the meanings previously explained, to conclude the discussion, and to demonstrate the excellence of praising that which brings about such establishment. Because this Dharma discourse is inconceivable and immeasurable, its maturation is also inconceivable; therefore, the intent of the statement "whoever holds this Dharma discourse" and so forth is that it is established. "Innumerable" is what is taught. The rest is what has been explained.

[3-156] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding this, "inconceivable" indicates that it is beyond the domain of thought, because it is beyond inference. "Incomparable" means it has no peer. "Immeasurable" means that even if all sentient beings were to calculate it, they would be unable to measure it. "Limitless" means that it cannot be measured even by great realms and the like, because it is even more vast than space. Alternatively, this and all the others are included as synonyms.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Thinking, "Does the Tathāgata also possess hatred and desire?" one asks, "For what reason?" In response, the words "Subhūti, one who aspires to the inferior" and so forth were spoken. This teaches that because the Tathāgata has love for all sentient beings just like an only child, he does not possess hatred or desire; however, he teaches those who have become vessels at the time they are ready, and not otherwise. If it were not so, then because he is omniscient, the Tathāgata would be rendered as not being omniscient; thus, it is taught in that way. "By those who aspire to the inferior" and so forth refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "By those who view things as self" and so forth refers to the non-Buddhists. "That is without basis" means that it is without opportunity. How could it be possible for ordinary beings to be capable of what even the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to hear? It is impossible that they could be capable of taking up and fully understanding what those others are unable to hear; that is the meaning. This leads one into the meditative absorption of yoga. If that is the case, how is the noble Subhūti able to hear this discourse on the Dharma? It is through the blessing of the Tathāgata, so there is no fault. The words "Subhūti" and so forth were also spoken to show the distinction of the gods and others who perform service, indicating that among all the lands, the single place where this sūtra is taught is to be praised. Previously, it was spoken to detach from attachment to external treatises, and now it is spoken to detach from the tasting of the flavor of meditative stability; thus, there is no repetition. It should be understood that there is no repetition because the different contexts are expressed solely by stating the meaning that encompasses everything. "Worthy of being offered to" refers to parasols, victory banners, pennants, and the like.

translation: Thinking, "How is it that some who are diligent in such a discourse on the Dharma still appear to be tormented?" and because this relies on the distinction of the complete purification of negative karma, the words "Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family" and so forth were spoken. Thinking, "How could such great beings be tormented?" the question "For what reason?" was asked, and in response, the words "Subhūti, those sentient beings'..." and so forth were spoken. "Of previous lives" refers to what was done in previous lives. "In this very life" refers to the life that is currently occurring.

Thinking, "How could such great beings be tormented?" the question "For what reason?" was asked, and in response, the words "Subhūti, those sentient beings'..." and so forth were spoken. "Of previous lives" refers to what was done in previous lives. "In this very life" refers to the life that is currently occurring.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: It should be stated that the abiding is completely pure. This is also divided into three types: abiding through deportment, abiding by having mastery over the world of vessels and sentient beings, and abiding by having no defilements whatsoever.

heading: གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The eye of wisdom exists regarding the object of the selflessness of persons and phenomena. Because the person is not, but rather it is merely the appearance of phenomena in conventional reality, the person is empty; thus, the eye of Dharma exists regarding the object of merely phenomena. The eye of a Buddha is said to be the knowledge of all objects of knowledge in every aspect; because this is present as a direct perception in the present, the teaching of the five eyes in valid conventional reality expresses the complete purity of what is perceived.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: When the Bhagavan abides in supramundane wisdom, it is not surprising that, due to being in a state of profound meditative equipoise, the perception of sentient beings and so forth does not arise. In order to show that even when he abides in mundane wisdom—at times when he is not in meditative equipoise—while bestowing the prophecy of liberation upon sentient beings, the perception of sentient beings and so forth also does not arise, and to indicate that this is the cause for establishing the instruction as having great meaning, thereby revealing that the Bhagavan’s perfect, unsurpassed mind is known, he spoke the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth, with the intention of teaching an instruction of great meaning.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Regarding the statement, "From that very basis, one generates merit that is extremely vast, incalculable, and immeasurable," the words "Subhūti, I have direct knowledge, and..." and so forth were spoken, thinking, "In what way should one understand it to be incalculable and immeasurable?" Here, it is shown to be incalculable and immeasurable by way of its power and its vastness. Among these, the words "Subhūti, I have direct knowledge that in the past, in an even more incalculable time than the incalculable eons..." and so forth, fully demonstrate its power. This is the power of that heap of merit, because it surpasses even this many heaps of merit that are extremely exalted and supreme. "From Dīpaṃkara onwards, for incalculable eons" means that the incalculable eons are those whose count is exhausted. The words "Even before Dīpaṃkara, in the time before that, I pleased eighty-four hundred thousand ten million Buddhas" refer to making offerings through the offering of practice. "I did not let them be interrupted" means that one did not abandon that practice even in the interim. "Whatever they were" refers to the specific types of actions.

Thinking, "How is it that some who are diligent in such a discourse on the Dharma still appear to be tormented?" and because this relies on the distinction of the complete purification of negative karma, the words "Subhūti, whatever son of noble family or daughter of noble family" and so forth were spoken. "To be tormented" means to be harmed by things such as scolding and exposing one's faults. "To be completely tormented" means to be harmed by things such as being killed or bound. Thinking, "How could such great beings be tormented?" the question "For what reason?" was asked, and in response, the words "Subhūti, those sentient beings'..." and so forth were spoken. "Of previous lives" refers to what was done in previous lives. "In this very life" refers to the life that is currently occurring.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In order to express the complete purity of knowledge, the text says, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The mind and mental factors of the three times are the continuum of the mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called "knowledge," and it is not called "seeing." Furthermore, one should understand the various natures of the afflicted and the purified, such as "a mind with attachment" and "a mind free from attachment."

The eye of wisdom exists regarding the object of the selflessness of persons and phenomena. heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The expression "as many world systems as that" is an indication, because [the Tathāgata] completely knows the continuum of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. In this way, in conventional reality, the Tathāgata possesses the eye of flesh and so forth; therefore, because he accomplishes [the goal] through that, a bodhisattva should abide in aspiration and prayer. This passage demonstrates both types of excellence.

The eye of a Buddha is said to be the knowledge of all objects of knowledge in every aspect; because this is present as a direct perception in the present, the teaching of the five eyes in valid conventional reality expresses the complete purity of what is perceived.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: In this regard, if one thinks, "If the Buddha is to be viewed as the Dharmakāya and not as the Rūpakāya, then how is it not contradictory to the scriptures that proclaim the Bhagavan’s four modes of deportment, his birth, his departure, and so forth?"—then, for the sake of such a person, focusing on the perfect abiding through deportment, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whatever..." The two terms "walking" or "coming" indicate the act of walking. The remaining terms indicate the other modes of deportment, such as standing, in their respective order. The mention of deportment is merely illustrative; therefore, it should be understood that birth and the rest are also indicated here. Those who cling to the literal meaning of the Bhagavan’s deportment and other activities as described in the scriptures are clinging to a perversion, and thus they do not understand the meaning intended by the Tathāgata. The Bhagavan is not a differentiation of the Rūpakāya; he is the purity of primordial wisdom. Because that primordial wisdom lacks a physical body, it is impossible for it to walk or perform other such actions in a conventional sense. Walking and the like are differentiated based on the specific location of the physical aggregates; therefore, those actions are spoken of in reliance upon the Bhagavan’s Nirmāṇakāya, not in reliance upon the Jñānakāya, for in that [Jñānakāya], walking and the like are impossible in both conventional and ultimate terms. Therefore, it is shown that a bodhisattva should abide through aspiration and prayer in such a state of perfect abiding through deportment. If one thinks, "If the Tathāgata does not possess walking and the like, then how is it taught that he is differentiated by 'having gone' (gata) as in the name 'Tathāgata'?"—having examined this thought, he said, "Why is that?" and this is to be connected with the statement, "They do not understand the meaning of what I have explained."

[3-161] translation already produced for this document:
"They will also attain the enlightenment of a Buddha" means that, having completely purified their negative karma, those who are diligent in meditation at another time will swiftly and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

[3-238] source:
བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་བརྗོད་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་དུ་དབྱེ་སྟེ། སྤྱོད་ལམ་གྱིས་བཞུགས་པ་དང་། སྣོད་དང་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འཇིག་བརྟེན་ལ་མངའ་བས་བཞུགས་པ་དང་། ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མི་མངའ་བས་བཞུགས་པའོ། །
[3-238] translation already produced for this document:
It should be stated that the abiding is completely pure. This is also divided into three types: abiding through deportment, abiding by having mastery over the world of vessels and sentient beings, and abiding by having no defilements whatsoever.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: If sentient beings were truly existent, they would become a cause for defilement; does the Tathāgata not think in this way? Or, having examined the thought of one who thinks, "Is it because there are no sentient beings?" he asked, "For what reason?" And, in order to show that because sentient beings, which are of the nature of the aggregates and the person, do not exist in the ultimate sense, they are not perceived in that way, he spoke the words, "Because there is no sentient being that the Tathāgata has liberated." By this, he has shown what is to be accomplished by the Bodhisattva through entering into such a meditative equipoise. Regarding the thought, "How is it known that they do not exist?" he spoke the words, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth. The intention here is this: the Tathāgata’s wisdom engages with knowable objects just as they are. If it were not so, how could he be the Tathāgata, having not abandoned the obscurations? Therefore, if sentient beings existed, then at that time the Tathāgata would perceive them clearly, for because he perceives the self directly, he is free from doubt. That very thing would become a firm grasping at a self of those beings. Therefore, because the binding of the entire net of defilements, which arises from the cause of grasping at a self, would be light or manifest, if at that time he had not abandoned the very firm obscuration of the binding of attachment and so forth, the Bhagavan would not have attained the rank of Tathāgata; yet, because the Bhagavan has attained that rank, it follows that he has abandoned all obscurations. By abandoning the obscurations, the entire mountain of grasping at a self is demolished. Therefore, it is not that he does not know that sentient beings do not exist.

[3-218] translation already produced for this document:
When the Bhagavan abides in supramundane wisdom, it is not surprising that, due to being in a state of profound meditative equipoise, the perception of sentient beings and so forth does not arise. In order to show that even when he abides in mundane wisdom—at times when he is not in meditative equipoise—while bestowing the prophecy of liberation upon sentient beings, the perception of sentient beings and so forth also does not arise, and to indicate that this is the cause for establishing the instruction as having great meaning, thereby revealing that the Bhagavan’s perfect, unsurpassed mind is known, he spoke the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth, with the intention of teaching an instruction of great meaning.

དྲིས་ནས་ལན་ལ་མ་བཞེངས་ཏེ། རིངས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ལྟར་ཉིད་ཀྱིས། རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་ལྟར་མི་བལྟའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོའི་རྒྱུ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

Having asked, he did not wait for an answer, but as if possessing a sense of urgency, he spoke the words "Subhūti, it should not be viewed in that way," and so forth. Therefore, this shows that a Bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer regarding such a cause for the Bhagavan’s perfect instruction of great meaning.

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
source: དེས་ན་དོན་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། མཉེས་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ལེན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། དེས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བག་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའི་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་གཉིས་ལས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་སྔ་མས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ཕྱི་མ་འདིའི་བརྒྱའི་ཆར་ཡང་མི་ཕོད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའོ། །འདི་སྙེད་པས་ཀྱང་ཉུང་བ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྟོང་གི་ཆ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །གྲངས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚུངས་པ་དེ་དག་ཁོ་ན་ལ་རིགས་པ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་གངས་ཅན་དང་གཉིས་པ་ནི་འབིགས་བྱེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཡུངས་ཀར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆ་ཤས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་རིགས་འདྲ་བའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་རི་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆ་ནི་རིའི་རྩེ་མོ་ཡིན་གྱི་རྩྭའི་རྩེ་མོ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བགྲང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་ཡང་མཚུངས་པ་དག་ཁོ་ན་ལ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྷུན་པོ་ཡང་རི་ཡིན་ལ། གངས་ཅན་ཡང་རི་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱའི་ཡུངས་ཀར་ཡིན་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དཔེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དཔེ་ཡང་འདྲ་བ་ཁོ་ན་ཡིན་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་བ་མེན་ལ་བ་ལང་དང་འདྲའོ་ཞེས་བྱའི་སྦྲང་མ་ལ་ནི་མི་བྱ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆུང་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་སྦྱང་བ་བྱས་པའི་དབང་གིས་ན་དེའི་བྱ་བ་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་ཟོར་བ་རྣོན་པོར་བྱས་ན་རལ་གྲི་ལ་བྱ་བ་བྱེད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ཟླ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་ཏེ། གླེབ་ཅིང་ཞེང་ཆེར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་རྙེད་དོ། །རྣོན་པོར་བྱས་ཀྱང་ཧ་ཅང་ཆུང་བས་མི་བཟོད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རྒྱུར་ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེའི་རྒྱུའི་དངོས་པོར་ཡང་མི་བཟོད་པའོ། །འདི་དག་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་བཀའ་ཁོ་ན་ལས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དབང་པོའི་ཡུལ་ལས་འདས་པའི་དོན་རྣམ་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་ནི། ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་བཀའ་ཁོ་ན་ཚད་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཞན་ཡང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའི་དུས་ན་ནི། དེའི་ཚེ་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཡིན་པས་ངོ་མཚར་མི་ཆེའི་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་དག་པའི་དུས་ན་སེམས་ཅན་དག་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་བསམ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་གྱུར་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་ཏོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རེ་ཞིག་མཐུའི་སྒོ་ནས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Therefore, the meaning is this: between the two, the heap of merit that is the essence of the imprints generated by faith and so forth, and the heap of merit that is the essence of pleasing [the Buddhas] and so forth, the former heap of merit does not amount to even a hundredth part of this latter heap of merit. Because even this amount indicates a smallness, the term "a thousandth part" was spoken. The word "count" is appropriate only for things that are similar; for example, it is not used for a mustard seed, saying "the Himālaya is the second, and the mustard seed is the first." The word "part" means a fraction. That, too, is of a similar kind; for example, a part of Mount Meru is a mountain peak, not a blade of grass. The word "reckoning" is also only for things that are similar; for example, one would not say that Mount Meru is a mountain and the Himālaya is a mountain, and then say that a mustard seed is a mountain. The word "example" is also only for things that are similar; for example, one says that a gaur is like a cow, but one does not say that of a fly. Thinking that even if it is small, by virtue of having been thoroughly purified, it will perform its function—just as if a sickle is made sharp, it performs the function of a sword—the word "fraction" was spoken, finding a method to make it flat and broad. The implication is that even if it is made sharp, because it is too small, it cannot endure. For that very reason, the word "cause" is also mentioned, meaning it cannot endure even as the substance of its cause. These things should be known only from the words of the Omniscient One, because for such matters that transcend the range of the senses, the words of the Omniscient One alone are the valid authority. Furthermore, at a time of complete purity, since all sentient beings are completely pure, it is not a marvel; but at a time of impurity, that sentient beings should have their thoughts become completely pure for even a single moment is a marvel. In this way, for the time being, it has been shown to be immeasurable by way of its power.

[3-162] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the statement, "From that very basis, one generates merit that is extremely vast, incalculable, and immeasurable," the words "Subhūti, I have direct knowledge, and..." and so forth were spoken, thinking, "In what way should one understand it to be incalculable and immeasurable?" Here, it is shown to be incalculable and immeasurable by way of its power and its vastness. Among these, the words "Subhūti, I have direct knowledge that in the past, in an even more incalculable time than the incalculable eons..." and so forth, fully demonstrate its power. This is the power of that heap of merit, because it surpasses even this many heaps of merit that are extremely exalted and supreme. "From Dīpaṃkara onwards, for incalculable eons" means that the incalculable eons are those whose count is exhausted. The words "Even before Dīpaṃkara, in the time before that, I pleased eighty-four hundred thousand ten million Buddhas" refer to making offerings through the offering of practice. "I did not let them be interrupted" means that one did not abandon that practice even in the interim. "Whatever they were" refers to the specific types of actions.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The eye of flesh and so forth, when analyzed by the nature of being one or many, are not found; furthermore, it is not reasonable to grasp them by knowing another object. If it were as previously analyzed, one might wonder how the Tathāgata could possess the eye of flesh and so forth, and how he could perfectly know the continuum of the mind. Considering this line of thought, the question "For what reason?" was asked. In order to show how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by entering into meditative equipoise regarding these two—the purity of the bodhisattva and [the nature of the mind]—the text says, "The continuum of the mind, the continuum of the mind," and so forth. The statement "there is no continuum" refers to the ultimate level.

མཁྱེན་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་ནི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་དུས་གསུམ་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡུལ་དེ་ཤེས་པ་ནི་མཁྱེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའི་གཟིགས་པ་ཞེས་ནི་མི་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་དང་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་དབྲལ་བའི་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བའི་ངོ་བོ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-185] translation already produced for this document:
In order to express the complete purity of knowledge, the text says, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The mind and mental factors of the three times are the continuum of the mind. Therefore, because the three times are the object, knowing that object is called "knowledge," and it is not called "seeing." Furthermore, one should understand the various natures of the afflicted and the purified, such as "a mind with attachment" and "a mind free from attachment."

དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་མཐའ་ཡས་པར་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཡོངས་སུ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལྟར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་ལ་སོགས་པ་མངའ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་དེས་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་གནས་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །གཞུང་འདིས་ནི་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཉི་ག་ཡང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

The expression "as many world systems as that" is an indication, because [the Tathāgata] completely knows the continuum of sentient beings belonging to infinite world systems. In this way, in conventional reality, the Tathāgata possesses the eye of flesh and so forth; therefore, because he accomplishes [the goal] through that, a bodhisattva should abide in aspiration and prayer. This passage demonstrates both types of excellence.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: In response, the expression "Tathāgata" and so forth is stated. This is said with the following thought: the designation is not distinguished by "going" (gśegs pa), but is distinguished by "realization" (thugs su chud pa), for the term "going" signifies the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of things exactly as it abides, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, just as the Buddhas of the past realized the suchness of things without error, so too has this one known and realized it, and thus he is the Tathāgata. That is also because, in terms of authentic conventional reality, there is no conceptualization regarding others in the nature of the wisdom-body. Furthermore, because there is no physical body, it is impossible for there to be any "going" or the like even in conventional reality. In the ultimate sense, because there is no birth, it is impossible for there to be any "going" at all. Therefore, because he has realized the nature of things as such, he becomes the lord of all the world, and because he is worthy of offerings, he is called an Arhat.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: Even though it is devoid of a self, there is a grasping at a self; does the defining characteristic of the view of a self not exist? Regarding the question, "Bhagavān, how should one not conceive of a self and so forth?" the passage beginning with "Subhūti, what is called 'grasping at a self'..." was spoken. If one were to grasp at any entity such as a self, then at that time, Bhagavān, a grasping at a self would arise for one who has abandoned the obscurations; however, because there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped as a self, the Tathāgata has taught that there is no grasping. Regarding the question, "Then what is meant by 'grasping at a self'?" the passage beginning with "That also..." was spoken. "Foolish beings" are those who, lacking learning and so forth, do not clearly understand what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. "Ordinary beings" are those who are distinct from the Āryas because they lack discernment. Since some ordinary beings, having listened to the authentic treatises and abiding in appropriate mental engagement, have faith in the selflessness of phenomena, they do not grasp at a self because they are firmly convinced of the truth; thus, "foolish beings" is stated in order to exclude them. If only "foolish beings" were mentioned, then since such ordinary beings who are learned in the aggregates and so forth have not yet generated the path of the Āryas, they are "foolish selves"; therefore, in order to indicate the distinction of foolish beings, [it is said that] even though that is a mistaken grasping at a self, because they have become foolish, it appears to them as if there is a grasping at a self. Therefore, due to the power of their conceptualization, it is taught in that way as "grasping at a self."

heading: ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མ་བསགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ཏེ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Regarding the thought of how it could be immeasurable by count, the words "Subhūti, if at that time..." and so forth were spoken. By this, it is indicated that it is extremely numerous. Through counting such merit, one becomes weary, and a specific type of mental illness arises in which the mind becomes confused and bewildered. Following that, there arises a mental disturbance born from that madness. By this, the profound and the extensive are indicated. Regarding the thought of how one might know that from this Dharma discourse there could be such a result possessing count and measure, the words "Subhūti..." and so forth were spoken; in all cases, the result is only in accordance with the cause. It is not observed that a nyagrodha tree or the like, even if small, would, by possessing great essence, become a great fruit called a branch, a leaf, or a tree.

heading: མཁྱེན་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Although they are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are spoken of in reliance upon conventional reality; for that very reason, it is said, "the continuum of the mind." The intention is that, otherwise, in ultimate reality, they would not be spoken of, because they transcend the entire scope of verbal expression. The mention of "the continuum of the mind" is an indication, for this is the occasion to state that the eye of flesh and so forth are also taught as being devoid of the nature of an eye; they are taught as being directly perceived. In order to show how the mind should be perfectly grasped in this regard, the question "For what reason?" was asked, and it is connected with the statement "there is no continuum." The mind of the past and so forth is not found, because it is not produced in ultimate reality; however, it is not the case that it is not found because it exists but is impossible to grasp. If that were the case, it would not be taught that there is no continuum of the mind, for the mere fact of not being found does not mean that things are devoid of intrinsic nature. How the mind of the three times does not exist in ultimate reality has been explained previously, and it will also be taught. The mention of "mind" is an indication, and therefore the eye of flesh and so forth, as well as the past and so forth, are also simply not found. With the words "there is no continuum" and so forth, the profound is expressed here. Through the remainder, the vast is expressed.

[3-187] translation already produced for this document:
The eye of flesh and so forth, when analyzed by the nature of being one or many, are not found; furthermore, it is not reasonable to grasp them by knowing another object. If it were as previously analyzed, one might wonder how the Tathāgata could possess the eye of flesh and so forth, and how he could perfectly know the continuum of the mind. Considering this line of thought, the question "For what reason?" was asked. In order to show how a bodhisattva should accomplish this by entering into meditative equipoise regarding these two—the purity of the bodhisattva and [the nature of the mind]—the text says, "The continuum of the mind, the continuum of the mind," and so forth. The statement "there is no continuum" refers to the ultimate level.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Because he has perfectly and completely realized [the truth], he is called a Samyaksambuddha. The thought here is that if it were not so, the form body would be of the nature of an insentient thing, and thus it would not be called by that name. By this, meditative equipoise and the perfect grasping of the mind are indicated. By all of these points, profundity is indicated. Because it is shown that, conventionally, the Tathāgata’s emanated form body relies upon going and so forth without obstruction throughout infinite world realms, vastness is also indicated. Since any emanated form body of the Tathāgata, as well as any mind-made body, is devoid of the nature of being one or many, it is shown to be false, like a Buddha emanated by magic; therefore, having analyzed the world of vessels and sentient beings, and having taken the state of abiding as the basis, the expression "Subhūti" and so forth is stated. Previously, it was shown that the bodhisattva on the stage of engaging through aspiration analyzes these, but now, by showing the abiding of the Bhagavan on the stage of a Buddha, there is no repetition of words. Here too, by realizing that [the Tathāgata] is devoid of the nature of being one or many through two types of methods, selflessness is taught.

[3-240] translation already produced for this document:
In response, the expression "Tathāgata" and so forth is stated. This is said with the following thought: the designation is not distinguished by "going" (gśegs pa), but is distinguished by "realization" (thugs su chud pa), for the term "going" signifies the meaning of realization. Because he has realized and understood the suchness of things exactly as it abides, he is the Tathāgata. Alternatively, just as the Buddhas of the past realized the suchness of things without error, so too has this one known and realized it, and thus he is the Tathāgata. That is also because, in terms of authentic conventional reality, there is no conceptualization regarding others in the nature of the wisdom-body. Furthermore, because there is no physical body, it is impossible for there to be any "going" or the like even in conventional reality. In the ultimate sense, because there is no birth, it is impossible for there to be any "going" at all. Therefore, because he has realized the nature of things as such, he becomes the lord of all the world, and because he is worthy of offerings, he is called an Arhat.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ།**
translation: That would not merely fail to be true, but would result in an absurdity; for why, by the application of terms such as "selfless," would one not also apprehend the self and the like as true? If there is no self, one might wonder, "To whom do the 'ordinary beings' refer?" In response to this, it is stated, "the childish ordinary beings," and so forth. In the ultimate sense, there are no beings; it is spoken in reliance upon the conventional, and thus there is no fault. By all of this, the elimination of the extremes of superimposition and denial is shown, thereby demonstrating how the mind is thoroughly grasped. By all of this, the profundity is directly expressed; and the teaching that the entire realm of sentient beings is the cause for establishing the great meaning of the instructions also demonstrates the vastness of the perfect mind.

Regarding the thought of how it could be immeasurable by count, the words "Subhūti, if at that time..." and so forth were spoken. By this, it is indicated that it is extremely numerous. Through counting such merit, one becomes weary, and a specific type of mental illness arises in which the mind becomes confused and bewildered. Following that, there arises a mental disturbance born from that madness. By this, the profound and the extensive are indicated. Regarding the thought of how one might know that from this Dharma discourse there could be such a result possessing count and measure, the words "Subhūti..." and so forth were spoken; in all cases, the result is only in accordance with the cause. It is not observed that a nyagrodha tree or the like, even if small, would, by possessing great essence, become a great fruit called a branch, a leaf, or a tree.

translation: By this, he teaches that if even a son or daughter of a noble family who gives away external objects, such as precious substances, comes to possess a great mass of merit, then why would the Tathāgata, who has practiced difficult deeds for countless, immeasurable eons and has cultivated them for many hundreds of ways, not possess the mass of merit? Because he has perfectly and completely realized [the truth], he is called a Samyaksambuddha. The thought here is that if it were not so, the form body would be of the nature of an insentient thing, and thus it would not be called by that name. By this, meditative equipoise and the perfect grasping of the mind are indicated. By all of these points, profundity is indicated. Because it is shown that, conventionally, the Tathāgata’s emanated form body relies upon going and so forth without obstruction throughout infinite world realms, vastness is also indicated. Since any emanated form body of the Tathāgata, as well as any mind-made body, is devoid of the nature of being one or many, it is shown to be false, like a Buddha emanated by magic; therefore, having analyzed the world of vessels and sentient beings, and having taken the state of abiding as the basis, the expression "Subhūti" and so forth is stated. Previously, it was shown that the bodhisattva on the stage of engaging through aspiration analyzes these, but now, by showing the abiding of the Bhagavan on the stage of a Buddha, there is no repetition of words. Here too, by realizing that [the Tathāgata] is devoid of the nature of being one or many through two types of methods, selflessness is taught.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Are infinitesimal particles not non-existent because they have distinct directional parts? Thinking, "How can they become an aggregation?" [the questioner] asks, "For that reason," and in response, the Bhagavan states, "If..." The thought here is this: the aggregation that is analyzed into infinitesimal particles merely as a method to reverse the grasping at a single entity is not something that the Bhagavan has stated to exist in the ultimate sense. If it were not so, since the aggregation of infinitesimal particles is famously evident to everyone, the Bhagavan would not have taught "an aggregation of infinitesimal particles," for it would be famous even without his teaching it. By this, it is shown that one should abide through aspiration and longing in such a state of abiding where the Tathāgata’s form is analyzed.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: If there were no childish ordinary beings, how could there be a Tathāgata possessing a perfect body adorned with the excellent marks and secondary signs? Thinking that ordinary beings, having generated the bodhicitta arising from the root of compassion and engaging in the perfections, become the perfect Tathāgata adorned with marks and the like, and that if those beings did not exist, there would be no root, and thus how could there be such a perfect Tathāgata—those in the assembly who have accumulated no small amount of realization, yet who are attached to forms and the like as real entities, think in this way. For their sake, focusing on the apprehension of the dharmakāya, the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth were spoken. Previously, the dharmakāya had not been established, but because this was spoken in order to establish the dharmakāya, there is no fault of verbal repetition. Realizing that the perfect marks, when examined in the ultimate sense, are not established as the essence of a composite entity or as an accumulation of atoms, and holding to the previous intention, the noble Subhūti replied, "It is not so." The Blessed One, in this very place, spoke of another justification, saying, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth.

[3-222] translation already produced for this document:
That would not merely fail to be true, but would result in an absurdity; for why, by the application of terms such as "selfless," would one not also apprehend the self and the like as true? If there is no self, one might wonder, "To whom do the 'ordinary beings' refer?" In response to this, it is stated, "the childish ordinary beings," and so forth. In the ultimate sense, there are no beings; it is spoken in reliance upon the conventional, and thus there is no fault. By all of this, the elimination of the extremes of superimposition and denial is shown, thereby demonstrating how the mind is thoroughly grasped. By all of this, the profundity is directly expressed; and the teaching that the entire realm of sentient beings is the cause for establishing the great meaning of the instructions also demonstrates the vastness of the perfect mind.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Having examined why the mass of merit is not established as existing in the ultimate sense, and in order to show both how a bodhisattva should accomplish this and how the mind should be well-grasped, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, if..." The word "if" is a synonym for "supposing."

By this, he teaches that if even a son or daughter of a noble family who gives away external objects, such as precious substances, comes to possess a great mass of merit, then why would the Tathāgata, who has practiced difficult deeds for countless, immeasurable eons and has cultivated them for many hundreds of ways, not possess the mass of merit? Therefore, although in the ultimate sense there is no mass of merit, because it exists in the conventional sense, he teaches that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish mastery over it; this also expresses its vastness.

heading: བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་མངའ་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The words "the Tathāgata does not speak" mean that he does not engage in verbal expression in the ultimate sense, for he intends that it will become known as such even without being taught. How the mass of merit does not exist in the ultimate sense has already been taught previously. By this, he teaches both that a bodhisattva who has entered into the path to accomplish the perfection of possessing the mass of merit of the Tathāgata should accomplish it by entering into meditative equipoise in which that is not perceived in the ultimate sense, and that the mind should be well-grasped by abandoning attachment to perceiving that in the ultimate sense; this also expresses its profundity.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Thinking that if there were no aggregation, why would the Bhagavan have stated, "Are those aggregations of infinitesimal particles numerous?" [Subhūti] asks, "For what reason?" The statement, "Because they are not aggregations," means that since those infinitesimal particles, which exist by being differentiated into directions such as east and north, are not established by their own nature, it is not logically sound for them to be an aggregation in the ultimate sense.

[3-243] translation already produced for this document:
Are infinitesimal particles not non-existent because they have distinct directional parts? Thinking, "How can they become an aggregation?" [the questioner] asks, "For that reason," and in response, the Bhagavan states, "If..." The thought here is this: the aggregation that is analyzed into infinitesimal particles merely as a method to reverse the grasping at a single entity is not something that the Bhagavan has stated to exist in the ultimate sense. If it were not so, since the aggregation of infinitesimal particles is famously evident to everyone, the Bhagavan would not have taught "an aggregation of infinitesimal particles," for it would be famous even without his teaching it. By this, it is shown that one should abide through aspiration and longing in such a state of abiding where the Tathāgata’s form is analyzed.

heading: བདག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Subhūti, because there is no such thing as that which is called 'one who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle,' this additional [teaching] serves to free one from grasping at a self." The explanation of the remainder is as before. If the Blessed One has already thoroughly explained that there is no self in persons or phenomena, how could it be that, even after that has been explained, grasping at a self on the part of a bodhisattva arises later at the time of realization? Since it is clear, why teach again what has already been taught? If, even though it is taught in this way, one remains confused, then the previous explanations would be endless. It is said: although it has been taught in this way, because of the power of having been strongly attached to a self since beginningless time, the confusion of some does not immediately cease, and therefore what has already been taught is taught again. By the very fact of teaching it again, the confusion of the assembly at that time ceases, so it does not become endless. The result of the Blessed One’s teaching is the turning away of the confusion of the beings to be trained; it is not without a result. Therefore, if the confusion is turned away, it does not follow that there is no result, and thus this is not a fault.

Therefore, from this inconceivable [Dharma], an inconceivable result in accordance with the causes and conditions will arise, for the power of the causes and conditions is omniscience, which is inconceivable. Here, the term "ripening" (vipāka) refers merely to the result; thus, it also includes results that are in accordance with the cause (niṣyanda-phala) and so forth. [3-167] translation already produced for this document:
Although the enjoyment of the flavor of meditative absorption (dhyāna) has been dispelled, when the time of realization (abhisamaya) draws near, those bodhisattvas who perceive their own distinction and think, "I have truly entered the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and I shall lead all sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," are free from grasping at a self. In order to teach how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should firmly grasp the mind at that time of realization, the text relies upon the fifteenth stage, and the noble Subhūti asked the Blessed One how one who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle should abide, and so forth. The teaching of the three, beginning with abiding, is exactly what the Blessed One had previously explained.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: If the Tathāgata were distinguished merely by the possession of perfect marks, then, because the reason for such a designation would be the same, why would a wheel-turning monarch not also be a Tathāgata? If one were to argue that the Blessed One’s perfect marks are distinct because they reside in a domain, are clear, and are complete, whereas those of a wheel-turning monarch are not, and therefore the latter is not called a Tathāgata, that too is unreasonable; for the distinctions of residing in a domain and so forth do not differ in any way from the nature of material things. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were distinguished by phenomena such as marks that are of the nature of material things, then a wheel-turning monarch would also be a Tathāgata, which is not the case. Thus, it is intended that the Tathāgata is distinguished solely by his realization of the nature of all phenomena exactly as they are. By this, it is shown that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in such a body, which has the Tathāgata’s wisdom as its cause. Now, in order to show that one should not be attached even to that wisdom of the Tathāgata in the ultimate sense, the dharmakāya is established, and the manner in which a bodhisattva should practice by entering into meditative equipoise is taught through two verses.

[3-223] translation already produced for this document:
If there were no childish ordinary beings, how could there be a Tathāgata possessing a perfect body adorned with the excellent marks and secondary signs? Thinking that ordinary beings, having generated the bodhicitta arising from the root of compassion and engaging in the perfections, become the perfect Tathāgata adorned with marks and the like, and that if those beings did not exist, there would be no root, and thus how could there be such a perfect Tathāgata—those in the assembly who have accumulated no small amount of realization, yet who are attached to forms and the like as real entities, think in this way. For their sake, focusing on the apprehension of the dharmakāya, the words "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth were spoken. Previously, the dharmakāya had not been established, but because this was spoken in order to establish the dharmakāya, there is no fault of verbal repetition. Realizing that the perfect marks, when examined in the ultimate sense, are not established as the essence of a composite entity or as an accumulation of atoms, and holding to the previous intention, the noble Subhūti replied, "It is not so." The Blessed One, in this very place, spoke of another justification, saying, "Subhūti, if..." and so forth.

heading: སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: If the mass of merit were non-existent, then the two types of perfect bodies of the Tathāgatas—the perfect body of excellent secondary signs and the perfect body of major marks—which are held to be born from unsurpassable merit, would also become non-existent because they would lack a cause.

[3-224] translation already produced for this document:
If the Tathāgata were distinguished merely by the possession of perfect marks, then, because the reason for such a designation would be the same, why would a wheel-turning monarch not also be a Tathāgata? If one were to argue that the Blessed One’s perfect marks are distinct because they reside in a domain, are clear, and are complete, whereas those of a wheel-turning monarch are not, and therefore the latter is not called a Tathāgata, that too is unreasonable; for the distinctions of residing in a domain and so forth do not differ in any way from the nature of material things. Therefore, if the Tathāgata were distinguished by phenomena such as marks that are of the nature of material things, then a wheel-turning monarch would also be a Tathāgata, which is not the case. Thus, it is intended that the Tathāgata is distinguished solely by his realization of the nature of all phenomena exactly as they are. By this, it is shown that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in such a body, which has the Tathāgata’s wisdom as its cause. Now, in order to show that one should not be attached even to that wisdom of the Tathāgata in the ultimate sense, the dharmakāya is established, and the manner in which a bodhisattva should practice by entering into meditative equipoise is taught through two verses.

heading: གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If it were the case that there is no such phenomenon as that which is called "one who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle," then how could the Blessed One have attained unsurpassed, truly perfect enlightenment after having received instructions from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara? If there were no attainment of perfect enlightenment, then those who think that there is no need to seek instructions because they desire to attain realization would be without instructions and separated from them; for the sake of those people, and focusing on the sixteenth location, he spoke [the words], "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. Previously, at the time of aspiring to attain the dharmakāya, the grasping at the phenomena that were taught was refuted. Now, at the time of perfect enlightenment, the attainment of perfect enlightenment is refuted; thus, this is not a repetition. In the ultimate sense, there is no phenomenon that is the nature of a knower and a known, just as was analyzed previously. Because of that, when examined, through the sequence of the arising of prajñā—beginning with that which arises from hearing, which is merely difficult—the Blessed One’s omniscience, which is self-arisen and included within the truly conventional, merely arises by its own nature. If one asks whether this is merely due to the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, even if that were the case, it is acceptable; however, the empowerment for that is common to all Buddhas, and it is not the case that it belongs only to the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara.

[3-168] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, because there is no such thing as that which is called 'one who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle,' this additional [teaching] serves to free one from grasping at a self." The explanation of the remainder is as before. If the Blessed One has already thoroughly explained that there is no self in persons or phenomena, how could it be that, even after that has been explained, grasping at a self on the part of a bodhisattva arises later at the time of realization? Since it is clear, why teach again what has already been taught? If, even though it is taught in this way, one remains confused, then the previous explanations would be endless. It is said: although it has been taught in this way, because of the power of having been strongly attached to a self since beginningless time, the confusion of some does not immediately cease, and therefore what has already been taught is taught again. By the very fact of teaching it again, the confusion of the assembly at that time ceases, so it does not become endless. The result of the Blessed One’s teaching is the turning away of the confusion of the beings to be trained; it is not without a result. Therefore, if the confusion is turned away, it does not follow that there is no result, and thus this is not a fault.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
source: གཅིག་པུར་འཛིན་པ་བསལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་གསུངས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དེ། དེ་བས་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་མེད་ན་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ལ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུ་རོལ་དང་། སྟེང་དང་འོག་དང་། ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པ་ནས་བསྐོར་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རྒྱས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཆ་ཉིད་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དུ་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེར་ཡང་དཔྱད་པ་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་གྱུར་ཀྱང་ཐུགས་མེད་དོ་ཞེ་ན། མི་རུང་སྟེ། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་ན་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་ཞིག་གྲུབ། ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་མི་འགྲུབ་སྟེ། དེ་བས་ན་ངེད་ཀྱི་འདོད་པ་ཉིད་གྲུབ་པོ། །ངེད་ནི་འདོད་རྒྱལ་དུ་རྡུལ་རྣམ་པ་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་སྨྲ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐུག་པ་མེད་ན་གང་གིས་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བརྗོད། ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཆ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཐ་དད་པ་ན་གནས་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པས་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཡན་ལག་དང་བཅས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐལ་བར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་དག་གིས་གཅིག་ཏུ་མ་ངེས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལུས་མེད་པས་ཕྱོགས་ན་མི་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་གནས་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་བས་ན། དེ་ནི་མིག་མིན་གཟུགས་ལ་མིན། །དེ་གཉིས་བར་ན་མི་གནས་ཏེ། །དེ་ནི་གང་ན་གནས་གྱུར་པ། །དེ་ནི་ཡོད་མིན་མེད་པ་མིན། །ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏེ་ཐལ་བས་ནི་ཆོག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་དང་བྲལ་བར་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ནས་སྣང་བ་མེད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཐབས་བསྟན་པས་རྣམ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དང་། སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དེ་མང་བ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ལྷག་མས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: It is merely stated to dispel the grasping at a single entity; therefore, it is called an "aggregation of infinitesimal particles." If there were no distinct directional parts, then infinitesimal particles would not be surrounded by other infinitesimal particles from the far side, the near side, above, below, and from distinct directional parts. Therefore, they would not become extensive, just as is the case with consciousness and mental factors. It is not logically sound to say that the parts themselves become infinitesimal particles, for the same analysis applies there as well. If you argue that even if they were to become so, they would have no contact, that is not acceptable; for if infinitesimal particles were to become partless in nature, what would you have established? A partless nature cannot be established as a real entity; therefore, our own position is established. We do not assert that particles are of the nature of many forms in an arbitrary way, so if infinitesimal particles have no contact, what is it that you claim is established? Since you admit that the infinitesimal particles you posit as partless entities reside in distinct directions such as east and north, you have admitted that they have directional parts; therefore, it follows that they possess limbs. Thus, because the consequence is proven, the basis of your logical reason is not established. It is also not the case that they are not fixed as one, like consciousness and mental factors, because they lack physical form and therefore do not reside in directions; they do not reside in directions such as east and north. Therefore, it is taught: "It is not the eye, nor is it form; it does not reside between those two. Where it resides, it is neither existent nor non-existent." The consequence is sufficient. By this, it is shown that having understood the absence of a nature of many, one should engage in the meditative equipoise of yoga and the firm grasping of the mind, which are the methods for making appearances non-existent. The statement, "Are those aggregations of infinitesimal particles numerous?" indicates vastness, while the remainder indicates profundity.

རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་ཐ་དད་པའི་ཕྱིར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནམ། དེ་དག་ཚོགས་སུ་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་ལ་དེའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་དང་། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། གཅིག་པུར་འཛིན་པ་བཟློག་པའི་ཐབས་ཙམ་དུ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དབྱེ་བར་ཚོགས་པ་དེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པའི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གྲགས་པར་གྱུར་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བཀའ་མི་སྩོལ་ཏེ། མ་གསུངས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་གྲགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་རྣམ་པར་གཞིག་པར་བཞུགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་། སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-243] translation already produced for this document:
Are infinitesimal particles not non-existent because they have distinct directional parts? Thinking, "How can they become an aggregation?" [the questioner] asks, "For that reason," and in response, the Bhagavan states, "If..." The thought here is this: the aggregation that is analyzed into infinitesimal particles merely as a method to reverse the grasping at a single entity is not something that the Bhagavan has stated to exist in the ultimate sense. If it were not so, since the aggregation of infinitesimal particles is famously evident to everyone, the Bhagavan would not have taught "an aggregation of infinitesimal particles," for it would be famous even without his teaching it. By this, it is shown that one should abide through aspiration and longing in such a state of abiding where the Tathāgata’s form is analyzed.

གལ་ཏེ་ཚོགས་མེད་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དེ་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་བཀའ་སྩལ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ཚོགས་མ་མཆིས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཤར་དང་བྱང་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་དབྱེ་བས་གནས་པ་དེ་དག་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པས་ཡང་དག་པར་ན་ཚོགས་སུ་མི་རིགས་སོ། །
[3-244] translation already produced for this document:
Thinking that if there were no aggregation, why would the Bhagavan have stated, "Are those aggregations of infinitesimal particles numerous?" [Subhūti] asks, "For what reason?" The statement, "Because they are not aggregations," means that since those infinitesimal particles, which exist by being differentiated into directions such as east and north, are not established by their own nature, it is not logically sound for them to be an aggregation in the ultimate sense.

heading: སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The body of major marks will be explained below, in the manner of the "ox and the bull." Regarding this, the intention of the noble Subhūti is as follows: just as the mass of merit is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of any inherent mass, so too is the form body unborn. Therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body in the ultimate sense. In the conventional sense, however, the form body exists just like a Buddha emanated by magic, and therefore it is appropriate for it to arise from the mass of merit. Thus, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that [form body] through such devotion to the form of a Buddha emanated by magic. There is no repetition of words here, for while at the stage of conduct through devotion one is at the time of aspiring to attain the form body and at the time of making offerings and service to the Tathāgata, one has abandoned such grasping; now, at the stage of the pure superior intention, this is taught in order to dispel the evil conceptualization of those in the retinue who claim that a bodhisattva who has entered the path to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata has grasping toward form.

དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཇི་ལྟར་འབད་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དཔེ་བྱད་བཟང་པོའི་སྐུ་ཡིན་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །

Therefore, in order to fully accomplish the two types of perfect bodies of the Tathāgata, and for the sake of the bodhisattva who thinks about how to exert effort toward that, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" with the intention of focusing on the perfect form body of the Tathāgatas. heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
source: ཇི་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། མཐོང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་དག་ཏུའོ། །སུ་དག་གིས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེ་ན། ལོག་པས་སྤོང་བར་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སོ། །གཟུགས་སུ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་གང་ཟག་གཟུགས་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ།དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་ལ་སོགས་པས་བརྒྱན་པ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་གི་གཟུགས་ཅན་དུ་མཐོང་བར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྒྲར་ཤེས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདག་གིས་སྒྲ་ལས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་དེ་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་འདི་འདྲ་བ་ཞིག་གོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་ཐོས་པར་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་འདི་གཉིས་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། དེས་ནི་བྱེ་བྲག་ཕྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་བསྡུའོ། །སྐྱེ་བོ་ལོག་པས་སྤོང་བར་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ལམ་ལོག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ང་ཡང་དག་པར་མི་མཐོང་ངོ་། །འདིས་སྤོང་བས་ན་སྤོང་བར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ་ལམ་ལ་བྱའོ། །དེ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པས་ལོག་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་བའི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འོ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཇི་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ལྟ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་གཤའ་མ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་གིས་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཟོད་མ་ནས་ཞི་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་དང་། ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་དང་། མཚན་མ་མེད་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རྣམ་གྲངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པའོ། །
translation: How should one not view him? By way of the conventional designations of seeing and so forth. Who are those by whom he is not seen? Those who have entered into the path of wrong abandonment. By the phrase "viewing him as form," this indicates the conventional designation of viewing a person who is attached to form as having the form of a person or a phenomenon, adorned in the ultimate sense with marks and so forth. The phrase "knowing him by sound" means that I know the Tathāgata in such a way, thinking, "He is like this, he is of this nature," based on sound. This indicates the conventional designation of hearing. These two conventional designations are illustrative; they also encompass differentiating and cognizing. Those beings who have entered into the path of wrong abandonment do not see me correctly because they have entered into a wrong path. Because this abandons, it is called "abandonment," which refers to the path. That is "wrong" because it has become perverted; that, too, is a cause for not seeing. If one wonders, "Then how should the Buddha be viewed?" the text states, "viewing him as the dharmatā," and so forth. The true nature of phenomena is what is called the dharmatā; because it is established by reasoning and scripture, it is the essence of what has been peaceful from the beginning. That very thing is expressed by synonyms such as "suchness," "dharmadhātu," "ultimate reality," "signlessness," and "the absolute."

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Now, focusing on the fact that the Tathāgata dwells by having deconstructed the world of sentient beings, the passage beginning with "the world system of the great trichiliocosm" was spoken. Since the world of the receptacle has already been explained, here the "world system" is understood as the world of sentient beings. The mention of "great trichiliocosm" in both cases signifies that the world systems are limitless. Therefore, the statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of them as not being world systems" means that the world of sentient beings, which is the nature of the five aggregates, is also devoid of the nature of being one or many, and is thus explained as before. By this, it is shown that a Bodhisattva should abide in such a state—where the Tathāgata dwells by having deconstructed the world of sentient beings—through aspiration and prayer. By making it devoid of appearance, it is also shown how this meditative equipoise is to be accomplished. Now, in order to show how the mind is to be firmly grasped, the question "Why is that?" is asked, and it is to be connected with the statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of them as not being world systems."

translation: If there were no manifest awakening to complete enlightenment, how could the Blessed One have been prophesied to attain complete enlightenment? Thinking this, he spoke the words beginning with "Subhūti, if..." The intention is this: If, in the ultimate sense, the Blessed One had manifestedly awakened to complete enlightenment exactly as the phenomena he realized for himself are, or if he had developed the pride of thinking, "I have manifestedly awakened to phenomena," then, because he would have already attained complete enlightenment and would be attached to a perversion, he would not have been prophesied by the Tathāgata. However, because at that time there was no manifest awakening to enlightenment for me, and no attachment to phenomena or the like, I was prophesied to abide on the path of authentic wisdom precisely because I was not perverted. The statement "there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is manifestedly awakened to" serves to point out that the conceptualization of having received instructions from Dīpaṃkara is a discordant factor, and in order to abandon that conceptualization, it also points to the aspiration and the making of vows. By mentioning Dīpaṃkara merely as a sign, all conceptualization of grasping at phenomena is turned back. By the statement "there is none," its profundity is also expressed.

heading: སྐུ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Thinking, "How then is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?" one asks, "For what reason?" and connects this with the statement, "One should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body, because it is perfected." This means it is not established; it is not established as the nature of a form body possessing limbs, nor as the nature of an accumulation of atoms, just as previously analyzed. By this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should accomplish it. The phrase "therefore" means that it exists conventionally. It is not that it is non-existent in every way, like the horns of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of nihilism, it is shown how the mind should be firmly grasped. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should exert themselves to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, the vast is also taught. Having taken the perfect body of major marks as the subject, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth; all the explanations here are the same as the preceding ones.

[3-196] translation already produced for this document:
The body of major marks will be explained below, in the manner of the "ox and the bull." Regarding this, the intention of the noble Subhūti is as follows: just as the mass of merit is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of any inherent mass, so too is the form body unborn. Therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body in the ultimate sense. In the conventional sense, however, the form body exists just like a Buddha emanated by magic, and therefore it is appropriate for it to arise from the mass of merit. Thus, it is taught that a bodhisattva should abide with aspiration and prayer in order to accomplish that [form body] through such devotion to the form of a Buddha emanated by magic. There is no repetition of words here, for while at the stage of conduct through devotion one is at the time of aspiring to attain the form body and at the time of making offerings and service to the Tathāgata, one has abandoned such grasping; now, at the stage of the pure superior intention, this is taught in order to dispel the evil conceptualization of those in the retinue who claim that a bodhisattva who has entered the path to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata has grasping toward form.

heading: གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By showing that the instructions were thoroughly sought for the sake of samyaksambodhi, the vastness of this [teaching] is expressed. This is because it is exceedingly superior to the instructions of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: In response, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "If." If the world of sentient beings were, as it is commonly reputed, to exist ultimately as a coarse, unitary entity, then at that time, the Tathāgata, having realized the reality of entities exactly as they abide, would be grasping it as a whole. Therefore, the cause of grasping at a self is merely the grasping at the nature of the aggregates as a whole; thus, that very thing becomes the Tathāgata’s firm grasping at a whole, and it is intended that this has not been abandoned. That is not the case. Therefore, the grasping at a whole which the Blessed One taught to childish beings as the cause of grasping at a self in another context is, in the ultimate sense, a lack of grasping, because there is no nature of a grasped whole that is either one or many.

Thinking, "How then is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?" one asks, "For what reason?" and connects this with the statement, "One should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body, because it is perfected." This means it is not established; it is not established as the nature of a form body possessing limbs, nor as the nature of an accumulation of atoms, just as previously analyzed. By this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should accomplish it. The phrase "therefore" means that it exists conventionally. It is not that it is non-existent in every way, like the horns of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of nihilism, it is shown how the mind should be firmly grasped. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should exert themselves to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, the vast is also taught. Having taken the perfect body of major marks as the subject, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth; all the explanations here are the same as the preceding ones.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
source: དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་ན་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོད་པས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་སྟེ། དེ་དག་གི་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་སོ། །ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པས་ཡང་དག་པ་སྟེ། དེའི་མཐར་གྱུར་པས་ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་འོ། །དེ་ལ་སྔོན་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དངོས་པོའི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་པས་མཚན་མ་མེད་པའོ། །ཡེ་ཤེས་དམ་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཡིན་པས་དོན་དམ་པའོ། །ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐུའི་སྒྲ་ནི་རང་བཞིན་ལ་བྱའོ། །དེས་ན་དོན་འདིར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གང་དག་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པ་དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཏེ། གང་དག་གང་གི་རང་བཞིན་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་དེའི་ངོ་བོར་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། གཞན་ལ་གཞན་གྱི་ངོ་བོར་བལྟ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་ནི་སྣང་བའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ན་དེས་མཚོན་པ་དེ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་སྙམ་པ་ལ་བརྟགས་ནས། ཆོས་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཅི་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་རིག་གམ། འོན་ཏེ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་ན་ཉེས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རམ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་མི་ནུས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་གྲུབ་ན་ནི་དེའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་ནུས་པ་ཞིག་ན་གང་གི་ཚེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཅན་རང་གི་ངོ་བོར་གྲུབ་པ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་རང་གི་རྒྱུད་འབའ་ཞིག་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ནུས་ཏེ། དེ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དགོངས་པའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཆོས་ཅན་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པས་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ཉེས་པ་མེད་དེ། གང་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའོ། །ཆོས་ཉིད་ནི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡིན་པས་དེ་ནི་དེ་དང་མི་མཐུན་པ་སྐྱེ་བ་འཛིན་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུང་། བུམ་པ་འཛིན་པས་ནི་དེའི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་འཛིན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་བ་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་དེ་སྐད་སྟོན་ཏོ། །
translation:
Because it exists in that way at all times, it is *tathatā* (suchness). Since all the qualities of a Buddha arise by taking that as their object, and because it serves as their cause, it is *dharmadhātu* (the expanse of phenomena). Because it is not erroneous, it is *yathārtha* (the real), and because it is the culmination of that, it is *bhūtakoṭi* (the ultimate limit). Because all marks of entities, such as blue and so forth, are absent in it, it is *animitta* (signless). Because it is the object of the supreme wisdom, it is *paramārtha* (the ultimate).

Thinking, "For what reason should it be viewed as *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena)?" the text states "Dharmakāya." The term "kāya" (body) refers to the nature. Therefore, the meaning here is as follows: those who are established as a Tathāgata, having the cause of perfect wisdom, are in the ultimate sense the nature of the *dharma*. One should view those things as being of the essence of that which they are the nature of; one should not view one thing as having the essence of another. If that were the case, then *dharmatā* would become the nature of appearances.

If that is not the case, then thinking, "How can one be capable of seeing those things indicated by it?" the text states "Dharmatā" and so forth. Is it that one does not see because one is incapable? Or is it that if one were to fully understand it, it would involve a fault? Thinking this, the text states "incapable" and so forth. If the nature of a *dharmin* (a phenomenon possessing properties) were established, then one might be capable of cognizing its *dharmatā*. However, at the time when, in the ultimate sense, there is no *dharmin* established as having its own essence, how could one be capable of cognizing that *dharmatā* as a separate continuum? The intention is that it does not exist as something separate.

If that is the case, then if the essence of perfect wisdom—the *dharmin*—and the Buddhas themselves are not established in the ultimate sense and thus are not seen, how then should one view it as *dharmatā*? There is no fault in that, for it is precisely by not seeing all *dharmins* in the ultimate sense that one sees *dharmatā*. Since *dharmatā* is of the essence of non-arising, how could it be grasped by grasping at arising, which is incompatible with it? Grasping at a vase does not constitute grasping at its non-arising. By this, it teaches that one should not view the Tathāgata as a *rūpakāya* (form body), but should view him as a *dharmakāya*.

Thinking, "How then is the form body of the Tathāgatas taught?" one asks, "For what reason?" and connects this with the statement, "One should not view the Tathāgata as being the form body, because it is perfected." This means it is not established; it is not established as the nature of a form body possessing limbs, nor as the nature of an accumulation of atoms, just as previously analyzed. By this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should accomplish it. The phrase "therefore" means that it exists conventionally. It is not that it is non-existent in every way, like the horns of a rabbit. By this, having refuted the extreme of nihilism, it is shown how the mind should be firmly grasped. By all these points, the profound is taught. By teaching that bodhisattvas should exert themselves to accomplish the perfect form body of the Tathāgata conventionally, the vast is also taught. Having taken the perfect body of major marks as the subject, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth; all the explanations here are the same as the preceding ones.
