heading: གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If there were no dharma to which the Tathāgata had fully and perfectly awakened as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then how could he be a Tathāgata? Just as the previous Buddhas attained full and perfect enlightenment, so too does he attain it here, and because he is called a Tathāgata, one might wonder: "Since there is no dharma whatsoever to be fully and perfectly awakened to, how can he be one?" It is because of this thought that the question was asked, and in response, the words "Subhūti, the Tathāgata..." and so forth were spoken. "Suchness" refers to the unerring nature of phenomena, which is the essence of being peaceful from the very beginning. Because this is common to all phenomena, the term "perfect" is added to distinguish it; "perfect" refers to the wisdom of the Tathāgata, as it is the meaning of being unerring. That which is the dharmatā of suchness, which is unborn in the ultimate sense, is called the Tathāgata, as it is said: "The dharma that is always unborn is the Tathāgata." Since the dharmatā is not, in the ultimate sense, other than the phenomena themselves, the intent is that the Tathāgata is the exalted wisdom that exists as a superimposition upon the perfect conventional reality, which is the realization of the dharmatā—the unborn nature of all phenomena in the ultimate sense—which is the essence of non-conceptual, singular joy. Furthermore, because it is unborn in the ultimate sense, there is nothing to be grasped or held, and thus, in the ultimate sense, there is no dharma whatsoever to which he has been fully and perfectly awakened; the intent is simply that, relying upon the perfect conventional, he is called a Tathāgata because of how he has been fully and perfectly awakened through that exalted wisdom.

heading: **ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ།**
translation: Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of possessing perfect physical marks, it is reasonable that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment arises from the causes of perfect physical marks. In order to dispel the doubt that a bodhisattva, having been seen by physiognomists as possessing perfect physical marks, was therefore prophesied by the Bhagavan to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" The intention is that if perfect physical marks were the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at that time a cakravartin would also become [a Buddha]. There is no fault in saying that the cause of the prophecy is not that physiognomists saw such signs. By this, the supreme cultivation of the mind is taught. By all of this, profundity is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which has realized the nature of all phenomena without exception in conventional reality, vastness is also taught.

translation: What is being taught? It is taught that the expression "grasping at a whole" is conventionally used, but because it does not exist in the ultimate sense, that phenomenon is inexpressible. If there is no such grasped whole, then at that time there is also no grasping of it; thinking, "How then can it be called 'grasping at a whole' conventionally?" one examines it, and it is taught that "it is grasped by childish, ordinary beings." Childish beings, due to the power of delusion, grasp at what does not exist as if it did exist; thus, the convention is applied based on their way of thinking, and it is intended that there is no contradiction. Therefore, they are called "childish beings"; if it were not so, how could they be childish beings, given that they apply conventions according to how things actually are? Here, how the mind is to be firmly grasped has already been taught. The extensive and the profound should also be applied here as before. By this, it is taught that when all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, empty of intrinsic nature, how could the Tathāgata’s form body and wisdom body be considered to have an ultimate nature, since at the root there are no sentient beings? Now, the passage beginning with "Subhūti, if some..." teaches the method by which one should be equanimous in all situations, having entered into the yogic meditative equipoise. The connection is to be applied as follows: if there is no grasping at a whole, then at that time there is no view of the transitory collection, which arises from the root; therefore, wondering how the Blessed One taught the view of the transitory collection among the five views, for that purpose, the passage beginning with "Subhūti, if some..." was spoken. By teaching here how to be non-conceptual, who is non-conceptual, what is to be non-conceptualized, by what one is non-conceptual, and what non-conceptualization is, the method of entering into yogic meditative equipoise is correctly taught. Regarding that, from "Subhūti, if some..." up to "therefore it is called 'view of a self'," this teaches how to be non-conceptual. How so? Other non-Buddhist schools explain a self, but the Blessed One, establishing that there is no self in the person, taught the "view of a self" in order to refute the self.

[3-247] translation already produced for this document:
In response, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "If." If the world of sentient beings were, as it is commonly reputed, to exist ultimately as a coarse, unitary entity, then at that time, the Tathāgata, having realized the reality of entities exactly as they abide, would be grasping it as a whole. Therefore, the cause of grasping at a self is merely the grasping at the nature of the aggregates as a whole; thus, that very thing becomes the Tathāgata’s firm grasping at a whole, and it is intended that this has not been abandoned. That is not the case. Therefore, the grasping at a whole which the Blessed One taught to childish beings as the cause of grasping at a self in another context is, in the ultimate sense, a lack of grasping, because there is no nature of a grasped whole that is either one or many.

heading: གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
source: དོན་དམ་པར་འཆད་པ་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཤད་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་ངས་ཆོས་བསྟན་ཏོ་སྙམ་དུ་མི་དགོངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཡིན་ན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་འཆད་པ་པོ་སྟེ་བདག་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱི་ནང་གི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པ་སྟེ། བྱེད་པ་གཟུགས་སམ་སྒྲའི་བདག་ཉིད་མེད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ནི་སྔར་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་ཟིན་ཏེ། དངོས་པོ་མཐའ་དག་ལ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཁྱབ་པར་སྔར་བསྒྲུབས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་འཆད་པ་པོ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། བཤད་པ་མ་བརྟགས་ན་དགའ་བས་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་པ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཏུ་ཟད་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དངོས་པོའི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་བསྟན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་ཁ་ཅིག་མགོ་རྨོངས་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་གསུམ་པོ་ཡོད་པར་སེམས་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་ཅིར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་པ་ལ། རབ་འབྱོར་སུ་ཞིག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །སྐུར་པ་ནི་དོན་མེད་པར་གླེང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་མེད་པ་དེས་གླེང་བར་ནུས་སྙམ་པ་ལ། ལོག་པར་འཛིན་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པས་ལོག་པར་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །འདིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྲག་ཅ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟ་བུར་ཤེས་པས་འཇུག་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་དེ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: In the ultimate sense, because there is no speaker, no object to be spoken of, and no speech, the Tathāgata does not think, "I have taught the Dharma." If it were not so, it would be a misconception, and therefore he would not be omniscient. As for the speaker—the self and so forth—the object to be spoken of—external and internal phenomena—and the speech—the act, whether in the nature of form or sound—that they do not exist has already been explained in detail, because it was previously established that all phenomena are pervaded by emptiness. In the conventional sense, the speaker, the object to be spoken of, and the speech are merely designations for the sake of convenience, which are acceptable when not analyzed, but they do not exist in the ultimate sense. If, even though the suchness of phenomena has been taught in this way, some are confused and think that the three exist in the ultimate sense, then what would happen? Thinking this, [the sūtra] states, "Subhūti, who..." and so forth. Denigration is because it speaks of what is non-existent. Regarding the thought of how one who is non-existent can speak, it states, "by grasping at what is false," meaning that because one is attached to a misconception, one grasps falsely, and thus it is said that it does not exist. By this, it is taught how a bodhisattva should abide, namely, that a bodhisattva who engages in the perfect speech of the Tathāgata should engage by knowing it to be like an echo and so forth.

translation: If, because all phenomena are non-existent in the ultimate sense, that reality cannot be cognized, then in that case you would become a proponent of nihilism.

Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of possessing perfect physical marks, it is reasonable that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment arises from the causes of perfect physical marks. In order to dispel the doubt that a bodhisattva, having been seen by physiognomists as possessing perfect physical marks, was therefore prophesied by the Bhagavan to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" The intention is that if perfect physical marks were the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at that time a cakravartin would also become [a Buddha]. There is no fault in saying that the cause of the prophecy is not that physiognomists saw such signs. By this, the supreme cultivation of the mind is taught. By all of this, profundity is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which has realized the nature of all phenomena without exception in conventional reality, vastness is also taught.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: By thoroughly dismantling the view of a self, one establishes the selflessness of phenomena; this is what is meant by the inquiry, "How did the Tathāgata speak of that which is not a view?" If one does not grasp that view of a self as being truly existent, then by engaging in this way, the bodhisattva enters into meditative equipoise; because there is no conceptualization, that is the method for entering into it.

heading: གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation:
Regarding the thought, "Why is it not said that he has perfectly awakened to buddhahood in dependence upon the ultimate?" he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whoever..." The phrase "Why is that?" is to be connected with the phrase "is not true." The remainder is easy to understand and is not explained. If one wonders, "Then what is the reality of that which is posited as the Tathāgata having perfectly awakened to buddhahood in terms of conventional truth?" he spoke the words "what phenomenon." "What" refers to phenomena characterized by form and so forth. The statement "there is no truth in that" means that because the mode of appearance is like an illusion, when examined, no power is produced. Because they are utterly non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit, there is also no falsehood, because in their unexamined nature they appear like an illusion. Alternatively, because no phenomenon is established in the ultimate sense, there is no truth. Since no truth to be analyzed is established, and because all phenomena are unborn, there is also no falsehood. By this, having blocked the extremes of superimposition and denigration, he establishes the middle way and leads one to enter into the meditative equilibrium of yoga. The phrase "therefore" means: because in the ultimate sense all phenomena are unborn, there is neither truth nor falsehood. The Tathāgata is also distinguished by the complete purity of the unborn nature of phenomena; therefore, because the unborn nature of phenomena is common to all:
"The Tathāgata is the constant source of phenomena;
All phenomena are like the Sugata.
Those with childish minds, grasping at marks,
Engage with phenomena that do not exist in the world."
By saying this and so forth, the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.

translation: If those three things, such as the explanation, did not exist, how could this diverse nature of words and speech, by which the Bhagavan taught the Dharma—teaching the selflessness of persons and phenomena—be renowned? If they do exist, then that which is to be taught by them, the explanation to be given, and the speaker who teaches them must also exist; thus, thinking that all three must exist by implication, the question "Why is that?" was asked, and here the answer is given as "the teaching of the Dharma." He thinks as follows: If the teaching of the Dharma existed ultimately, would it be an entity of its own characteristic or an entity of a general characteristic? The first alternative is not the case, because all ultimate own-characteristics have been clarified extensively before. The second is also not the case, because if there were no own-characteristic, there would be no basis, and thus nothing at all. If one accepts a general characteristic as a real entity, it is included solely within the own-characteristic, and since that is clarified, the former is also clarified. If one thinks that a general characteristic is an imputed entity by excluding others, then the teaching of the Dharma would be meaningless, and one would be proving what is already established. Even if one were to allow that an own-characteristic exists ultimately, it would not be reasonable for it to teach the Dharma, because the imputation of words by others upon an imputed entity, such as a clear sound, is contradictory in terms of performing a function through sequence or non-sequence; being devoid of all efficacy, it has no connection to consciousness or anything else, and how could it become words while doing nothing at all? Even the impermanence of an own-characteristic is not reasonable as words, because when it is conventionally designated, it is seen, but when it is conventionally established, there is no continuity. It is not reasonable that the conventional designation and the conventional establishment are different, for that would lead to an absurd consequence.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation:
Because of the doubt that the Tathāgata also does not exist, and therefore a non-abiding nirvāṇa is not established, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think, those who have truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle," in order to focus on not abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. There is no analysis that destroys what has occurred, because one realizes the nature of phenomena just as it abides. Therefore, it is said:
"In this, there is nothing to be removed,
And nothing to be established.
Truly seeing the truth itself,
One who sees truly is liberated."
There is no analysis of nihilism that obstructs the arising of future phenomena, because the nature of phenomena is taught just as it abides. Since it is accepted that all phenomena, when not analyzed, arise according to conditions as they are, the Buddha Bhagavan, by the power of great compassion, possesses emanations and so forth in the nature of true conventional reality; and because it is accepted that he does not cut the stream of entering saṃsāra by teaching methods just as they are for the sake of those to be trained, by this, the Bhagavan’s non-abiding in nirvāṇa is taught, and the necessity of abiding in such a body of the Bhagavan through aspiration and prayer is also taught. Because it is considered that if it were accepted that the Bhagavan enters saṃsāra in that way, he would become saṃsāra itself, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Again, Subhūti," in order to teach the state of not abiding in saṃsāra.

[3-228] translation already produced for this document:
Even though the Tathāgata is not of the nature of possessing perfect physical marks, it is reasonable that the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment arises from the causes of perfect physical marks. In order to dispel the doubt that a bodhisattva, having been seen by physiognomists as possessing perfect physical marks, was therefore prophesied by the Bhagavan to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he spoke [the words] beginning with, "Subhūti, what do you think?" The intention is that if perfect physical marks were the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then at that time a cakravartin would also become [a Buddha]. There is no fault in saying that the cause of the prophecy is not that physiognomists saw such signs. By this, the supreme cultivation of the mind is taught. By all of this, profundity is taught. By teaching the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which has realized the nature of all phenomena without exception in conventional reality, vastness is also taught.

[3-229] source:
གལ་ཏེ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པར་མི་ནུས་ན་དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་ཁྱེད་ཆད་པར་སྨྲ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-229] translation already produced for this document:
If, because all phenomena are non-existent in the ultimate sense, that reality cannot be cognized, then in that case you would become a proponent of nihilism.

heading: གདམས་ངག་དང་མི་ལྡན་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If these phenomena are exclusively unproduced, then how can one think of them as "all phenomena"? In response to this, the statement beginning with "Subhūti, 'all phenomena'..." was spoken. The meaning here is as follows: it is not that they are designated as such because they exist in an ultimate sense; although phenomena such as form do not exist in an ultimate sense, they are called "all phenomena" because, relying upon unexamined conventional reality that is not ultimate, one grasps their specific and general characteristics. They are not so in an ultimate sense, for even when one sees everything that resides therein, all conventional designations are absent. By this, the subduing of distraction is taught.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Subhūti, the phrase "has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptuality. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that toward which one is to be non-conceptual. The phrases "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" express by what means one is to be non-conceptual. By what means is one to be non-conceptual? By knowledge, by vision, and by resolution. Regarding these, knowledge is the wisdom arising from hearing. Vision is the wisdom arising from reflection, for it is that which brings about realization. Resolution is the wisdom arising from meditation; here, the term "resolution" is intended to express a superior aspiration. That is accomplished through the power of meditation; therefore, the wisdom arising from meditation is spoken of as "resolution" when in the stage of the factors concordant with certainty.

[3-250] translation already produced for this document:
By thoroughly dismantling the view of a self, one establishes the selflessness of phenomena; this is what is meant by the inquiry, "How did the Tathāgata speak of that which is not a view?" If one does not grasp that view of a self as being truly existent, then by engaging in this way, the bodhisattva enters into meditative equipoise; because there is no conceptualization, that is the method for entering into it.

heading: གསུང་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Therefore, because there is no subsequent progression, it is not reasonable to express even its own intrinsic nature. If one were to claim that a general entity is also something to be expressed, then because it has become the essence of what is to be expressed, it is the essence of its own intrinsic nature, and thus there is no progression to another object. It is also not reasonable for a single entity to pervade many distinct particulars that are separated by place, time, and so forth. For if the entire self were to be complete in one particular, then at that time, there would be no other nature connected to other particulars that could be understood by whatever nature of that one entity was fully imagined; for the single entity would be lost. If it were to pervade by a single part, it would result in the fault of being composed of parts and not being fully grasped. Thus, if one holds that as many distinct particulars as there are, they are established as being pervaded by a single part of it, then grasping one particular would be grasping a single part, and one might wonder if it is appropriate to grasp it in that way. However, since there is no simultaneous grasping of distinct particulars—which are separated by age, place, time, and so forth—by grasping them from a single particular, it results in there being no conceptualization. Therefore, the expressed and the expression are reasonable only as the essence of a superimposed form, not as they are in reality. For that very reason, the Tathāgata has stated elsewhere: "Whatever names are used to express whatever phenomena, those names do not exist in them; that is the suchness of phenomena." Furthermore, the explanation is also false; thus, the teaching to be explained and the indication that there is an explainer also come from that same door, and are therefore merely particulars. The Tathāgata did not teach them separately as if they were devoid of both. By this, it is shown how a Bodhisattva should practice and how the mind should be well-grasped. By all of this, the profound is shown.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: "Selflessness" means that, like an illusion, it is dependent upon others. It is not the nature of a self by itself, for if it were permanent, it would be contradictory as a cause due to [the issues of] sequence and non-sequence; and if it were not a cause, it would do nothing, and thus it would be impossible for it to be a bestower of blessings. There is also no self that has been blessed by another. Therefore, in both ways, all phenomena are selfless. As it is said: "O monks, childish beings who lack learning designate and engage in 'self' and 'mine,' but in this [reality], there is no 'self' or 'mine'." By this, the patience regarding the selflessness of the person is shown for all phenomena. By the phrase "non-arising," the patience regarding the selflessness of phenomena is shown. If entities were to arise, would they arise from having no cause or from having a cause? If one speculates that they arise from having a cause, would they arise from a permanent cause or an impermanent cause? Regarding that, since entities appear occasionally, the first speculation is not tenable, for if they were independent, there would be no distinction in any respect, and they would be permanently existent or non-existent, just like the time of existence and non-existence. Therefore, because they arise occasionally, the second position is also not tenable, for if the power of permanent things cannot be differentiated by other auxiliary conditions, and if they are dependent on nothing, then why would they produce results sequentially rather than simultaneously? It is not reasonable that a result whose causes are complete would not appear occasionally; why then would it arise sequentially? Those who assert that there is an intrinsic nature as the cause of entities are also, in reality, admitting that there is no existence, for if an intrinsic nature were established, it would be a cause, but if it is not established, it is not, because it is characterized by being devoid of all power.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: The statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of that as being without perception" is presented here as a logical reason. Because that which is to be perceived is itself empty of the nature of being one or many, in the ultimate sense, it is without perception. The Tathāgata spoke of it in another way by relying upon the conventional. The intention is that if one knows it to be false and abides in that, how could one become conceptually attached? The method for entering into meditative equipoise in all situations has been explained. The absence of defilement is also of two types: the absence of defilement in teaching and the absence of defilement in cyclic existence.

[3-251] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, the phrase "has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptuality. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that toward which one is to be non-conceptual. The phrases "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" express by what means one is to be non-conceptual. By what means is one to be non-conceptual? By knowledge, by vision, and by resolution. Regarding these, knowledge is the wisdom arising from hearing. Vision is the wisdom arising from reflection, for it is that which brings about realization. Resolution is the wisdom arising from meditation; here, the term "resolution" is intended to express a superior aspiration. That is accomplished through the power of meditation; therefore, the wisdom arising from meditation is spoken of as "resolution" when in the stage of the factors concordant with certainty.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If there is no phenomenon whatsoever that the Tathāgata has perfectly realized, then how can a bodhisattva take up the instructions and realize the selflessness of phenomena and persons? Thinking this, the statement beginning with "Just as, for example..." was spoken to demonstrate realization. This teaches realization through the attainment of primordial wisdom and the absence of pride. What is the nature of this attained primordial wisdom? It relies on two types of primordial wisdom: the primordial wisdom that fully grasps the lineage, and the primordial wisdom of equality. Among these, the primordial wisdom that fully grasps the lineage is that which, once attained, causes one to be born into the lineage of the Tathāgata and be certain of the lineage of the Buddha. By being born of it, one possesses a body. "Possessing" means that which is made one's own; the "body" is the body of the Tathāgata, and whoever attains that possesses the body. Thinking, "How is it known that this primordial wisdom is attained?" the phrase "great body" was spoken. By this, it is shown that having attained the primordial wisdom of equality through the selflessness of persons and phenomena, one realizes [the truth]; therefore, it is taught as the primordial wisdom of the lineage. Through that primordial wisdom of equality, one realizes that all sentient beings are selfless in terms of persons and phenomena, and thus one gathers them into the self alone. Therefore, because it gathers the bodies of all sentient beings into the self, it is a "great body." This is not merely a literal meaning, for in this way, because all sentient beings are gathered into the self, it is called a "body." And because they are extremely numerous, it is a "great body," so it is not merely a literal meaning. By this, the vastness of this state is expressed.

[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
If these phenomena are exclusively unproduced, then how can one think of them as "all phenomena"? In response to this, the statement beginning with "Subhūti, 'all phenomena'..." was spoken. The meaning here is as follows: it is not that they are designated as such because they exist in an ultimate sense; although phenomena such as form do not exist in an ultimate sense, they are called "all phenomena" because, relying upon unexamined conventional reality that is not ultimate, one grasps their specific and general characteristics. They are not so in an ultimate sense, for even when one sees everything that resides therein, all conventional designations are absent. By this, the subduing of distraction is taught.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
source: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་བདུན་ཏེ། དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་དང་། ཆོས་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ་དང་། བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའོ། །
translation: The perfection of the mind consists of seven distinct aspects: the foundations of mindfulness, the attainment of perfect awakening, the designation of the great meaning of the Dharma, the designation of the great meaning of the instructions, the complete apprehension of the dharmakāya, the non-abiding in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, and the complete purity of dwelling.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: The intention is this: the realization of a Bodhisattva is distinguished merely by the arising of superior primordial wisdom that relies upon valid conventional reality; in the ultimate sense, however, there is neither a realizer nor anything to be realized. To teach this, the noble Subhūti addressed the Tathāgata, saying, "The Tathāgata possesses a human body," and so forth. By this, he indicates in essence the discordant factor of being attached to having a body and a great body. In order to abandon that, he teaches that one should abide through aspiration and prayer.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation:
If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is established, then one must admit that it is established without a cause; for if one does not accept that there is some other, distinct cause, how could it not be causeless? Since a phenomenon is not other than its intrinsic nature, if it is established, it is established as such, and thus it becomes causeless. If it were not so, then since it would not be established when it is established, how could it be of an intrinsic nature that is non-distinct from that? Therefore, the refutation of the position that asserts causelessness is the same here as well.

It is also not appropriate to posit a third position, because it is contradictory for a cause to exist either simultaneously or non-simultaneously with the effect. For if it were to become a cause in this way, one might wonder whether it would be simultaneous with the effect or at a different time. It cannot be simultaneous, because the entity itself, not having attained its own state, is devoid of all capacity and thus has no connection to any effect whatsoever. The entity itself is merely the intrinsic nature of the state of having attained the effect simultaneously with it, according to its own nature; there is no connection of that to the effect.

If they are at different times, then it would be separated by another time, and it would become like the Vaibhāṣikas, who accept the cause of maturation as a cause, or it would arise from an offering; or perhaps it would be like the Sautrāntikas, who claim that the destruction and arising of cause and effect are equal, like the rising and falling of the pans of a scale. If the effect arises after being separated by another time, then one would have to admit that it arises from the very state of destruction. Since that is devoid of all capacity, it is not reasonable for destruction to be the entity of a cause.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: In this regard, if there is no perception of phenomena, then when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, if that perception arises, how could there be no thorough affliction? Thinking, "If one abides until the end of cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion, how could one not be thoroughly afflicted by the perception of phenomena?" and having examined this, the Tathāgata, through that very perfection of his mind, teaches that there is no thorough affliction in teaching, and through the verse, he shows that there is no thorough affliction in cyclic existence; for this reason, he says "Subhūti" and so forth. Previously, in other contexts, the praises of world-systems were taught to express merit, but now, in the context of there being no thorough affliction, he does not state the merit when teaching the infinite world-systems, so that the words do not become repetitive. Here too, the reasoning should be stated as before. "Having taken up" means having recited it by heart. "Grasping" refers to the words. "Reading" refers to reading from a book or the like. "Comprehending" is a synonym for grasping the meaning. By this, he fully demonstrates that because this Dharma is of great significance, a Bodhisattva must inevitably abide with aspiration and prayer in such a great and significant teaching of the Dharma.

དེ་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་གསུངས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་གཏན་ཚིགས་སུ་གསུངས་སོ། །འདུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཕྱོགས་གཞན་དུ་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་བརྫུན་པའི་དོན་དུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་གནས་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞེས་དགོངས་པའོ། །གནས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པའི་ཐབས་ནི་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ།། །།ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མི་མངའ་བ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། འཆད་པ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མི་མངའ་བ་དང་། འཁོར་བའི་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མི་མངའ་བའོ། །
[3-253] translation already produced for this document:
The statement "the Tathāgata has spoken of that as being without perception" is presented here as a logical reason. Because that which is to be perceived is itself empty of the nature of being one or many, in the ultimate sense, it is without perception. The Tathāgata spoke of it in another way by relying upon the conventional. The intention is that if one knows it to be false and abides in that, how could one become conceptually attached? The method for entering into meditative equipoise in all situations has been explained. The absence of defilement is also of two types: the absence of defilement in teaching and the absence of defilement in cyclic existence.

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: In this regard, the assembly now lacks conviction, thinking, "In the future, when this profound Dharma is obscured by the thicket of wrong views, how could it possibly be fruitful?" In order to dispel the lack of conviction of those who think in this way, the noble Subhūti, taking as his basis the foundation of mindfulness from among the perfections of the mind, addressed the Blessed One, beginning with the words, "Blessed One..."

ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཐ་དད་པ་བདུན་ཏེ། དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་དང་། ཆོས་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། གདམས་ངག་དོན་ཆེན་པོར་གདགས་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ་དང་། བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའོ། །
[3-203] translation already produced for this document:
The perfection of the mind consists of seven distinct aspects: the foundations of mindfulness, the attainment of perfect awakening, the designation of the great meaning of the Dharma, the designation of the great meaning of the instructions, the complete apprehension of the dharmakāya, the non-abiding in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, and the complete purity of dwelling.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By stating "possessing a body and a great body," he merely expresses a sign, through which he causes the Bodhisattva to turn away from attachment to all phenomena. He also establishes them in the ultimate sense, and he leads them into meditative equipoise in that. He also expresses the profound. He also abandons the extreme of superimposition. By the former, he has blocked the extreme of denigration. If the Tathāgata were to teach that that very body does not exist, then, at that time, those Bodhisattvas who have attained realization might think, "Since I have attained the realization of a Bodhisattva, I shall now liberate sentient beings." Because they lack the pride of realization, having examined the noble conceptualization of others, he spoke the words "what is a Bodhisattva" in order to teach realization.

དགོངས་པ་ནི་འདི་ཡིན་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་འདི་ཡང་ཡང་དག་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་འབྱུང་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་ནི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པར་ བྱ་བ་གང་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མི་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསོལ་ཏོ། །འདིས་ནི་དོན་གྱིས་ན་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལུས་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་སྤང་པའི་ཕྱིར་འདུན་པ་དང་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟོན་ཏོ། །
[3-176] translation already produced for this document:
The intention is this: the realization of a Bodhisattva is distinguished merely by the arising of superior primordial wisdom that relies upon valid conventional reality; in the ultimate sense, however, there is neither a realizer nor anything to be realized. To teach this, the noble Subhūti addressed the Tathāgata, saying, "The Tathāgata possesses a human body," and so forth. By this, he indicates in essence the discordant factor of being attached to having a body and a great body. In order to abandon that, he teaches that one should abide through aspiration and prayer.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation:
If that is not the case, how could a non-acting entity become something that is destroyed? If one were to offer worship to the entirety of an object, then at that very moment, the worship would become simultaneous; there is no other way for two partless entities to be worshipped in their entirety except by becoming simultaneous. Therefore, just as if atoms were to be cut in their entirety, they would become mere atoms, so too it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that an eon also becomes a mere moment. If one worships with only one part, then it would possess limbs. Therefore, all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn; they merely appear as if they arise due to the falsity of unexamined delight, similar to the nature of what appears to a deluded consciousness. By what logic can one argue that conventional consensus is not a valid cognition, and that it is therefore unreasonable to deconstruct it because it is accepted by everyone from cowherds upwards as the cause and effect of phenomena? It is because conventional consensus regarding forms and the like is deconstructed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavan states in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
Having refuted valid cognitions such as the eye,
The eye, the ear, and the nose are not valid cognitions.
The tongue, the body, and the mind are not valid cognitions.
If these faculties were valid,
What would there be for the noble path to do?

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Although it has been explained, in order to show how it is explained that there is no thorough affliction, he says, "How does he correctly and thoroughly teach?" and so forth. The intention is this: although it is taught that all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn and inexpressible, those phenomena are not explained as having the nature of being inexpressible. This is taught in the following way: he teaches in such a way that the person being trained thinks, "All phenomena are unborn from the very beginning and are therefore inexpressible; hence, they are not things to be taught by anyone." In this way, he teaches without being afflicted, because it is for the sake of the non-erroneous meaning. If it were not so, he would be teaching erroneously and thus would be afflicted. Therefore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, although he enters into pure worldly wisdom and perceptions of phenomena as such arise, because he has no grasping at them as being truly real, he does not incur the fault of being afflicted. By this, he demonstrates meditative equipoise, the thorough holding of the mind, and profundity. By the former, he demonstrated vastness.

[3-254] translation already produced for this document:
In this regard, if there is no perception of phenomena, then when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings, if that perception arises, how could there be no thorough affliction? Thinking, "If one abides until the end of cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion, how could one not be thoroughly afflicted by the perception of phenomena?" and having examined this, the Tathāgata, through that very perfection of his mind, teaches that there is no thorough affliction in teaching, and through the verse, he shows that there is no thorough affliction in cyclic existence; for this reason, he says "Subhūti" and so forth. Previously, in other contexts, the praises of world-systems were taught to express merit, but now, in the context of there being no thorough affliction, he does not state the merit when teaching the infinite world-systems, so that the words do not become repetitive. Here too, the reasoning should be stated as before. "Having taken up" means having recited it by heart. "Grasping" refers to the words. "Reading" refers to reading from a book or the like. "Comprehending" is a synonym for grasping the meaning. By this, he fully demonstrates that because this Dharma is of great significance, a Bodhisattva must inevitably abide with aspiration and prayer in such a great and significant teaching of the Dharma.

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: Did the Blessed One not previously state, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth? Now, in order to show that one should not become attached to the notion that these exist as a unity, nor that they do not exist, he did not say "they exist," but in order to negate the two extremes, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those..." and so forth. Because in the ultimate sense, the essence of the aggregates, the person, and so on, is not observed, they are not sentient beings; by this, the extreme of reification is negated. Because they exist in a conventional sense as objects of pleasant experience, they are not non-existent; by this, the extreme of nihilism is negated. By teaching that "they will arise," he shows what the unerring foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One is like for sentient beings, and he teaches that a bodhisattva should dwell in that perfect foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One through aspiration and prayer. The phrase "they are not sentient beings" indicates the meditative absorption of yoga. If they were not sentient beings, then, having reflected on how the Blessed One could have said, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth, he asked, "For what reason?"

The perfection of the mind consists of seven distinct aspects: the foundations of mindfulness, the attainment of perfect awakening, the designation of the great meaning of the Dharma, the designation of the great meaning of the instructions, the complete apprehension of the dharmakāya, the non-abiding in either nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, and the complete purity of dwelling.

In this regard, the assembly now lacks conviction, thinking, "In the future, when this profound Dharma is obscured by the thicket of wrong views, how could it possibly be fruitful?" In order to dispel the lack of conviction of those who think in this way, the noble Subhūti, taking as his basis the foundation of mindfulness from among the perfections of the mind, addressed the Blessed One, beginning with the words, "Blessed One..."

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: This shows that one who thinks, "I shall liberate sentient beings," and who thinks, "I am a Bodhisattva," is, in the ultimate sense, not a Bodhisattva, because they possess the pride of realization. The phrase "For what reason?" is an inquiry into the logical grounds for understanding this here. The term "phenomena" refers to the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of the person and so forth. The noble Subhūti also replied, "They do not exist," because when those phenomena are examined through reasoning, they are not seen. Since that reasoning is common to both, the Blessed One spoke the words "Therefore" in order to establish the lack of self in both. The phrase "no sentient beings" and so forth is an indication; one should also view them as lacking intrinsic nature. By this, the subduing of mental wandering is taught. The realization has been explained.

[3-177] translation already produced for this document:
By stating "possessing a body and a great body," he merely expresses a sign, through which he causes the Bodhisattva to turn away from attachment to all phenomena. He also establishes them in the ultimate sense, and he leads them into meditative equipoise in that. He also expresses the profound. He also abandons the extreme of superimposition. By the former, he has blocked the extreme of denigration. If the Tathāgata were to teach that that very body does not exist, then, at that time, those Bodhisattvas who have attained realization might think, "Since I have attained the realization of a Bodhisattva, I shall now liberate sentient beings." Because they lack the pride of realization, having examined the noble conceptualization of others, he spoke the words "what is a Bodhisattva" in order to teach realization.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
source: འདི་ལྟར་དབང་པོ་འདི་དག་ཆད་མིན་ཏེ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བེམས་པོ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན། །དེ་ཕྱིར་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པའི་ལམ་འདོད་གང་། །དེས་ནི་འཕགས་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་བྱ་བ་བྱོས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །སློབ་དཔོན་དག་གིས་མངོན་སུམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་གསུངས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཡང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་མངོན་སུམ་སྟེ། དོན་དམ་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ནི་མཐུན་པར་བརྒལ་ཞིང་བརྟག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་བརྟག་མི་བཟོད་པའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་སཱ་ལུ་ལྗང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་བདག་དང་གཞན་ལས་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་བ་བཀག་གོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། འཕགས་པ་ལང་ཀར་གཤེགས་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བློ་གྲོས་ཆེན་པོ་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་ལས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་མ་སྐྱེས་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་གསུངས་པ།རབ་འབྱོར་ཆོས་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མ་སྐྱེས་པ་དེ་ནི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤེས་རབ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་སྐད་དུ། དཀོན་མཆོག་འབྱུང་གནས་ཀྱི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། གང་ལ་རང་བཞིན་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །རང་བཞིན་མེད་པས་གཞན་རྐྱེན་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར། །རང་བཞིན་མེད་པས་གཞན་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྐྱེད། །རྒྱུ་དེ་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པས་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡང་། དངོས་པོ་སྐྱེ་བ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ། །

It is stated:
"In this way, these faculties are not valid cognitions,
For by their very nature they are inert and indeterminate.
Therefore, whoever desires the path to nirvāṇa,
Let them perform the task of the noble path."
Whatever definition of direct perception the masters have provided is also direct perception only conventionally; it should be viewed as a means of entering into the ultimate. Conventionally, one does not dispute or examine; therefore, because it is taught conventionally, it cannot withstand analysis. For this reason, the Bhagavan has refuted the arising of phenomena from self or other in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* and similar texts. As it is said in the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra*: "Great Sage, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unborn." It is stated in the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā*: "Subhūti, that which is not even slightly born is called 'non-arising'." The wisdom that is present regarding that is called "forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena." As it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
"That which has no intrinsic nature,
How could it be conditioned by another?
Without intrinsic nature, how could it produce another?
This cause has been well taught by the Sugata."

If that is not the case, how could a non-acting entity become something that is destroyed? If one were to offer worship to the entirety of an object, then at that very moment, the worship would become simultaneous; there is no other way for two partless entities to be worshipped in their entirety except by becoming simultaneous. Therefore, just as if atoms were to be cut in their entirety, they would become mere atoms, so too it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that an eon also becomes a mere moment. If one worships with only one part, then it would possess limbs. Therefore, all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn; they merely appear as if they arise due to the falsity of unexamined delight, similar to the nature of what appears to a deluded consciousness. By what logic can one argue that conventional consensus is not a valid cognition, and that it is therefore unreasonable to deconstruct it because it is accepted by everyone from cowherds upwards as the cause and effect of phenomena? It is because conventional consensus regarding forms and the like is deconstructed by valid cognition. Therefore, the Bhagavan states in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
Having refuted valid cognitions such as the eye,
The eye, the ear, and the nose are not valid cognitions.
The tongue, the body, and the mind are not valid cognitions.
If these faculties were valid,
What would there be for the noble path to do?

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: Now, he sets forth the entire body of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and by means of a verse, he demonstrates that there is no thorough affliction of *saṃsāra*. This verse fully demonstrates four types of characteristics of the conditioned: the characteristic of nature, the characteristic of the object of experience, the characteristic of realizing the drawbacks, and the characteristic of realizing the definitive emergence. Regarding that, the nature of the five *skandha*s, which are entities as they appear, are dependent and interconnected; because they are produced by the gathering of causes and conditions, they are called "conditioned." The nature of all of these should be viewed like the stars. Just as stars appear at night but do not appear during the day, conditioned phenomena appear when there is the darkness of the fault of ignorance, but they do not appear when the light of the sun of wisdom arises; therefore, they should be viewed as having the nature of stars. Conditioned phenomena that have the nature of grasping at persons and phenomena should be viewed like a cataract, because they are the cause of the appearance of what is non-existent. The characteristic of consciousness should be viewed like a butter lamp, because it burns in dependence upon the wick of karma and the oil of craving. In this way, by means of these analogies, he fully demonstrates the characteristic of the nature of the conditioned.

Although it has been explained, in order to show how it is explained that there is no thorough affliction, he says, "How does he correctly and thoroughly teach?" and so forth. The intention is this: although it is taught that all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, unborn and inexpressible, those phenomena are not explained as having the nature of being inexpressible. This is taught in the following way: he teaches in such a way that the person being trained thinks, "All phenomena are unborn from the very beginning and are therefore inexpressible; hence, they are not things to be taught by anyone." In this way, he teaches without being afflicted, because it is for the sake of the non-erroneous meaning. If it were not so, he would be teaching erroneously and thus would be afflicted. Therefore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, although he enters into pure worldly wisdom and perceptions of phenomena as such arise, because he has no grasping at them as being truly real, he does not incur the fault of being afflicted. By this, he demonstrates meditative equipoise, the thorough holding of the mind, and profundity. By the former, he demonstrated vastness.

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: The statement "because they are taught to be without sentient beings" means that in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a sentient being.

[3-205] translation already produced for this document:
Did the Blessed One not previously state, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth? Now, in order to show that one should not become attached to the notion that these exist as a unity, nor that they do not exist, he did not say "they exist," but in order to negate the two extremes, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those..." and so forth. Because in the ultimate sense, the essence of the aggregates, the person, and so on, is not observed, they are not sentient beings; by this, the extreme of reification is negated. Because they exist in a conventional sense as objects of pleasant experience, they are not non-existent; by this, the extreme of nihilism is negated. By teaching that "they will arise," he shows what the unerring foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One is like for sentient beings, and he teaches that a bodhisattva should dwell in that perfect foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One through aspiration and prayer. The phrase "they are not sentient beings" indicates the meditative absorption of yoga. If they were not sentient beings, then, having reflected on how the Blessed One could have said, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth, he asked, "For what reason?"

heading: **དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ།**
translation: They are spoken of in reliance upon the existence of the essence of the aggregates that are established conventionally; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" because they exist conventionally. If it were not so, and they did not exist even conventionally, there would be no speech about them. By this, the mind being well-grasped is shown. By all of this, the profound is expressed. By the Blessed One showing that the foundation of mindfulness is unobstructed toward all sentient beings, the vast is shown.

[3-205] translation already produced for this document:
Did the Blessed One not previously state, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth? Now, in order to show that one should not become attached to the notion that these exist as a unity, nor that they do not exist, he did not say "they exist," but in order to negate the two extremes, he spoke the words, "Subhūti, those..." and so forth. Because in the ultimate sense, the essence of the aggregates, the person, and so on, is not observed, they are not sentient beings; by this, the extreme of reification is negated. Because they exist in a conventional sense as objects of pleasant experience, they are not non-existent; by this, the extreme of nihilism is negated. By teaching that "they will arise," he shows what the unerring foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One is like for sentient beings, and he teaches that a bodhisattva should dwell in that perfect foundation of mindfulness of the Blessed One through aspiration and prayer. The phrase "they are not sentient beings" indicates the meditative absorption of yoga. If they were not sentient beings, then, having reflected on how the Blessed One could have said, "In the future, there will be those who possess ethical conduct and possess qualities," and so forth, he asked, "For what reason?"

heading: སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱ་ས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: From this point onward is the investigation of the Buddha, and that Buddha is also comprised of seven perfections. The seven perfections are: the perfection of the completely pure field, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed vision, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed knowledge, the perfection of the mastery of the accumulation of merit, the perfection of the body, the perfection of speech, and the perfection of the mind.

འདིས་ནི་གང་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ། །བདག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་འོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དེ་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་དུ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མ་ཡིན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འདིར་ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲི་བའོ། །ཆོས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དམ་གང་ཟག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་དེ་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་མ་མཐོང་བས་དེ་ནི་མ་མཆིས་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསོལ་ཏེ། །རིགས་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐུན་མོང་པས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉི་ག་ལ་གཟུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསུངས་སོ། །སེམས་ཅན་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་མཚོན་པ་སྟེ། རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཡང་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །འདིས་ནི་རྣམ་པར་གཡིང་བ་ཚར་གཅད་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ།། །།
[3-178] translation already produced for this document:
This shows that one who thinks, "I shall liberate sentient beings," and who thinks, "I am a Bodhisattva," is, in the ultimate sense, not a Bodhisattva, because they possess the pride of realization. The phrase "For what reason?" is an inquiry into the logical grounds for understanding this here. The term "phenomena" refers to the nature of form and so forth, or the nature of the person and so forth. The noble Subhūti also replied, "They do not exist," because when those phenomena are examined through reasoning, they are not seen. Since that reasoning is common to both, the Blessed One spoke the words "Therefore" in order to establish the lack of self in both. The phrase "no sentient beings" and so forth is an indication; one should also view them as lacking intrinsic nature. By this, the subduing of mental wandering is taught. The realization has been explained.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation: The analogy of an illusion fully demonstrates the characteristic of the object of experience, because it appears in a deceptive manner. Regarding that, the two types of characteristics of realizing the drawbacks are the nature of the conditioned: realizing them as impermanent and realizing them as suffering. The analogy of dew demonstrates realizing them as impermanent, because they do not remain for a long time. The analogy of a bubble demonstrates realizing them as suffering, because feelings are like a bubble in water, and it is said that whatever feeling there may be, that is suffering here. By way of the three types of suffering, all feelings should be understood as suffering; therein, the feeling of pain is the suffering of suffering. Those conditioned factors that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. The feeling of pleasure is the suffering of change. Those phenomena that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. Feelings that are neither suffering nor pleasant, and those entities that are in accordance with them, are the suffering of conditioning by virtue of the characteristic of arising and ceasing. In this way, one should view all conditioned phenomena as being possessed of suffering.

Now, he sets forth the entire body of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and by means of a verse, he demonstrates that there is no thorough affliction of *saṃsāra*. This verse fully demonstrates four types of characteristics of the conditioned: the characteristic of nature, the characteristic of the object of experience, the characteristic of realizing the drawbacks, and the characteristic of realizing the definitive emergence. Regarding that, the nature of the five *skandha*s, which are entities as they appear, are dependent and interconnected; because they are produced by the gathering of causes and conditions, they are called "conditioned." The nature of all of these should be viewed like the stars. Just as stars appear at night but do not appear during the day, conditioned phenomena appear when there is the darkness of the fault of ignorance, but they do not appear when the light of the sun of wisdom arises; therefore, they should be viewed as having the nature of stars. Conditioned phenomena that have the nature of grasping at persons and phenomena should be viewed like a cataract, because they are the cause of the appearance of what is non-existent. The characteristic of consciousness should be viewed like a butter lamp, because it burns in dependence upon the wick of karma and the oil of craving. In this way, by means of these analogies, he fully demonstrates the characteristic of the nature of the conditioned.

heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: If the Blessed One had not taught any dharma whatsoever, then he would not have attained complete and perfect buddhahood; therefore, the efforts of the bodhisattvas to establish the Tathāgata’s complete and perfect enlightenment would be in vain.

They are spoken of in reliance upon the existence of the essence of the aggregates that are established conventionally; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" because they exist conventionally. If it were not so, and they did not exist even conventionally, there would be no speech about them. By this, the mind being well-grasped is shown. By all of this, the profound is expressed. By the Blessed One showing that the foundation of mindfulness is unobstructed toward all sentient beings, the vast is shown.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: "In the ultimate sense, there is no intrinsic nature," it is also said. If one were to ask, "Is this said with the intention that all these things are of the nature of the conceptually constructed?" the answer is no, because all intrinsic natures have already been refuted by valid cognition. By this, it is taught that if even others who possess only a small root of virtue do not experience the suffering of cyclic existence, then why would a Bodhisattva, who has attained forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena, who has given rise to a great accumulation of wisdom, and who has attained the generation of an unsurpassed accumulation of merit, experience the suffering of cyclic existence? In this way, suffering is experienced in cyclic existence in two forms, characterized by physical and mental distress. The former is the result of negative karma, and the latter arises from ignorance, that is, it arises from wrong views. For a Bodhisattva who has attained forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena, both causes of suffering—negative karma and ignorance—are absent. Without the causes, it is impossible to be touched by the latent tendencies of suffering. By this, it is taught how a Bodhisattva should practice. One might wonder: "Even if one has already generated an extremely vast accumulation of merit, will one not still be in cyclic existence like sentient beings who engage in form and so forth? How is it taught that merely by generating a vast accumulation of merit, one does not abide in cyclic existence?" To address this doubt, the words "Subhūti" and so forth were spoken.

It is stated:
"In this way, these faculties are not valid cognitions,
For by their very nature they are inert and indeterminate.
Therefore, whoever desires the path to nirvāṇa,
Let them perform the task of the noble path."
Whatever definition of direct perception the masters have provided is also direct perception only conventionally; it should be viewed as a means of entering into the ultimate. Conventionally, one does not dispute or examine; therefore, because it is taught conventionally, it cannot withstand analysis. For this reason, the Bhagavan has refuted the arising of phenomena from self or other in the *Śālistamba-sūtra* and similar texts. As it is said in the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra*: "Great Sage, because they do not arise from existence or non-existence, all phenomena are unborn." It is stated in the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā*: "Subhūti, that which is not even slightly born is called 'non-arising'." The wisdom that is present regarding that is called "forbearance for the unborn nature of phenomena." As it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
"That which has no intrinsic nature,
How could it be conditioned by another?
Without intrinsic nature, how could it produce another?
This cause has been well taught by the Sugata."
Furthermore: "The arising of phenomena is conventional;

heading: ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In this regard, if there were any such entity called a bodhisattva, then who would strive to accomplish the purification of a buddha-field? To dispel such doubts, and focusing on the perfection of the completely pure buddha-field, he spoke the words beginning with, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." The phrase "one should speak in that way" is intended to mean that one should not say, "This is a bodhisattva," because of the presence of conceit; it is because one engages in conceit, thinking that one has realized the non-self of persons and phenomena when one has not. In this way, by thinking "I am," one has not realized the non-self of persons. By engaging in conceit regarding the buddha-fields, thinking they exist when they do not, one has not realized the non-self of phenomena. This teaches how a bodhisattva should abide by having faith that the buddha-fields are like an illusion. If, in the ultimate sense, those buddha-fields did not exist, one might wonder how the Blessed One could have spoken of them; thus, the question "Why is that?" is asked, and the explanation for this is as before. This does not result in a repetition of words, for the former was to dispel the conceptualizations of a bodhisattva who is abiding on the stage of engaging through faith, at the time when he is aspiring for the purification of a bodhisattva-field. Now, it is taught in order to dispel the conceptualizations of those who, when entering upon the path to accomplish the purification of a buddha-field, think that they are entering with such attachment. At that time, because such conceptualizations do not arise in others, it does not result in an infinite regress. This teaches how a bodhisattva should accomplish this.

From this point onward is the investigation of the Buddha, and that Buddha is also comprised of seven perfections. The seven perfections are: the perfection of the completely pure field, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed vision, the perfection of the completely pure unsurpassed knowledge, the perfection of the mastery of the accumulation of merit, the perfection of the body, the perfection of speech, and the perfection of the mind.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: By this, even if one has generated a mass of merit, because one clings to it as a perversion, one possesses an grasping of the mass of merit; since the root of all defilement—the perversion—has not been abandoned, even if one attains a superior state of existence, it is classified as being within saṃsāra. A bodhisattva, having attained the patience for the unborn nature of phenomena, has no clinging to the mass of merit as being truly real; therefore, because the root of all defilement—profound ignorance—has been abandoned, it is taught that they do not abide in saṃsāra.

heading: **བཞུགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ།**
translation:
Regarding that, the characteristic of realizing definitive emergence is the realization that persons and phenomena are empty. Because of that object of focus, there is definitive emergence, and thus the Bhagavan taught two types of objects of focus for definitive emergence. As it is stated in the *Ārya-samādhirāja-sūtra*:
If one investigates the selflessness of phenomena individually,
And having investigated them, if one meditates upon them,
That is the cause for attaining the result of nirvāṇa;
Any other cause will not lead to peace.
All conditioned phenomena possess two types of selflessness. In this way, conditioned phenomena are of three types by the distinction of past, present, and future. Regarding that, those that are past exist only as memory; because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty of phenomena and persons, and they have not been blessed by a self. Therefore, the analogy of a dream demonstrates the realization of those two types of selflessness. The analogy of lightning demonstrates the realization of the present, because it does not possess the nature of being a single substance or multiple substances, and thus its nature cannot be grasped. The future is of the nature of not having arrived; the analogy of a cloud demonstrates the two types of selflessness because it generates their seeds in a mind that is like the sky through the power of latent tendencies.

སྒྱུ་མའི་དཔེས་ནི་རོ་མྱང་བའི་ཡུལ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ནོར་བའི་རྣམ་པར་སྣང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་ཉེས་དམིགས་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ནི་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཏེ། མི་རྟག་པར་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པ་དང་། སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པའོ། །ཟིལ་བའི་དཔེས་ནི་མི་རྟག་པར་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཡུན་རིང་དུ་མི་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཆུ་བུར་གྱི་དཔེས་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་རྗེས་སུ་རྟོགས་པ་བསྟན་ཏེ། ཚོར་བ་ནི་ཆུའི་ཆུ་བུར་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་གང་ཅི་ཡང་རུང་བ་དེ་ནི་འདིར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱིས་ཚོར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དུ་རིག་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་ཚོར་བ་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ། །གང་དག་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པའི་འདུ་བྱེད་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ། །བདེ་བའི་ཚོར་བ་ནི་འགྱུར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ། །གང་དག་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་མཐུན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་བདེ་བ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་། དེ་དང་མཐུན་པའི་དངོས་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་འཇིག་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་ལྡན་པར་བལྟའོ། །
[3-257] translation already produced for this document:
The analogy of an illusion fully demonstrates the characteristic of the object of experience, because it appears in a deceptive manner. Regarding that, the two types of characteristics of realizing the drawbacks are the nature of the conditioned: realizing them as impermanent and realizing them as suffering. The analogy of dew demonstrates realizing them as impermanent, because they do not remain for a long time. The analogy of a bubble demonstrates realizing them as suffering, because feelings are like a bubble in water, and it is said that whatever feeling there may be, that is suffering here. By way of the three types of suffering, all feelings should be understood as suffering; therein, the feeling of pain is the suffering of suffering. Those conditioned factors that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. The feeling of pleasure is the suffering of change. Those phenomena that are in accordance with that are also suffering by virtue of being in accordance with that. Feelings that are neither suffering nor pleasant, and those entities that are in accordance with them, are the suffering of conditioning by virtue of the characteristic of arising and ceasing. In this way, one should view all conditioned phenomena as being possessed of suffering.

heading: **མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ།**
translation: For the sake of those who think, "If one desires to attain complete and perfect buddhahood, then at that time there must also be a teaching," he spoke with the intention of complete and perfect enlightenment, saying, "Subhūti, what do you think?" and so forth. The noble Subhūti, grasping the previous intention, replied, "That is not so." He thinks this because he believes the Blessed One has negated the teaching by intending the ultimate sense. As was previously shown, because in the ultimate sense there is no dharma taught, there is also no complete and perfect buddhahood. Conventionally, however, the Blessed One’s teaching of dharma, the perfect enlightenment, and the path that is its cause do indeed exist. Therefore, a bodhisattva should strive to establish the essence of the unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment in its true conventional sense; by this, it is shown how a bodhisattva should abide. Previously, at the time of seeking the instructions, the conceptualization of the bodhisattva who thinks that complete and perfect enlightenment is in the ultimate sense was dispelled; now, at the time of seeking the buddha-ground, because such conceptualization of others is dispelled, there is no fault of repeating the words. Regarding the thought of what that unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment, which the Blessed One has established in the true conventional sense, is like, he spoke, "Even a little," and so forth.

དེ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་མེད་པར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །
[3-206] translation already produced for this document:
The statement "because they are taught to be without sentient beings" means that in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a sentient being.

[3-207] source:
ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་གནས་པའི་ཕུང་པོའི་ངོ་བོ་ཡོད་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེ་དག་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་པས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡང་མེད་ན་ནི་གསུང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་བཟུང་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །འདི་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཟབ་པ་བརྗོད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཐོགས་པ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པས་ནི་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[3-207] translation already produced for this document:
They are spoken of in reliance upon the existence of the essence of the aggregates that are established conventionally; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" because they exist conventionally. If it were not so, and they did not exist even conventionally, there would be no speech about them. By this, the mind being well-grasped is shown. By all of this, the profound is expressed. By the Blessed One showing that the foundation of mindfulness is unobstructed toward all sentient beings, the vast is shown.

[3-208] source:
གལ་ཏེ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་གང་ཡང་མེད་ན་དེའི་ཚེ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་འབད་པ་དོན་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-208] translation already produced for this document:
If the Blessed One had not taught any dharma whatsoever, then he would not have attained complete and perfect buddhahood; therefore, the efforts of the bodhisattvas to establish the Tathāgata’s complete and perfect enlightenment would be in vain.

heading: ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Thinking, "What kind of being is called a bodhisattva?" the text states, "Subhūti, whatever bodhisattva..." and so forth. The fact that "phenomena are selfless" is stated twice indicates that phenomena are shown to be selfless by way of the two types of selflessness. The fact that "bodhisattva, mahāsattva" is stated twice indicates that one realizes those very two types of selflessness. Alternatively, one instance of "bodhisattva" is a repetition. The subsequent phrase, "it is called a bodhisattva," is the method. Therefore, how is it explained? It will be shown that they are called bodhisattvas because they have understood both the absence of grasping at a person and the like, thinking "by whom will it be accomplished," and the absence of grasping at the "array of buddha-fields" as a phenomenon. By this, the firm grasping of the mind is shown. By all of this, profundity is shown. Because it is shown that bodhisattvas engage with faith in order to accomplish those buddha-fields which are like illusions, vastness is expressed.

heading: **མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་འཁོར་བ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: In order to dispel the conceptualizations of others, the noble Subhūti expresses a contradiction, asking, "Should one not embrace it just as the Bhagavan has not embraced the intention?" His thought is this: "The Bhagavan has stated in various sūtras that a bodhisattva should embrace the mass of merit, yet here he states that it should not be embraced; how can this not be a contradiction?" The Bhagavan, in order to show the intention by which both were stated, said, "One may indeed embrace it." The statement "embrace it" refers to the method of embracing characterized by accomplishment. Here, however, the characteristic of grasping wrongly is being dispelled, so there is no contradiction. Grasping wrongly is grasping the path wrongly. By this, the mind is shown to be well-embraced through the abandonment of that conceptualization. Furthermore, beginning with "Subhūti, whatever son or daughter of noble family," the vast aspect is taught. The remaining previous sections taught the profound aspect. By all these points, the extremes of permanence and annihilation are blocked, and the Middle Way is expressed. The non-abiding in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa has already been explained.

[3-236] translation already produced for this document:
By this, even if one has generated a mass of merit, because one clings to it as a perversion, one possesses an grasping of the mass of merit; since the root of all defilement—the perversion—has not been abandoned, even if one attains a superior state of existence, it is classified as being within saṃsāra. A bodhisattva, having attained the patience for the unborn nature of phenomena, has no clinging to the mass of merit as being truly real; therefore, because the root of all defilement—profound ignorance—has been abandoned, it is taught that they do not abide in saṃsāra.

heading: གཟིགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: If there were any phenomenon whatsoever called a "bodhisattva," then at that time, the Tathāgata would be devoid of perfectly pure vision and devoid of perfectly pure knowledge. For if that which is born from the bodhisattva does not exist, how could that [Tathāgata] be possible? To be without a cause would result in the meaning of being eternally existent and so forth.
